title: B16 Takedown 2026-03-25_ATM
section: B16 Tumor processing protocol obtained from Nicole. Thanks Nicole
text:
B16 Tumor processing protocol obtained from Nicole. Thanks Nicole

Tumor tissue dissociation
Use scissors and chop tumor into small pieces inside 50ml falcon turned on its side (should look like mush).
Add 10ml collagenase solution, washing scissors off and tissue down the side of the tube.
Incubate for 30 min @ 37°C in shaking incubator.
Pour through cell strainer into a new 50mL conical, mash through cell strainer, and add 10mL RP5 (RPMI +5% serum) to wash cells down.
Put tubes on ice while processing other tumors.
Before spinning, add 2mL 1x ACK to each tube, and vortex each tube for 30 seconds to further disassociate lymphocytes from tumor cells.
Spin down at 1600 rpm for 6 min.

title: B16 Takedown 2026-03-25_ATM
text:
Percoll

Make sure you see a pellet, then pour supernatant out.
Resuspend each sample in 5 mL 44% percoll solution, make sure pellet is well resuspended, and transfer to a 15ml round bottom tube (bacteria culturing tube).
Place glass pasteur pipette in conical and add 2 mL 67% percol solution to top of pipette to make a bottom layer. Don’t disturb after adding!
Spin at 21°C at 2000 rpm for 20 min, set acceleration to 3 and brake to 0
Check for an interphase between the two layers and transfer it to 15 mL conical (usually about 2 mL).
Fill to top with RP5 then spin at 1600 rpm for 4 min.

title: B16 Takedown 2026-03-25_ATM
text:
Ficoll

Make sure you see a pellet, then pour supernatant out.
Resuspend each sample in 5 mL RP5, place glass pasteur pipette in conical and add 2 mL Ficoll (Corning Lymphocyte Separation Media MT25072CV) to top of pipette to make a bottom layer. Don’t disturb after adding!
Spin at 10°C at 2000 rpm for 15 min, set acceleration to 9 and brake to 9
Check for an interphase between the two layers and transfer it to 15 mL conical (usually about 2 mL).
Fill to top with RP5 then spin at 1600 rpm for 4 min.
Resuspend pellet in 1mL RP5 - cells are now ready to transfer to plates for staining.

title: Bleeding Mice for transduction check_ATM
text: Procedure

title: Bleeding Mice for transduction check_ATM
text:
Preparing Blood

Get blood tubes - 1 for each mouse.
Label blood tubes so that you know which mouse is bled into each.
Bleed animal into blood tube with 1 ml of PBS + EDTA.
Store blood at 4 C for one dahy if you are not going to use it that day. PAUSE
Spin the blood at 6000 rpm for 4-5 min.
Aspirate and discard supernatant.
Add 1 ml Ack and resuspend the pellet.
Incubate at room temp for 5 - 10 min.
Spin at 6000 rpm for 4-5 min.
Aspirate and discard supernatant. Be careful not to aspirate the pellet.
Resuspend pellet in 200 ul FACS buffer.
Transfer to a labelled 96 well V-bottom plate.
Make antibody master mix by preparing a 1:200 dilution of each antibody in FACS buffer.
50 ul of FACS buffer per sample + 100 ul in addition (just in case)
Spin 96-well plate at 2000 rpm for 2 min.
Discard supernatant be flicking once over the sink.
Add 50 ul antibody master mix to the wells and resuspend. Keep on ice.
Incubate on ice or at 4 C in the dark for 15 min.
Add 150 ul FACS buffer.
Spin at 2000 rpm for 2 min and discard the supernatant by flicking once over the sink.
Add 200 ul FACS buffer and resuspend.
Spin at 2000 rpm for 2 min and discard supernatant by flicking once over the sink.
Add 200 ul of FACS buffer, resuspend cells, and transfer to FACS tubes on ice.

THURSDAY, 4/17/2025
Plating Plat-E Cells from Frozen
1. Check if we have D10 media. 2. Get a 50 ml conical, put 30 ml D10 and put in water bath. 3. Use a 15 mL conical tube and add 10 mL D10. 4. Put the conical tube in a 37°C water bath. 5. Move liquid nitrogen container from the southwest rack – 4th box from top. 6. Grab Plat-E cells. 7. Place the frozen Plat-E vial in the water bath until thawed (1–2 min max). 8. Add 1 mL warmed media dropwise. 9. Transfer back into 15 mL tube. 10. Spin – can count right here. 11. Plate in 2 Plat-E plates,
○ 2.5 × 105 cells per 10 cm plate.
● Don’t change the culture medium during the first three days. It is normal to see some cells floating after the first 24 hours. • Don’t culture cells to complete confluency. Split cells 4X to 6X every two to three days when the culture reaches 70-90% confluency.

title: Human PBMC Ex vivo Dynabead multiday stim_PMArestim
text:
Ex vivo anti-CD3/28 Dynabead multiday stim and PMA restimulation of human PBMC to measure cytokine production
Donor Vial info:
PBMC cell count:
If using fresh PBMC:
PBMC isolation from whole blood in CPT tube

Invert CPT tube 2-4 times
Centrifuge CPTs at 1800 G for 30 minutes at room temperature, 9-1 acceleration/deceleration (handle with care and keep tubes upright after centrifuging). 
Remove plasma layer being careful not to disrupt cell layer (cloudy layer between CPT gel and plasma).   
Pour remaining plasma and cells from CPT tubes into a 50 mL Falcon tube 


NOTE:  No more than 6 CPTs per 50mL Falcon tube, if you have more than 6 divide them evenly into 2 or more Falcon tubes (they can be combined at the lyse step). 


Rinse CPTs 2-3x using ≈ 7mL of RPMI by pipetting up and down.
Dispense each wash from the CPTs into the 50 mL Falcon tube along with the cells in step 4
Bring Falcon tube volume up to 50 mL using RPMI 
Centrifuge at 1500RPM for 5 minutes at RT, aspirate the supernatant, mechanically disrupt pellet by raking
Resuspend cells in 10 ml High Yield Lyse (Thermofisher) and incubate at RT for 10 mins.
Bring volume up to 50 mL using RPMI, mixing gently. 



Centrifuge at 1500RPM for 5 minutes at RT, aspirate the supernatant, mechanically disrupt pellet by raking, resuspend in 2 mL to count cells. Cell count: average dilution 1:5 in 4% trypan blue (80ul trypan plus 20uL cells)

If using frozen PBMC:
Thawing cryopreserved PBMC for immunophenotyping
Protocol modified from here: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6060642/

Place a cryopreserved PBMC vial in a 37°C water bath. Submerge the cryovial halfway and thaw for 60 seconds.
PBMCs were frozen at 6-7 million cells in 1ml of freezing medium for 1 min.
Add 1 mL of warmed (37°C) complete RPMI slowly dropwise to the thawed PBMCs against the side of the cryovial using a transfer pipette.
Pipette the thawed PBMCs into 5 mL (per vial so 10 ml if thawing two vials) of complete RPMI in a 15ml conical tube that has been warmed to 37°C (no pipetting). Make sure to wipe down the tube
Rinse the cryovials once with 1 mL of warm complete RPMI, pipette the PBMCs into the conical tube with the cell mixture.
Incubate the PBMCs for 5 minutes in the 37°C water bath.
Take aliquot to count cells.

Cell Count Pre-Rest: 1.76e6/ml. 98% viability. 2.5 mls. 4.4e6 cells total.

Centrifuge the PBMCs for 10 minutes at 300xg at room temperature.
Pour off the supernatant. This will leave a small amount of complete RPMI behind that aids in pellet resuspension.
Add 1 mL of pre-warmed complete RPMI. Mix by flicking or racking the tube (avoid pipetting up and down).
Incubate the PBMCs for one hour at 37°C in a CO2 water jacketed incubator (37°C, 5% CO2, 95% humidity). Leave the cap of the conical tube slightly loose so that gas transfer can occur.
Centrifuge the PBMCs for 10 minutes at 300xg at room temperature.
Resuspend in complete RPMI to 10e6/ml.
Take aliquot to count cells

Cell Count Post-Rest:
Multi-day anti-CD3/28 Dynabead stimulation


Prepare CD3/CD28 beads (Invitrogen Dynabeads Human T-Activator CD3/CD28) 


Vortex 30 seconds 


Add beads to 1.5 mL conical (15 ul per 1 ml sample in manufacturer protocol)


Add 1 mL FACS 


Vortex 30 seconds 


Place on magnet 1-2 minute 


Remove supernatant


Add equal parts R10 to the bead volume used in step 4 (resulting concentration beads to R10 ratio is 1:1)


Add media to well of 48 well plate, correct up to 1 ml (1 ml – 100 ul cells – 15 ul beads = 885 ul of media


Plate 1-1.2 million cells in 100 ul into R10 in 48 well plate *Easier on cells to add media first then cells then beads*


Add washed beads to cells in media in 48 well plate. 15ul of anti-CD3/28 beads per well of 1 ml media.


Add protein, antibody of interest or PBS as a control to respective wells.


Incubate 1-3 days


4 hour PMA restimulation

Pipette up and down thoroughly to resuspend cells and transfer to flow tubes and place on magnet 1-2 min to remove Dynabeads 
Aspirate supernatant (including cells; leaving beads behind) and transfer to clean flow tubes 
Wash flow tubes still containing beads by washing well in 48 well plate with 500 ul of FACS, then transfer FACS used to wash well into the respective tube on the magnet
Take tube off magnet, vortex, and put the tube back on the magnet and let sit on magnet for 1-2 min 
Repeat steps 3-4 once more
Aspirate the supernatant while tube is still on the magnet as in step 2 and add supernatant to appropriate flow tubes already containing cells debeaded in step 2.
Discard tubes containing CD3/CD28 beads 
Spin flow tubes with cells at 1500 RPM for 5 min 
Dump supernatant, wash in 1 ml of FACS, and dump supernatant 
Resuspend samples in 500 ul of R10 media only (for unstim controls), or 500 ul of R10 with 1 mg/ml of PMA, 0.7 mg/ml of ionomycin, and 1 ul/ml of GolgiStop into each tube besides unstim.

Surface stain

After 4 hrs, spin and dump supernatant.
Add surface stain master mix to samples. Ab at 1:100
Stain all samples in surface antibody cocktail at room temp for 20 minutes, covered in foil. Make comps and FMOs during this time.
Add 1 ml of FACS, spin, dump supernatant. Repeat.

Live/Dead staining

Stain each sample with 1 ml live dead (1 ul L/D Aqua per 1 ml PBS)

LIVE/DEAD™ Fixable Aqua Dead Cell Stain Kit, for 405 nm excitation Thermofisher, L34965 *Live/dead stain is on same channel as CD14, CD19 to serve as a dump channel on BV510*

Incubate at room temp for 10 mins, covered in foil.
Wash 1x with FACS

Cytokine and transcription factor staining

Make fixation buffer (1:3 fix to diluent)
Add 250uL/sample. Fix perm= 5mL fix, 15mL diluent
Incubate for 20min at 4C in dark.
At end of fixation incubation, wash 1x with 1X perm buffer (1:10 dilution with diH20)
Stain with fluorochromes for 25-30 min at 4C in dark in perm buffer.
Wash 1X with perm buffer. Wash 1X with FACS.
Resuspend samples in 100uL FACS, transfer to microtubes, and flow.

Centrifuge at 1500RPM for 5 minutes at RT, aspirate the supernatant, mechanically disrupt pellet by raking, resuspend in 2 mL to count cells. Cell count: average dilution 1:5 in 4% trypan blue (80ul trypan plus 20uL cells)

If using frozen PBMC:
Thawing cryopreserved PBMC for immunophenotyping
Protocol modified from here: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6060642/

Place a cryopreserved PBMC vial in a 37°C water bath. Submerge the cryovial halfway and thaw for 60 seconds.
PBMCs were frozen at 6-7 million cells in 1ml of freezing medium for 1 min.
Add 1 mL of warmed (37°C) complete RPMI slowly dropwise to the thawed PBMCs against the side of the cryovial using a transfer pipette.
Pipette the thawed PBMCs into 5 mL (per vial so 10 ml if thawing two vials) of complete RPMI in a 15ml conical tube that has been warmed to 37°C (no pipetting). Make sure to wipe down the tube
Rinse the cryovials once with 1 mL of warm complete RPMI, pipette the PBMCs into the conical tube with the cell mixture.
Incubate the PBMCs for 5 minutes in the 37°C water bath.
Take aliquot to count cells.

Cell Count Pre-Rest: 1.76e6/ml. 98% viability. 2.5 mls. 4.4e6 cells total.

Centrifuge the PBMCs for 10 minutes at 300xg at room temperature.
Pour off the supernatant. This will leave a small amount of complete RPMI behind that aids in pellet resuspension.
Add 1 mL of pre-warmed complete RPMI. Mix by flicking or racking the tube (avoid pipetting up and down).
Incubate the PBMCs for one hour at 37°C in a CO2 water jacketed incubator (37°C, 5% CO2, 95% humidity). Leave the cap of the conical tube slightly loose so that gas transfer can occur.
Centrifuge the PBMCs for 10 minutes at 300xg at room temperature.
Resuspend in complete RPMI to 10e6/ml.
Take aliquot to count cells

Cell Count Post-Rest:
Multi-day anti-CD3/28 Dynabead stimulation


Prepare CD3/CD28 beads (Invitrogen Dynabeads Human T-Activator CD3/CD28) 


Vortex 30 seconds 


Add beads to 1.5 mL conical (15 ul per 1 ml sample in manufacturer protocol)


Add 1 mL FACS 


Vortex 30 seconds 


Place on magnet 1-2 minute 


Remove supernatant


Add equal parts R10 to the bead volume used in step 4 (resulting concentration beads to R10 ratio is 1:1)


Add media to well of 48 well plate, correct up to 1 ml (1 ml – 100 ul cells – 15 ul beads = 885 ul of media


Plate 1-1.2 million cells in 100 ul into R10 in 48 well plate *Easier on cells to add media first then cells then beads*


Add washed beads to cells in media in 48 well plate. 15ul of anti-CD3/28 beads per well of 1 ml media.


Add protein, antibody of interest or PBS as a control to respective wells.


Incubate 1-3 days


Four hours prior to harvest, add GolgiStop at 1 ug/ml


Surface stain

After 4 hrs, spin and dump supernatant.
Add surface stain master mix to samples. Ab at 1:100
Stain all samples in surface antibody cocktail at room temp for 20 minutes, covered in foil. Make comps during this time. Make FMOs!
Add 1 ml of FACS, spin, dump supernatant. Repeat.

Live/Dead staining

Stain each sample with 1 ml live dead (1 ul L/D Aqua per 1 ml PBS)

LIVE/DEAD™ Fixable Aqua Dead Cell Stain Kit, for 405 nm excitation Thermofisher, L34965 *Live/dead stain is on same channel as CD14, CD19 to serve as a dump channel on BV510*

Incubate at room temp for 10 mins, covered in foil.
Wash 1x with FACS

Cytokine and transcription factor staining

Make fixation buffer (1:3 fix to diluent)
Add 250uL/sample. Fix perm= 5mL fix, 15mL diluent
Incubate for 20min at 4C in dark.
At end of fixation incubation, wash 1x with 1X perm buffer (1:10 dilution with diH20)
Stain with fluorochromes for 25-30 min at 4C in dark in perm buffer.
Wash 1X with perm buffer. Wash 1X with FACS.
Resuspend samples in 100uL FACS, transfer to microtubes, and flow.

Notes

title: Human TIL Ex vivo Dynabead multiday stim
text:
Human TIL stimulation
Cell preparation

If using fresh TIL, see tumor digestion protocol
If using frozen TIL, see frozen PBMC protocol
After these steps, continue to protocol here

 
Anti-CD3/28 Stimulation

Prepare CD3/CD28 beads (Invitrogen Dynabeads Human T-Activator CD3/CD28) 

Vortex 30 seconds 
200 μL beads into 1.5 mL conical 
Add 1 mL FACS to wash
Vortex 30 seconds 
Place on magnet 1-2 minute 
Remove supernatant 
Add 200 μL of R10 to 200 μL beads (this can be done at varying amounts; resulting concentration beads:FACS is 1:1) 

Plate 1e6 cells per well in a 24 well plate
Supplement to 1 ml of R10 in each well
Add 25 ul of equilibrated CD3/CD28 beads to each well per 1 ml of R10. Mix thoroughly. *Make sure to include an unstimulated (no CD3/28 beads) control*
Incubate in 37°C incubator
At desired harvest time (48 hours later in this expt) remove cells from incubator 
Add Golgi Plug to each well of sample at 1 ul per ml of media. Add 5 ul of CD107a-APC antibody here as well because CD107a is internalized and needs to be added during stim for optimal staining. Pipette well up and down a few times and place back into the incubator
Incubate again at 37C for 4 hours
At end of 4 hours, collect cells from well by gently pipetting. Wash well 2x with 1 ml of R10 and add to cells.
Place cells + R10 on magnet 1-2 min to remove beads 
Aspirate supernatant (including cells; leaving beads behind) and transfer to clean flow tubes 
Wash flow tubes still containing beads 2x with 500 μL R10 each time, letting sit for 1-2 min 
Transfer R10 used to wash beads to new flow tubes containing cells
Discard tubes containing CD3/CD28 beads
Spin flow tubes with cells at 1500 RPM for 5 min 
Wash 1x with FACS
Transfer cells from flow tubes to 96 well plate

Surface Stain

Make surface antibody master mix in FACS. Make FMOs at this time.
Resuspend cells in 100 ul of surface stain master mix
Mix cells + master mix by light vortex.
Incubate cells for 20 min at room temp in the dark.
Wash 1x with FACS

L/D Stain

Wash 1x with PBS
Resuspend samples in 1 ml of PBS + L/D stain (made from -20 stock at a 1:1000 dilution)
Incubate cells for 10 min at room temp in the dark
Wash 2x with FACS

Cell Fixation and Intracellular TF and cytokine staining

Fix cells using 100 ul fixation buffer diluted 1:4 (i.e. 5 mls concentrate, 15 mls diluent) from eBioscience Foxp3 Transcription Factor Staining kit and resuspend thoroughly.
Incubate in dark at 4C for 20 minutes.
Wash with 100 ul 1x perm wash (from 10x stock).
Make intracellular antibody master mix in perm wash, using 1:100 for all antibodies, except Ki67, use 10 ul per sample of 1e6 cells (i.e. add 60 ul if doing three samples). Make FMOs at this time for: Granzyme B, IL2, TNF, IFNg, and Ki67.


*Hopefully unstimulated control can be used for these markers in the future, but unstimulated TILs may have residual staining for these markers, making the gate hard to make. If we see no differences between FMOs and unstim controls in these markers, we can definitely just use unstim control going forward!*


Resuspend cells in 50 μl intracellular stain and stain at RT or 30 minutes covered in foil.
Wash with 100 ul 1x P/W buffer, spin.
Rewash with 100 ul FACS, resuspend and run flow

title: ICS_GP33 peptide restim
text:
Intracellular cytokine stain/peptide restim
Reconstitute peptide

Dissolve gp33-41 in DMSO. If 1 mg of peptide, reconstitute peptide in 250 ul media to get 4 mg/ml

Lymph node and spleen collection

Take all lymph nodes and spleen
Process through 70 and 40 um filters
Flow stain or start peptide stim
Count cells
To start peptide stim, plate 5% of spleen (250 ul from 5 ml of spleen resuspended in media) into well in 96 well u-bottom plate
If some samples are a little lower or higher, this is okay. Use a standard volume across samples (use cell count to relate back to spleen)
Spin plate at 1500 RPM for 3 min

Make stim media (gp33 + Golgi Plug)

Calculate the amount of media you will need by multiplying your number of samples by 200 ul. Account for unstim here. You can make an unstim sample for each mouse (just golgi plug in media no gp33) or a pooled unstim sample per tissue.
Add Golgi Plug to media at 1:500 (500x cocktail)
Partion off the amount you will need for stim vs unstim into two separate tubes
To the stim tube, add peptide. To the unstim tube, add nothing.

Prepare peptide for stim

When time to use the peptide, make an intermediate dilution of 1:10 with media to get to 0.4 mg/ml (0.4 ug/ul
Then, add 1 ul (at 0.4 mg/ml) for every 1 ml of media to bring final concentration to 0.4 ug/ml
Flick plate and resuspend in media supplemented with gp33 + golgi plug (stim samples) or golgi plug (unstim samples)
Incubate at 37C for 4-6 hours

title: ICS_OVA peptide restim
text:
Ex vivo peptide restim: OVA/OT-I
Plate cells from dLN, tumor, spleen

Plate cells. 2 million cells per sample is a good starting point. Add spleen (~5% which is 250 of 5 ml), lymph nodes (all), tumors (all). Plate however many plates you need according to map. Remember to include unstim wells as these will be the best control for cytokines.
Spin plate at 1500 RPM for 3 min and flick. Resuspend in R10 +/- peptide detailed below.
Proceed with ICCS plate first and setting up ex vivo stim and then while ICCS plate is incubating, proceed with surface staining

Ex vivo stimulation 
Reagents needed:

Golgi plug (Golgi plug has BFA and Golgi stop has monensin)
OVA 257-264 peptide
R10 media




Make up dilution of R10 +stim condition (no stim, OVA257-264 peptide)


Make enough for 200 ul per well (R10 + golgi plug for unstim controls, R10 + golgi plug + peptide for experimental wells, or R10 + golgi plug + PMA for positive control).


Add in a 1:1000 dilution of Golgi Plug into media before distributing to three groups. I have 10 mls for each condition, so 30 mls total (e.g. add 30 ul of GP into media and then divide into each condition)




Unstim: do not add peptide but should have golgi plug
For OVA 257-264: From -80 stock make an intermediate 1:1000 dilution in R10 to go from 3 mM to 3 uM (e.g. 3 ul into 3 mls). Then add into media as a 1:300 solution (e.g. add 33.3 ul of 1:1000 solution into 10 mls of R10) 




Add 200uL of each master mix to appropriate wells. Mix well. 


Incubate cells at 37 for 4 hours. 


During 4-hour incubation, continue protocol with other panels. After 4-hour incubation, proceed with protocol with surface staining + ICCS plate.

title: Jurkat electroporation
text:
Jurkat Electroporation with Lonza Electroporator

Place 1.5 mls of antibiotic free R10 in each well of a 12 well plate (one for each cuvette sample) and equilibrate at 37C for 15-30 min.
Collect Jurkats from 6 T75 flasks and place into 2 50 ml conicals. Take aliquots to count cells.

Cell count: 1.3e6, 80 mls. 104 million cells (2 tubes total), 97% viability

Aliquot number of cells needed (10 million cells per sample (n=7)) 70 million.
Spin at 100xg for 10 min.
During Jurkat centrifugation, take out plasmids from -20C. *IMPORTANT NOTE: plasmid solution added should not exceed 10% of reaction volume, 100 ul in this case so can only add 10 ul of plasmid max.

Pmaxgfp = positive control, use 2 ug per solution (4 ul)
MF12 (plasmid + BirA + GFP) = 2.05 ug/ul
5 ug = 2.44 ul of MF12
10 ug = 4.88 ul of MF12
20 ug = 9.75 ul of MF12
MF15 (plasmid + BirA + GFP + Fcgr2b) = 2.48 ug/ul
5 ug = 2.01 ul of MF15
10 ug = 4.02 ul of MF15
20 ug = 8.04 ul of MF15

During centrifugation, make nucleofector solution. Add 82 ul of nucleofector solution V and 18 ul of supplement 1 for each sample. _7_ samples = (82 * 7) = 574 ul of nucleofector solution V. _7_ samples = (18 * 7) = 126 ul of supplement 1.
Aspirate all of supernatant (very important to get all of supernat)
Resuspend in # of samples * 100 ul (700 ul) room temp nucleofector solution (nucleofector solution V + supplement 1 at a 4.5 to 1 ratio)
Aliquot 100 ul into different tubes and add respective plasmid
Add solution to cuvette slowly, making sure there are no air bubbles in cuvette and that the media gets to the bottom of the cuvette. Tap lightly if necessary.
Clean off metal panels on cuvette with a chemwipe.
Run Jurkat high viability protocol on the electroporator. It is fast, but I swear it does electroporate!
Return to hood and slowly add 500 ul of prewarmed antibiotic free media from 37C
Use supplied Pasteur pipette to take all the solution out. Be careful not to pipette up and down. Just slowly draw the solution out of the cuvette and into the 12 well plate.
Repeat for each sample *IMPORTANT NOTE: nucleofector solution is toxic to cells so cells will die as time progresses (no more than 15 min) so batch samples accordingly.
Swirl plate gently and incubate at 37C overnight.

Transfection validation

Take plate and transfer media to tubes
Spin cells down, dump supernatant.
Add pool left in tube to wells in a 96 well plates
Wash 1x with FACS.
Resuspend cells in 50uL of master mix in FACS wash.
Incubate at 4C for 20 minutes.
Wash cells 1x with FACS wash.
Repeat but wash with PBS instead of FACS.
Make up L/D Blue solution by diluting 1:1000 of the stock to stain with 100uL per sample in PBS
10 samples= 1mL PBS, add 1uL L/D stock.
For the comp, use 1 drop Arcs+ beads, 100uL PBS, and 1uL L/D stock. Let stain for 20-30min.
Resuspend in 100uL L/D solution.
Incubate in dark at 4C for 25min.
Add 100uL FACS buffer to cells and spin down and flick plate.
Wash 1X with FACS.

title: TCR signaling phospho-flow
text:
Phospho-flow of TCR signaling
Day -1
Coat Plate

Make a 5 ug/ml anti-CD3 solution and 2 ug/ml anti-CD28
Add 50 ul of PBS to 96 well flat bottom plate and incubate overnight at 4C

Day 0
Cell Stimulation

Transfer cells after isolation or culture from well to 50 ml conical vials and wash well 2x with media by spinning cells 1500 RPM for 5 min
Dump media and resuspend wells in serum-starved media.
Make conditions of interest such as protein that induces cell death, promotes proliferation, etc. Use PBS or buffer as a control.
Plate 2e6 cells to uncoated wells for unstim controls and then to anti-CD3/28 coated wells (+/- protein of interest) for 5, 10, 15, 30 min stim. Ideal to have different plates if you can to not disrupt the other time frames.
Incubate at 37C for 5, 10, 15, 30 minutes
With each timepoint, aspirate cells, wash well 1x with 100 ul FACS and put into 96 U bottom wells

Samples

Starved media unstim controls
5 ug/ml CD3, 2 ug/ml anti-CD28 in starved media



Phospho-protein controls: pERK isotype, pSLP76 isotype, pZap70 isotype, pS6 isotype
Whole protein controls: ERK, SLP76, S6, ZAP70

MeOH Fix/perm for phospho-flow (Byron Au-Yeung lab)

Wash 1x with FACS
Aspirate all FACS and resuspend in 4% paraformaldehyde
Fix cells for 10 min with 4% paraformaldehyde (150 ul) in the dark at 4C or on ice.
Spin down and wash cells 1x with FACS and aspirate sup
Perform surface staining
Wash 1x with FACS
Add 40 ul of ice cold 90% MeOH (kept in freezer, diluted with water) dropwise, vortex (repeat 3x)
Incubate on ice for 30 min
Wash with FACS, spin, aspirate.
Rehydrate with 50 ul of FACS for 15-20 min
Wash with FACS, spin, and aspirate.
Stain with intracellular master mix for 30 min at 4C.
Wash 2x with FACS
Flow

Altered peptide ligand in vitro stim of OT-I
Day 0
Harvest and baseline flow

Harvest splenocytes from OT-I mice
Stain and flow the cells for baseline, zero time.
Stain the cells with Live/Dead dye at 1:1000 dilution, for 15 min at RT. Wash 2x. Prepare a tube for compensation: overheating the cells (~0.5 million) at 95°C for 3 min, then stain with Live/Dead dye.
Stain all cells with surface antibodies mixture for 30 min at 4C. Wash 2x

text:
Genotyping OT-I mice by flow cytometry

Bleed mice to type animals and coordinate with ear punch so we know which mice is what genotype in the cage
Put blood into FACS tubes with 2 mls of RBC lysis buffer
Wash 2x with lysis buffer
Stain with master mix diluted in RBC lysis buffer for 20 minutes at 4C.

title: LCMV-Cl13 blood phenotyping
text:
Phenotyping time course of P14 from blood of LCMV-Cl13 infected mice
Day 4, 8, 12, 15, 30 post infection
Blood draws


Bleed mice with 5mm lances and collect about 50 ul of blood in green microvette blood collection tubes


Transfer blood immediately into 3mL lysis buffer in FACS tube


NOTE: if this is not how you typically bleed, that’s fine. Just make sure that all the days are the same and that the same amount of blood is collected from each animal.

title: CD8 isolation and activation
text:
CD8 Isolation and Activation
Coat Plates for activation
For goat anti-hamster coated plates

Prepare Antibody-Coated Plate (Start 2+ hrs before plating)
Preparing a 1:30 dilution of Goat Anti-Hamster IgG antibody in sterile PBS.
Coat wells by adding 550 µL of the diluted GAH-IgG solution to each required well of a 6-well round-bottom plate.
Gently tap the plate to ensure the bottom of each well is fully coated.
Place the plate in a 37°C incubator for at least 2 hours (or overnight at 4°C).

Spleen/lymph node harvest and homogenization

Grab spleen and lymph nodes (inguinal, brachial, and axilliary, avoid mLN if you can) and put in a tube with R10
Prepare Single-Cell Suspension by washing spleen/lymph nodes over a 70 uM filter in a petri dish
When spleen in homogenized, place 70 um filter over 50 ml conical
Wash filter by washing the petri dish 2x with 1 ml of RP5
Wash cells 1x at 1600 RPM for 4 min
Dump and add 1 ml ACK lysis and incubate for 4 min
Add 40 ml MACS buffer and spin at 1600 RPM for 4 min
Prepare Biotinylated Antibody Cocktail. The volumes below are per sample (adjust as needed based on cell number, typically for up to  total cells).







Antibody Target






Cell Type Marked for Depletion






Example Volume










NK1.1






NK cells






3 µL








MHC Class II






APCs (B cells, Monos, DCs)






3 µL








CD4






Helper T cells






3 µL








B220 (CD45R)






B cells






3 µL








Ter119






Erythroid lineage cells






3 µL








Ly-6G/Ly-6C (Gr-1)






Granulocytes (Neutrophils)






3 µL








MACS buffer








600 µL







Note: This cocktail targets major non-CD8+ T cell populations. Adjust cocktail based on specific experimental needs or available antibodies.

Negative Selection Staining & Bead Incubation

Resuspend the cell pellet in 500 µL of the freshly prepared Biotinylated Antibody Cocktail (adjust volume based on cell number if necessary, typically ~100 µL per 10^7 cells).
Incubate for 15 minutes at 4°C (in the fridge), protected from light.
Fill the tube with MACS buffer (~10-14 mL). Centrifuge at ~400 x g for 4 minutes. Discard the supernatant.
Resuspend the pellet in 500 µL MACS Buffer. Add 50 µL of streptavidin magnetic beads.
Incubate for 15 minutes at 4°C, protected from light.
Fill the tube with MACS buffer. Centrifuge at ~400 x g for 4 minutes. Discard the supernatant. During centrifuge step, wash MACS column (e.g. LS column) in the magnet by rinsing with 3 ml of MACS buffer. Discard flow through. Don’t let filter dry so add more if needed during centrifuge step.
Resuspend the pellet in 500 µL MACS buffer.





Magnetic Column Separation

Apply the cell suspension onto the column.
Collect the unlabeled cells that pass through the column. This fraction contains the enriched, untouched CD8+ T cells.
Wash the column three times (3x) with 3 mL of MACS buffer each time. Collect these washes and combine them with the initial flow-through.
Centrifuge the collected flow-through at 1600 RPM for 4 minutes. Discard the supernatant.
Resuspend the purified CD8+ T cell pellet in a small volume (e.g., 500 µL) of R10. Count the cells using a hemocytometer or automated counter. Determine cell viability (e.g., using Trypan Blue).
Stop here and check CD8 T cell purity by flow (pre and post isolation)

We had 89% purity post isolation of CD8 T cells and 44e6 cells total. Resuspend to 2e6 cells/ml. Plate 1 ml.

Run flow to check purity (can assume 90-95% if in a hurry but always better to flow check)
Stain aliquot of cells with FITC-CD8b (1:100)
Wash 1x with FACS and run on flow.






Cell Plating and Activation

Retrieve the GAH-IgG or anti-CD3 coated plate from the incubator. Carefully aspirate the coating solution from the wells.
Wash each well twice with 1 mL of R10 to remove any residual unbound antibody. Aspirate thoroughly after the final wash.
Dilute anti-CD3 and anti-CD28 antibodies each 1:500 in R10 for GAH-IgG coated wells. Dilute anti-CD28 for the anti-CD3 plate coated wells at 1:250 so there will be 1 ug/ml anti-CD28 in final well.
Add 1 ml of the CD8 T cell suspension (containing cells) to each prepared well.
Add 1 ml of the anti-CD3/CD28 antibody (or just anti-CD28) mixture to each well containing cells (total volume per well = 2 mL). Gently pipette up and down or swirl the plate to mix.

Final concentration: 1 x 106 cells/mL
Final antibody dilution: 1:1000 (effective concentration depends on stock)

Place the plate in a 37°C, 5% CO2 incubator for 18-24 hours.

title: Propagate LCMV Clone 13
text:
Propagate LCMV Clone 13 virus
BHK media (500 mL):


500 mL DMEM (high glucose, liquid)


50 mL FBS (10%)


5 mL L-glutamine (100x)


5 mL Pen-strep (100x)


25 mL Tryptose phosphate broth (Gibco)


Day -1:


Plate BHK to be ~40-50% confluent the following day. Seed about 5x10 6 BHK cells in a T175 flask the day before infection. The cells will grow to a confluency of 40-50%, corresponding to ~1x107.


Note
BHK cells grow at different rates in different labs and seem to be pretty sensitive. Consider setting up flasks at target multiple confluencies to try to hit the right one on the infection day.
Day 0:


Take photos of the T175 flasks on the light microscope if possible - try to record what a good confluency looks like.


Pipet off media and infect with virus in a limited volume (6 mL for a T175, 3 mL for a T75). The MOI used in the field seems to vary; many people use 0.001-0.01, but Teijaro lab uses an MOI of 0.1.



The lore is that it is important to use a high titer virus to inoculate, but unclear where this line is drawn.


Teijaro adds 5 uL of 2x10 8 PFU/mL stock to 6 mL BHK media to hit a target of MOI 0.1 for 107 cells in a T175.


Allen lab has a stock at 2.58e8/ml (Floor 2 lab -80, rack 00156, box 01649). I added 4 ul per 6 mls of media per flask or 24 ul per 36 mls for 6 T175 flasks



Incubate at 37 Celsius for 90 minutes. Gently tilt and rock the flask every 10-15 minutes.


After 90 minutes, add 19 mL warm BHK media (total 25 mL final).


Incubate for 72 hours.


Day 3
Keep the virus cold for all following steps!


Pipet supernatant into 15 mL conical tubes. The supernatant contains the virus. Be careful, this is a LOT of LCMV. Have bleach handy in case of a spill.


Separate any remaining BHK cells that were aspirated from virus.



Spin at 2000 rpm in a benchtop centrifuge (~800-850 g depending on centrifuge in IMPL-K) for 15 minutes.


Collect the supernatant, transfer to a fresh tube.


Repeat for a total of two centrifugation steps.



Keeping the virus cold, aliquot and snap freeze in liquid nitrogen. Pre-chill cryo-tubes in cold room.


Protocol yields ~20-25 mL virus containing supernatant at a target of ~2x108 pfu/mL.



Infecting at 2x10 6 pfu/mouse (100 uL of 2x10 7 pfu/mL), this corresponds to enough virus to infect 2000 mice per T175 of LCMV Clone 13.



Titrate the virus. Make sure to titrate an aliquot that has been frozen and thawed to get a representative value for what the titer will be when you inject from a thawed aliquot (rather than titrating the supernatant directly).

title: Treg isolation
text:
Treg isolation
Spleen/LN processing:

Sac WT B6 mice. Process LN and spleen from each mouse through 70 and 40 um.
Count cells.

Treg MACS isolation
Magnetic labeling of non-CD4+ cells + labeling of CD25+ cells
*Work fast and keep all reagents on ice
MACS enrichment of Tregs/Tconvs: primary labeling reagent will leave all non-CD4+ T cells bound on the LD column. Secondary labeling reagent will label CD25+ cells so flow through from LD column = Tconvs on column = Tregs.

Determine cell number:






Centrifuge cells at 300xg for 10 min, aspirate supernatant completely
Resuspend pellet in 40uL of MACS buffer per 107 cells:

WT: ___ million cells, Resuspend in ___ ul of MACS

Add 10uL of the CD4+CD25+ Regulatory T cell Biotin antibody cocktail per 1e7 cells






Incubate for 10 min in the fridge (2-8C)
Add 38uL of MACS buffer, 20uL of anti-biotin MACS beads, and 2uL of CD25 PE antibody per 1e7 cells






Mix well and incubate for an additional 15 min in the fridge

Magnetic separation: Depletion of non-CD4+ T cells

Place LD column in the magnet, rinse with 3 ml of MACS buffer
Apply cell suspension onto the column
Collect the cells that pass through – THIS IS THE CD4+ T CELL POPULATION
Wash the column with 2x1mL of MACS buffer and collect
Take off column from magnet and wash 2x with 1 ml to get the non-CD4 T cell population

Magnetic Labeling of CD25+ T cells

Centrifuge suspension for 5 min at 300xg, aspirate completely
Resuspend cell pellet in 90uL of buffer
Add 10uL of anti-PE microbeads
Mix well and incubate for 15 min in the fridge
Bring to 500uL volume in MACS buffer
Magnetic Separation: positive selection of CD4+CD25+ Regulatory T cells
Place MS column in the magnetic field, rinse with 500 uL of MACS buffer
Apply cells to column: FT IS TCONVS –SAVE
Wash with 2x 500 uL MACS buffer – SAVE
Remove column from separator and add place on a collection tube
Add 1mL of buffer to column and immediately flush out beads by firmly pressing on column with plunger (2x)
Confirm Treg isolation by flow

title: Western blot
text:
Western blot
Sample Prep
1. Add 2-ME (under chemical fume hood) to lysates at 1:10 concentration into Laemmli sample buffer at time of sample prep.
2. Boil samples in thermal cycler at 95C for 5 minutes
3. Prepare and load 30 ug (10-100ug total protein per well) samples (refer to excel sheet from BCA) into wells and proceed with WB. Dilute as needed with sample buffer to ensure equal protein loading across wells. If you have extra empty wells, fill with buffer + loading buffer to ensure even running of the gel
Protein ladder in Coopersmith freezer- using 5-6 ul is sufficient
SDS-PAGE
4. Run gel at 90V for the first 30 min. After the band has consolidated and made it through the stacking gel section, you can bump up gel to 150V for remaining time (20-40 min). Keep an eye on the gel.
5. When blue bands reach black line on the gel cassette, stop electrophoresis chamber.
6. Take out cassette and crack open using green key
7. Image gel on the imager if interested in protein concentration (similar to Coomassie)
After turning machine on, navigate to Application 🡪 Protein gels 🡪Stain free gel
Exposure: faint bands
Expose gel by hitting camera in bottom right of screen
Transfer
8. While gel is being exposed, prepare the transfer sandwich
9. Pour transfer buffer in one container and 100% methanol in another
10. Dip sandwich pads into transfer buffer and place one stack at bottom of transfer sandwich in the Turboblot platform.
11. Prepare the PVDF membrane next by soaking membrane in 100% methanol until membrane becomes clear (30s-1min) and then dip into transfer buffer before putting membrane onto the transfer stack.
*Make sure there are no bubbles under the membrane
12. Place gel on top of membrane and make sure there are no bubbles here either. Use roller to gently roll out any bubbles between membrane and gel.
*Picture on sheet above Turbo transfer if you have questions about these steps*
13. Place top sandwich stack on top of the gel and close the cassette
*Make sure the iron prongs in the back are present (sometimes they come off)
14. Run the Turboblot on the mixed MW protocol (7 min) and select the number of gels you are transferring
Membrane Blocking
15. During transfer, prepare 2.5% BSA TBS-T
16. After transfer, place membrane (check to make sure ladder has transferred to the membrane) in a box to block for 1 hour in 2.5% BSA TBS-T
*If membrane dries out, soak in methanol and then transfer buffer prior to putting it into the blocking solution
17. After blocking, wash membrane 3x for 5 min each rocking at RT (one by Yvonne’s bench and chemical fume hood in Ford lab) with TBS-T
Primary and Secondary Ab Incubations
18. Dilute primary abs according to manufacture instructions in 1% BSA-TBST and place on rocker at 4C overnight.
Use 1:500 – 1:1000 p.AKT antibody (CST, 4060S) in 1% BSA
19. The next morning, wash membrane 3x for 5 min each rocking at RT (one by Yvonne’s bench and chemical fume hood in Ford lab) with TBS-T
20. Dilute secondary abs according to manufacture instructions in 1% BSA-TBST and place on rocker at RT for 1 hour
Use 1:5000 goat anti-rabbit (abcam, ab205718) in 1% BSA
21. At end of incubation, wash membrane 3x for 5 min each rocking at RT
Imaging
22. During last wash, bring membranes to Coopersmith lab and use the ECL reagents to image
23. Make an ECL substrate mix of 1:1 with the clear and brown bottles (to the left of the electrophoresis chamber)
*Can use Clarity max instead of Clarity if you want brighter bands
24. Drain membrane well and add ECL reagent and tilt the box back and forth for 1 min
25. During 1 min, turn on imager
26. After turning machine on, navigate to Application 🡪 Blots 🡪Chemiluminescence
Optimal exposure (if nothing shows up you can expose for longer amounts of time)
Expose gel by hitting camera in bottom right of screen
27. Export the membrane image using a flash drive and quantify using Biorad software if desired.

title: Antibody titration
text:
Antibody titration
Plate cells

Take aliquot of in vivo day 7 cells and in vitro stimulated P14. Take around 60e6 and then verify by cell count. Plate 2e6 cells/well.
Plate 2e6 cells/well in 96 well plate
Wash 1x with PBS

Live/dead & Fc block

Resuspend in 50 ul of Fc block/well and then 50 ul of 1:500 APC-Cy7 live/dead dye
Incubate for 15 min at RT in the dark
Wash 1x with 100 ul of FACS

Surface stain

Resuspend cells in 50 ul of surface stain/well with antibodies diluted accordingly in FACS buffer.
CD45.2 – BV510 (1:100)
CD45.2 – BV786 (1:100)
Incubate for 20 min at 4C in the dark
Wash 2x with 100 ul FACS

Use Intracellular staining (Foxp3 eBioscience kit if intranuclear molecules such as transcription factors, Cytofix/Cytoperm BD kit if cytoplasmic molecules such as cytokines want to be stained)
Cell fixation & intracellular staining (Foxp3 eBioscience kit)

Prepare fixation buffer by diluting 1:4 of fix perm to diluent (1 ml of fix perm, 3 ml of diluent)
Prepare 1x perm buffer from 10x by diluting buffer with H2O (1 ml perm buffer, 9 mls water)
Resuspend cells in 100 ul fixation buffer
Incubate for 20 min at 4C in the dark
While cells are incubating, make serial diluted antibodies in a 96 well plate by adding 100 ul of perm buffer in the first well and 50 ul of perm buffer in each successive well.
Then add antibody (one at a time for titering) at 1:25 to the first well, mix, and then transfer 50 ul successfully to each well afterwards all the way until you reach 1:400 (which is really 1:800 dilution).
Do not add antibody to the last well, this is your blank control. *Make each dilution twice as concentrated bc you are going to be diluting it 2x in each well bc there’s 50 ul already in each well. * Go down the column with these dilutions

1:50

Resuspend cells in intracellular staining antibodies diluted in perm buffer and incubate for 30 min at 4C in the dark.
After incubation wash 1x with perm buffer and 1x with FACS and you are ready to flow. Use QC voltages from Giovanni when you titer.

title: Mouse Genotyping Protocol
text:
Thaw tail juice from −20°C before going downstairs.
Label a 96-well plate with cage numbers and N/L/R for each mouse.
Take the blood tube from above Anh’s desk and add 100 µL to each well; prepare extra wells as needed.
Label microcentrifuge tubes with cage numbers and N/L/R for each mouse.

title: Mouse Genotyping Protocol
text:
Thaw tail juice from −20°C before going downstairs.
Label a 96-well plate with cage numbers and N/L/R for each mouse.
Take the blood tube from above Anh’s desk and add 100 µL to each well; prepare extra wells as needed.
Label microcentrifuge tubes with cage numbers and N/L/R for each mouse.

title: Mouse Genotyping Protocol
text:
Tail and bleed mice

Scruff mice and ear punch them with N/L/R for each mouse.
Hold the mouse by the scruff and the base of the tail with your ring finger.
Snip the tail into a tube.
While holding the tail base, squeeze down the tail to release blood into the well.
Dry the tail on a paper towel.

title: Mouse Genotyping Protocol
text:
Process tails

Add 400 µL tail juice to each tail tube.
Shake at 55°C and 1,000 rpm for 1 hour.
Add 150 µL 5 M NaCl to each sample and vortex.
Centrifuge at maximum speed for 5 minutes.
Transfer 400 µL supernatant to a new tube.
Add 250 µL isopropanol to each sample and vortex.
Centrifuge at maximum speed for 5 minutes.
Pour off the supernatant.
Wash the pellet with 500 µL 70% ethanol and vortex.
Centrifuge at maximum speed for 5 minutes.
Pour off the supernatant.
Dry tubes upside down over paper towels in a chemical hood for 1 hour.
Resuspend in 200 µL ultrapure water and store at −20°C until use.

title: Mouse Genotyping Protocol
text:
Process blood

Add 100 µL 1× ACK to each well and incubate 5 minutes at room temperature.
Centrifuge at 2,000 rpm for 1 minute and discard supernatant.
Add 50 µL Fc block to each well and incubate 10 minutes at 4°C.
Add 150 µL FACS buffer to each well, centrifuge as above, and discard supernatant.
Add 100 µL antibody cocktail per sample and incubate 15 minutes at 4°C in the dark:

CD8a PE-Cy7 (1:200)
CD45.1 eFluor 450 (1:200)
CD45.2 FITC (1:200)
APC Vα2 (1:200)

Add 150 µL FACS buffer to each well, centrifuge, and discard supernatant.
Prepare compensation controls: use half a drop of vortexed beads with 1 µL antibody per color; incubate 15 minutes at room temperature in the dark; add 200 µL FACS buffer to bullet tubes and refrigerate until running.
If fixing: add 100 µL fixation buffer and incubate 15 minutes at 4°C; add 150 µL FACS buffer, centrifuge, discard supernatant, then add 100 µL FACS buffer and transfer to bullet tubes.
If not fixing: add 100 µL FACS buffer and transfer to bullet tubes.

title: Mouse Genotyping Protocol
text:
Run PCR

Resuspend 10 µL primer stock in 90 µL ultrapure water.
Make master mix according to the appropriate sheet.
Combine 24 µL master mix with 1 µL tail DNA.
Run PCR:

AR: use TOUCHDOW on the rightmost machine, or an equivalent touchdown protocol.
UBC-Cre: use GENO_TD on the middle machine.

The run takes approximately 90 minutes.

title: Mouse Genotyping Protocol
text:
Run gel
While PCR is running, make the gel.

Set out the gel tray, gel basin, and required combs.
For a small 2.5% gel, combine 2.5 g agarose with 100 mL 1× TAE in a 250 mL flask.
For a large 2.5% gel, combine 5 g agarose with 200 mL 1× TAE in a 500 mL flask.
Microwave for 1 minute; swirl. Microwave for 30 seconds; swirl. Microwave for 20 seconds; swirl until flash boiling stops. Confirm agarose is fully melted, then cool under running cold water while swirling until the flask is safe to handle.
Add 4 µL EtBr for a small gel or 8 µL for a large gel and swirl.
Pour into the gel basin. If it leaks, place ice around the sides to stop the leak.
Let harden for about 20 minutes. Meanwhile, fill the main running basin to the line with TAE.
Remove combs once hardened. Place gel in the running apparatus and add enough TAE to cover it.
Load 7 µL ladder and 10 µL samples.
Run at 100 V and image. Orient red to red and black to black: the red lead is at the lower end of the gel and the black lead is toward the ladder.

AR gel: 45 minutes.
UBC-Cre gel: 45 minutes.

title: Liberase Skin Protocol
text:
Each vial of Liberase TL research grade (Roche 5401020001) makes 20 mL Liberase solution. Normally prepare 3–4 vials at a time.
Add 2 mL RPMI plus supplementary complement per vial of lyophilized enzyme and place on ice to reconstitute for 20 minutes.
Add 5 mL RPMI plus supplementary complement to each vial after reconstitution (7 mL total). Mix with a stripette before transferring to a 50 mL tube.
Bring to 20 mL per vial with 13 mL RPMI plus supplementary complement. For example, if pooling two vials, bring the 50 mL tube to 40 mL total.
Add 100 µL of 1 mg/mL DNase per 20 mL Liberase solution (200 µL for 40 mL). Use Sigma bovine DNase.

title: Liberase Skin Protocol
text:
Each vial of Liberase TL research grade (Roche 5401020001) makes 20 mL Liberase solution. Normally prepare 3–4 vials at a time.
Add 2 mL RPMI plus supplementary complement per vial of lyophilized enzyme and place on ice to reconstitute for 20 minutes.
Add 5 mL RPMI plus supplementary complement to each vial after reconstitution (7 mL total). Mix with a stripette before transferring to a 50 mL tube.
Bring to 20 mL per vial with 13 mL RPMI plus supplementary complement. For example, if pooling two vials, bring the 50 mL tube to 40 mL total.
Add 100 µL of 1 mg/mL DNase per 20 mL Liberase solution (200 µL for 40 mL). Use Sigma bovine DNase.

title: Liberase Skin Protocol
text:
Harvest

Shave the right and left flanks, then perfuse mice with 10 mL HBSS.
Harvest both ears, separate dorsal and ventral sides, and place in 1 mL Liberase solution.
Harvest 3 cm flank skin (1.5 × 2 cm area) into 1.5 mL Liberase solution.

title: Liberase Skin Protocol
text:
Process flank skin

Incubate for 30 minutes at 37°C in a water bath in Liberase solution.
Peel epidermis from dermis and return it to the same Liberase tube.
Chop the skin.
Incubate for a further 80 minutes at 37°C in a water bath.
Transfer to 3 mL RP-10 and triturate 30 times with a transfer pipette.
Filter through a 70 µm nylon filter cone into a fresh tube, rinsing the filter with RP-10.
Centrifuge and aspirate RP-10 from the pellet. The pellet is ready to stain.

title: Liberase Skin Protocol
text:
Process ear skin

Incubate for 120 minutes at 37°C in a water bath in Liberase solution.
Chop the ears.
Transfer to 3 mL RP-10 and triturate 30 times with a transfer pipette.
Filter through a 70 µm nylon filter cone into a fresh tube, rinsing the filter with RP-10.
Centrifuge and aspirate RP-10 from the pellet. The pellet is ready to stain.

title: Liberase Skin Protocol
text:
Notes

Flank skin has two incubations: 30 minutes before peeling/chopping, then 80 minutes at 37°C. Ear skin has one 120-minute incubation before chopping and filtering.
Peel flank skin gently but thoroughly enough to see the white, stringy epidermal material removed.
Do not over-chop the skin: chop vigorously for no more than 40–60 seconds to protect viability.

text:

Maintenance for the -80:

Must be defrosted at minimum once a year
The middle of the freezer must always be full
If freezer is not completely full, fill it with empty shelves
Clean the filter in the front every month

Slide out the metal guard
Slide out the filter
Wash with warm water and dry overnight
Replace filter and guard next morning

Clean the filter on the bottom every month

Slide out the 2inch filter under the front side of the freezer
Wash with warm water and dry
Replace the filter that same day

Shave off ice once a month
Clean the compressors and system on the side of the -80 annually

AGR will do this as part of their service

If it is not maintaining temperature or losing temperature quickly, call AGR Mechanical

They come out the same day or next day and will monitor the machine and give a diagnostics report

Service the machine regularly

title: Blood prep for phenotyping
text:
Preparation for blood - genotyping


Bleed animal into 50 μl EDTA in a microfuge tube
If the blood is fresh, spin at max for 30 seconds. If you are not going to use it that day, put it at 4°C for one day.
If the blood is a day old, there should already be a pellet, so you don’t need to spin it down.
Aspirate and discard supernatant
Add 0.5 ml Ack and vortex
Incubate at room temp for 5 minutes
Spin at max for 30 seconds
Aspirate and discard supernatant
Wash with ~1 ml FACS buffer and vortex
Spin at max for 30 seconds
Aspirate and discard supernatant

If you are not FC blocking go to step 15.
If you are not FC blocking and are not biotin labeling, go to step 20.

Make master mix of 50 μl FACS buffer/sample plus 0.25 μl FC block/sample (e.g., if you have 8 samples, mix 400 μl FACS buffer + 2 μl FC block)
Add 50 μl of your master mix to each sample to resuspend the pellet and vortex
Incubate on ice for at least 5 minutes

If you are NOT biotin labeling your samples, proceed to step 20.

Add 0.5 μl of your biotin antibody per sample
Incubate on ice for 15 minutes
Wash with ~1.5 ml FACS buffer and vortex
Spin at max for 30 seconds
Aspirate and discard supernatant
Make master mix of 50 μl FACS buffer/sample
Add 50 μl of your master mix to each sample to resuspend the pellet and vortex
Incubate on ice for 10 minutes in the dark
Wash in ~1.5 ml FACS buffer and vortex
Spin at max for 30 seconds
Aspirate and discard supernatant
Add 50 μl FACS fix buffer and vortex
Put sample on ice or at 4°C until you run flow cytometry

title: DNA extaction from tails
text:
Extraction of DNA from mouse tails

Place small piece of tail or ear in 400 μl of tail juice and incubate overnight at 55° C. Vortex and proceed to step 3.

2. If frozen, thaw sample in incubator.

Add phenol-chloroform IMA (25:24:1) to tail juice mixture at approximately 1:1 ratio (~400μl) in fume hood, mix well.
Spin samples in centrifuge for 5 min. at 12,000 rpm (room temperature).
Add 100μl TE (pH 8.0) to one well for every sample in a clean 96 well plate.


6. Obtain a new set of eppendorf tubes and pipette in ~400 μl of ethanol.


Remove tubes from centrifuge and pipette top layer (aqueous-phase DNA) into the tubes with ethanol, avoiding any phenol layer or interface (sludge).
Mix tubes with DNA + ethanol until white clumps of DNA are visible.
Use pipette tip to remove each clump of DNA into a well containing the TE. If difficult to remove DNA, centrifuge in order to force the DNA to pellet.
Cover wells and seal sides with tape until further use. 4° C for near term or -20° C for longer storage.
Dispose of phenol-chloroform in container in fume hood, return to refrigerator.

text:
Memory CD8+ T cells and Long-Term Hematopoietic Stem Cells Share a Transcriptional Profile of Self-Renewal
Chance John Luckey*,1,2, Ananda W Goldrath*,3, Patrick Autissier4, Christophe Benoist1, and Diane Mathis1.
*These authors contributed equally to this work
1Joslin Diabetes Center, Department of Immunology, Harvard Medical School, 1 Joslin Place, Boston, MA 02115, USA.
2Department of Pathology, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA 02215, USA.
3Division of Biology Section of Molelcular Biology, University of California San Diego, 9500 Gilman Drive, San Diego CA, 92093-0377, USA.
4Division of Viral Pathogenesis, Department of Medicine, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Harvard Medical School, 330 Brookline Avenue,Boston MA 02215, USA.
Abstract
The only cells in the adult hematopoietic system that undergo self-renewal are long-term hematopoietic stem cells and memory T and B cells. We set out to determine whether this similar characteristic arises from a common molecular program. The transcriptional profiles of memory, naïve and effector CD8+ T cells were compared with long-term hematopoietic stem cells, short-term hematopoietic stem cells, and lineage committed progenitors. Transcripts enriched in memory CD8+ T cells relative to naïve and effector T cells were also selectively enriched in long-term hematopoietic stem cells relative to their short-term and lineage committed counterparts. Thus, the capacity for self-renewal shared by memory T cells and long-term hematopoietic stem cells correlates with a common molecular program. Several of these shared transcripts have been shown to be involved in self-renewal. We propose that these common transcripts provide a unique insight into the molecular pathways involved in homeostatic self-renewal within the adult hematopoietic system. Study of these molecular pathways will be essential in understanding the molecular basis for the maintenance of long-term immunological memory as well as steady state hematopoiesis.
Introduction
One hallmark of the adaptive immune response is it’s the ability to respond more effectively upon re-encountering a pathogen—thus “remembering” a prior pathogenic exposure. The ‘memory’ response that results upon re-exposure to a pathogen is larger and more rapid than the initial ‘naïve’ response, providing a more robust control of the infection. Memory responses to most pathogens require the development of memory T and B cells, which along with long-lived antibody secreting B cells called plasma cells provide the cellular basis for successful vaccination.
Recent developments in the enumeration and characterization of antigen-specific CD8+ T cell populations have allowed for a more detailed picture of the cellular dynamics underlying the formation and maintenace of T cell memory (reviewed in [1-4]).
Prior to initial infection, antigen-inexperienced, “naïve” T cells that may recognize a given infectious agent exist at very low frequencies and rarely if ever divide [6, 7].. Upon pathogen exposure, those rare naïve T cells capable of recognizing the pathogen via their TCR undergo a process of rapid clonal expansion as well as differentiation. These stimulated T cells divide as rapidly as every 6-8 hours and acquire the necessary functional activity to eliminate the pathogen; these cells are termed “effector” T cells (make this all CD8+ specific) [8, 9]. Effector T cells demonstrate a more rapid response to antigen stimulation and the ability to traffic throughout the body. CD8+ effector T cells undergo a dramatic contraction in numbers following antigen clearance (with 90-95% of the antigen specific CD8+ T cells undergoing apoptosis within two weeks of initial infection [10].
For CD8+ T cells, a subset of the antigen-specific persists long after initial antigen exposure and are known as memory cells. The lineage relationship between effector T cells and memory T cells has been the subject of several recent papers. Initial reports indicated that naive progeny destined to become memory T cells underwent a stage in which they adopted effector-like phenotype and gene expression patterns, suggesting that memory T cells were derived stochastically from a homogeneous effector T cell pool [11]. However, more recent work has demonstrated that the precursors destined to become memory cells can be identified among the effector T cell population by the surface expression of IL-7R and CD8 alpha/alpha homodimer [12-14]. IL-7R and CD8 alpha/alpha expression distinguishes memory-destined effector T cells from the majority of effector T cells that are fated to die in the contraction phase of the immune response. Thus it appears that all effector T cells are not created equally, with only a subset expressing the necessary transcripts that allow for the progression to long-lived memory T cells.
Followinginfection, memory CD8+ T cells are maintained at relatively constant cell numbers often for the lifetime of an individual [9, 10]. Once formed, memory CD8+ T cells undergo a process of homeostatic self-renewal or basal homeostatic proliferation which is dependent on IL-15 . Thus, memory T cells numbers are maintained through a process involving a homeostatic balancing of low level turn-over and survival with death. [1, 6]. (you said this already) It is this persistentence of an increased precursor frequency long-lived memory cells, combined with their rapid ability to differentiate into secondary effectors, that provides the basis for the robust recall response to re-infection in successful vaccination.
We are particularly interested in understanding the molecular events that allow memory T cells to persist and thus provide long lasting antigen-specific protection over the lifetime of an individual. The ability of memory T cells to proliferate in response to homeostatic signals without further differentiation is strikingly reminiscent of the self-renewal observed in hematopoietic stem cell populations [15]. The capacity for self-renewal observed by both memory CD8+ T cells and long-term hematopoietic stem cells appears to support the maintainance of relatively constant numbers throughout the life of the animal. Furthermore, memory T cells and Lt-HSC also maintain the ability to differentiate into progeny which are incapable of self renewal. While these phenotypic similarities have been pointed out previously [2, 16, 17], no direct evidence that either supports or contradicts these general observations has been reported. We, therefore, set out to directly test the hypothesis that memory T cells and long-term hematopoietic stem cells share a portion of their respective transcriptional profiles. We hypothesized that those transcripts expressed in memory T cells would be enriched in long-term hematopoietic stem cells and would likely be involved in the molecular pathways of self-renewal.
Results
In order to compare the overall transcriptional profiles of memory CD8+ T cell populations with hematopoietic stem cell populations, we employed Affymetrix Genechip analysis. As a source of monoclonal populations of naïve, effector, and memory CD8+ T cells, we used the OTI TCR-transgenic adoptive transfer and viral infection model described previously (manuscript in press). Purified naïve, effector, and memory populations expressed the expected cell surface phenotypic markers and demonstrated functional activities indicative of naïve, effector and memory CD8+ T cells (data not shown). For stem cell populations, we chose the phenotypically well-characterized and functionally defined mature hematopoietic stem cell data published by Ivanova et.al. [18].
Having established functionally defined cellular populations, we grouped together the raw data (.cel files) and collectively pre-processed them with the “rma” method in the “affylmGUI” statistical analysis package developed by the collaborative, open source project www.bioconductor.org [19-22]. The rma method uses an improved algorithm for probe level background correction, normalization, and summary that dramatically reduces observed statistical noise both in published control data sets [19-21] as well as among replicates within our own data (data not shown). Differential expression of individual genes was calculated using the LIMMA (LInear Models for MicroArray data) within the affylmGUI package [23]. LIMMA uses empirical Bayesian methods to provide stable results even when number of replicates between arrays is relatively small, as is the case with these data sets.
We confirmed that our data set accurately depicts the expression profiles of naïve, effector, and memory cells by showing that known transcripts behave as expected (manuscript in preparation). Furthermore, our expression profiles are remarkably similar to those generated independently using a different TCR transgenic and viral infection model by Kaech et.al. [11], providing an important external validation of our techniques and cell purity. Finally, we demonstrated that memory CD8+ T cells generated in our model are self-renewing by following memory cell numbers from a cohort of mice over the course of several months. OTI memory CD8+ T cells maintained constant cell numbers, cell surface phenotypes, and cytokine secretion profiles (data not shown). Our findings are consistent with the published reports demonstrating that CD8+ memory T cells homeostatically self- renew over the life of an individual [9, 10].
In order to test whether memory CD8+ T cells and Lt-HSC share a transcriptional profile, we first compared memory versus naïve T cells and the long-term versus short-term hematopoietic stem cells. These pairs were chosen because they represented the closest relatives to each other when all genes were compared either by MVA plots or cluster analysis (data not shown). Furthermore, since both Lt-HSC and St-HSC populations are pluripotent, the only known functional difference between them is the inability of St-HSC to self-renew [15]. Finally, memory T cells divide more frequently than naïve cells while St-HSC divide more frequently than Lt-HSC, thus any similarities observed between memory T cells and Lt-HSC not likely to be the result a proliferative molecular signature. These comparisons therefore represented a focused look at self-renewing potential.
Interestingly, those genes that were differentially enriched in memory T cells were dramatically skewed toward Lt-HSC, with 73% of the transcripts enriched relative to St-HSC (Figure 1A). In addition to the number of transcripts, there was a clear skewing towards more significant P values among the Lt-HSC enriched genes. The reverse comparison was similarly skewed. Of the transcripts differentially enriched in long- versus short-term hematopoietic stem cells, 62% were also enriched in memory T cells relative to naïve T cells and showed a trend towards more significant P values (Figure 1B). This demonstrates a significant overlap between the expression profiles of self-renewing memory cells and self-renewing long-term hematopoietic stem cells, at least when they are compared to their closest non-renewing relatives: naïve T cells and St-HSC.
We next took a broader look at how the memory-enriched genes in Figure 1 were expressed across all mature hematopoietic precursor populations. Consistent with the idea that memory-enhanced genes relative to naive are shared with Lt-HSC and not other hematopoietic precursor populations, memory enriched genes demonstrated a positive skewing in the Lt-HSC versus LCP (68%), with less visual skewing but similar percentages of St-HSC versus LCP (67%) comparisons (Figure 2A). This demonstrates that memory genes enriched relative to naïve cells are selectively enriched in long-term hematopoietic stem cells.
Despite the clear correlation of memory-enriched genes with Lt-HSC in all pair-wise comparisons, the converse did not hold to be true. Specifically, Lt-HSC enriched genes were not strongly correlated with memory T cells when compared to effector T cells (51%) (Figure 2B). Indeed, the enrichment seen in the memory versus naïve cells was comparable to that observed for effector relative to naïve (56%). It appears that while the set of transcripts most up regulated in memory T cells are generally up in Lt-HSC, the transcripts most up regulated in Lt-HSC are actually negatively correlated with naïve expression.
As outlined in the introduction, recent reports have demonstrated that effector CD8+ T cells are heterogeneous [12-14]. A subset of effector T cells at the peak of the initial burst already express a few memory cell surface markers (IL-7R and CD8 alpha/alpha), and these effectors appear to go one to become self-renewing memory cells. We therefore hypothesized that the positive correlation observed between Lt-HSC and effectors was a result of correlation with the subset of IL-7R+ memory-destined effectors that might themselves express a more memory-like phenotype. We sorted day 8 effector T cells into IL-7R+ and IL-7R- populations and subjected them to Affymetrix Genechip analysis. To our surprise, there was no selective enrichment of the Lt-HSC transcripts in IL-7R+ effector cells relative to their IL-7R- counterparts (Figure 3A). Furthermore, Lt-HSC specific genes where selectively enriched in IL-7R- effectors relative to naïve cells (Figure 3B). This confirmed our previous observation that much of what is up-regulated in Lt-HSC vs. St-HSC actually represents genes that are selectively down-regulated in naïve cells relative to both memory and all effector populations.
Given the above results, we wanted to ensure that the shared transcripts between memory and Lt-HSC observed in Figure 1A were not solely the result of the comparison to naive and St-HSC cells, i.e. a denominator effect. We therefore looked at the relative expression of the subset of genes that met our definition of differential expression in memory T cells in both the naïve as well as the effector comparisons. Of the 46 transcripts that met these criteria, there was again a significant skewing of both numbers and P values towards Lt-HSC compared with St-HSC (65%) (Figure 4). Thus a significant fraction of memory specific transcripts were selectively enriched in Lt-HSC. This demonstrates that a common molecular signature is shared between memory CD8+ T cells and long-term hematopoietic stem cells.
In order to gain further insight into these shared transcripts, we made a list of all transcripts which were up-regulated in memory cells compared to naïve and effector cells as well as up-regulated in Lt-HSC relative to St-HSC (Table I). Our inclusion criteria of fold change of 1.4 was based on within-replicate analyses providing empirical estimation of experimental noise (data not shown). By quantitative PCR, we have found that this cutoff correctly predicts differential expression 93% of the time, with the GeneChip data often dramatically underestimating true fold changes (manuscript in preparation). Such underestimation is consistent both with general array data and further reflects the fact that the ‘rma’ algorithm consistently underestimates true fold changes; with the decrease in the accuracy of the algorithm serving as a tradeoff for a dramatic increase in its precision [19-21].
We were pleased to discover that Mel18 was among those shared transcripts between memory and Lt-HSC. Mel18 is a polycomb family member which, like its closest homolog BMI1, has been shown to be involved in the self-renewal of hematopoietic stem cells [24] and is involved in inhibition of the of Ink4a/ARF complex [25]. Interestingly, Mel18 knockout mice also demonstrate a T cell differentiation defect during thymic and CD4+ differentiation, but its role in memory CD8+ T cells has yet to be addressed [26, 27]. There were several other shared transcripts with known functionsconsistent with their potentially playing a role in stem cell self-renewal. Both TnfR2 and Traf1 are known to associate within the cell, and signaling via this pathway results in inhibition of apoptosis (reviewed in [28, 29]. Finally, the stromal-derived cytokine EDR has been shown to play a role in the survival of several different cell types [30]. Taken together, the presence of these transcripts previously been shown to play a role in self-renewal and/or survival supports the general hypothesis that the shared transcripts in both memory CD8+ T cells and Lt-HSC represent a self-renewal molecular signature.
We were interested in determining whether the transcripts shared between memory and Lt-HSC were also enriched in other stem cell comparisons. In order to address this issue, we pooled together our T cell data with the complete published data sets from Ivanova et.al., including their adult and fetal hematopoietic stem cells as well as embryonic and neural stem cells [18]; the data sets from Ramalho-Santos et. al. which included adult hematopoietic stem cells as well as neural and embryonic stem cells [31]; and the data sets from Akashi et. al. which included adult LtHSC and StHSC populations [32]. These data sets were normalized together and analyzed as above using affylmGUI. Intriguingly, the vast majority of those genes whose expression we had previously identified as enriched in memory T cells and LtHSC were also enriched in the adult hematopoietic stem cell populations from Ramalho-Santos et.al. and Akashi et.al. (Table II). Furthermore, most of the shared transcripts were also enriched in fetal liver hematopoietic precursor populations. This provided important external confirmation of our findings, suggesting that this shared signature holds true for all hematopoietic self-renewing populations tested. However, there was not a consistent enrichment in either NSC or ESC populations (data not shown). Therefore this signature does not seem to be conserved with stem cell populations outside of the hematopoietic system.

Discussion
Several authors have posited that memory T cells are similar to stem cells in their ability to both self-renew and maintain the ability for further differentiation [2, 16, 17]. However, there has been no previous evidence to support that these shared phenotypes result from a shared molecular program. Given that Long-term hematopoietic stem cells and memory T and B cells are the only cells of the adult hematopoietic system which undergo homeostatic self-renewal, we tested whether Lt-HSC and memory CD8+ T cells shared a common molecular profile.
We have shown that Lt-HSC and memory CD8+ T cells share a significant portion of their transcriptional profiles when compared to their closest non-renewing counterparts: St-HSC and naïve CD8+ T cells. Further analysis demonstrated that many of these shared transcripts were also selectively enriched in effector CD8+ T cells relative to naïve cells, suggesting that a subset of Lt-HSC enriched transcripts are selectively down-regulated in naïve CD8+ T cells relative to their memory and effector counterparts. This was surprising given the relative quiescence of both naïve [33] and Lt-HSC populations [32]. We suggest this correlation reflects a fundamental difference in the overall transcriptional accessibility of the two populations, with naïve cells in a closed chromatin state relative to the known open state of Lt-HSC (reviewed in [34]).
Given our interest in directly comparing Lt-HSC with memory T cells, we further differentiated memory specific transcripts based on their enrichment relative to both naïve and effector T cells. Once again, memory specific transcripts were enriched in Lt-HSC. Further analysis of the specific shared transcripts demonstrated that several are known to play a role in self-renewal and/or cell survival. This provides the first evidence that Lt-HSC and memory T cells share a common molecular program. Furthermore, we suggest that these shared transcripts represent a self-renewal signature for the hematopoietic system.
There has been a great deal of debate within the literature concerning the validity and reproducibility of defining a general molecular signature of stem cells [18, 31, 35, 36]. We took several steps to minimize potential differences due to analytical methods. We chose to analyze only those data files where we were able to obtain the original Affymetrix cell intensity file (.cel file). All cel files were normalized and summarized at the probe level together, and were statistically analyzed in exactly the same manner. In contrast to the previous attempts to broadly define a stemness profile, we chose to focus on the more limited phenotype of self-renewal within the hematopoietic system. We feel that by using memory T cells, which arguably share only this phenotypic characteristic with other stem cell populations, we might gain a unique and focused insight into self-renewal. Indeed, our analysis demonstrates that those transcripts shared between memory CD8+ T cells and Lt-HSC are generally enriched in other adult, and to a lesser degree fetal, hematopoietic stem cell populations. However, they are not enriched in NSC and ESC populations, consistent with the idea that the specific transcripts involved in self-renewal are only conserved within a particular differentiation system [35].
We feel that the shared transcripts identified in the study are excellent candidates for playing a direct functional role in stem cell and memory T cell self-renewal. Mel18 has been shown to affect Lt-HSC self-renewal, but its role in memory has not been explored. While TnfR2 and Traf1 are known to be involved in anti-apoptotic signaling; their role in the self-renewal of either T cells or HSC has not been directly addressed. Similarly, the stromal derived cytokine EDR has been shown to support the survival of multiple hematopoietic cell types in vitro but its role in vivo has not been addressed. In addition, the presence of several specific members of the RAS/MAP-Kinase pathway suggests that selective activation of individual members of this diverse signaling pathway are invoved in self-renewal.
While IL-7R has been shown to be essential for the long-term survival of memory CD8+ T cells [1], its presence in the Lt-HSC transcriptional profile points to one of the limitations of the current study. Our data relies solely on transcriptional information, and the IL-7R protein is not expressed on the surface of Lt-HSC [32]. Obviously, relative protein expression and protein interactions/ modifications would be a more informative comparison. Given the small numbers of cells available from the populations studied, such comparisons will require advancement in the sensitivity and dynamic range of current mass-spectrometric proteomic technologies. For now, transcriptional profiling remains one of the more tractable quantitative methods for global comparative analysis between rare cellular populations.
We have demonstrated that most of the transcripts uniquely enriched in memory CD8+ T cells are also enriched in long-term hematopoietic stems cells, implying they represent a signature for the molecular process of self-renewal. We believe the subset of memory enriched genes that are also enriched in long-term hematopoietic stem cells are excellent candidates for a common molecular signature of self-renewal within the hematopoietic system. Further analysis of the functional requirement for these individual transcripts for the self-renewal of both memory T cells and Lt-HSC should prove enlightening.
