Frozen HISTOLOGY of the GUT
01/2020 - LLB
Procedure for OCT sections:
1) Take down one mouse at a time (it’s a time-sensitive thing! Gut will lose its architecture super fast). 
2) Pull out gut (I typically grab the intestine by the stomach, cut it from the stomach and pull it vertically). Cut the 3-5cm piece you are interested in (I typically do ileum, but you can do duodenum, jejunum, ileum, colon). Put tissue on a paper tissue, squirt some PBS1x with pasteur pipette and remove feces by gently pushing with scissors. Cut/open the gut longitudinally, mucus facing up and muscle down. Keep it relatively moist with pasteur pipette+PBS1x. **Don’t worry about removing fat, it’s part of the natural structure of the gut and won’t hurt for OCT sectioning.
     *Don’t do any washing steps. Unnecessary and they will damage structure!
3) Have a cassette filled with OCT ready.
4) Make swiss roll with wooden stick (I use cotton swab sticks): place stick below (on the muscle side). Now roll gut put muscle touching stick, mucus is in the outside. 
     *When rolling don’t force tissue into roll. Move stick forward instead of force-rolling the tissue around it (tissue is super soft)
5) Once rolled place in cassette filled with OCT by putting stick vertical on cassette and pushing tissue down with forceps. Try to embed it flat. Add more OCT on top. 
- Procedure for Paraffin sections:
1) Take down one mouse at a time (it’s a time-sensitive thing! Gut will lose its architecture super fast). 
2) Pull out gut, remove feces by gently pushing with scissors, put on tissue and cut/open longitudinally, mucus facing up and muscle down. Keep it relatively moist with pasteur pipette+PBS.
     *Don’t do any washing steps. Unnecessary and they will damage structure!
3) Cut in 2-3cm pieces (one distal, medial, proximal). Have a cassette ready with 2 sponges with holes made by the cut plastic stick. 
4) Make swiss roll with wooden stick: place stick below (on the muscle side). Now roll gut put muscle touching stick, mucus is in the outside. 
     *When rolling don’t force tissue into roll. Move stick forward instead of force-rolling the tissue around it (tissue is super soft)
5) Once rolled place in cassette in between sponges (to flatten it). Remove stick, close cassette and dump in fixative (this has to be done within 10min after death). Fix in 10% Formalin solution (=4% Paraformaldehyde) +1mM CaCl2 in PBS1x for 24h at RT (24h preserves epitopes pretty well. Some people fix for 48h, but you risk losing epitopes).
6) After fixation, dump PFA in appropriate biohazard container, and wash with deoinized water twice (dump fixative, fill bottle with water - let sit for 5min for every wash).  
7) Place in 70% EtOH (70% EtOH preserves tissue for longer than just PBS).
8) Bring to the core for embedding/sectioning in 70% Ethanol. (Tissues can remain in ethanol for days/weeks before being sent in to the core)

                                   Introduction
About the product
Neon® The Neon® Transfection System is a novel, benchtop electroporation device Transfection that employs an electroporation technology by using the pipette tip as an electroporation chamber to efficiently transfect mammalian cells including System primary and immortalized hematopoietic cells, stem cells, and primary cells. The Neon® Transfection System efficiently delivers nucleic acids, proteins, and siRNA into all mammalian cell types including primary and stem cells with a high cell survival rate. The transfection is performed using as few as 1 × 104 or as many as 5 × 106 cells per reaction using a sample volume of 10 µL or 100 µL in a variety of cell culture formats (60 mm, 6-well, 48-well, and 24-well). The Neon® Transfection System uses a single transfection kit (Neon® Kit) that is compatible with various mammalian cell types including primary and stem cells thereby avoiding the need to determine an optimal buffer for each cell type. The Neon® Transfection System offers open and transparent protocols that are optimized for ease of use and simplicity. The Neon® device is preprogrammed with one 24-well optimization protocol to optimize conditions for your nucleic acid/siRNA and cell type, or you can program and store up to 50 cell-specific protocols in the Neon® device database. Optimized protocols for many commonly used cell types are also available on www.lifetechnologies.com/neon for your convenience to maximize transfection efficiencies for your cell types. See page 3 for details on various parts of the system.
System The Neon® Transfection System consists of: components • Neon® Device The Neon® Device is a simple, user friendly benchtop electroporation device that employs the pipette tip as an electroporation chamber to efficiently transfect mammalian cells including primary and immortalized hematopoietic cells, stem cells, and primary cells. The device is preprogrammed with a 24-well optimization protocol and supports a database to store up to 50 user-specified protocols. See page 3 for details. • Neon® Pipette Station The Neon® Pipette Station is a unique component of the system and holds the Neon® Pipette during electroporation and protects the user from any electrical shock exposures. The Neon® Tube which has an electrode near the bottom is inserted into the pipette station to transfer the electric field from the electrode inside the Neon® Tip. See page 3 for details. • Neon® Kits (not supplied with the device) The Neon® Kits contain the Neon® Tips, Neon® Tubes, and buffers for electroporation. The Neon® Kits are available in two formats for electroporation of 10 µL or 100 µL samples (page 40 for ordering information). See page 3 for details on Neon® Tips and Tubes.
Neon® Transfection System 1
System overview   Unlike standard cuvette based electroporation, the Neon® Transfection System
                  uses a unique electroporation reaction chamber, the Neon® Tip that delivers a
                  high electric field to the biological sample. The Neon® Tip maximizes the gap
                  size between the two electrodes while minimizing the surface area of each
                  electrode. As a result, the sample experiences a more uniform electric field,
                  minimal pH change, less ion formation, and negligible heat generation.
                  This next generation electroporation technology overcomes many of the
                  limitations associated with standard cuvette based electroporation thereby
                  increasing transfection efficiency and cell viability, and providing an ergonomic
                  workflow.

                                                         V




                  The transfection occurs in the uniquely designed Neon® Tip using simple 3-step
                  procedure.
                  1. Load a mixture of harvested cells and molecules to be delivered (e.g., DNA,
                     RNA, siRNA) into the Neon® Tip.
                  2. Plug the Neon® Pipette with Neon® Tip into position in the Neon® Pipette
                     Station with Neon® Tube; select your protocol on the device, and press
                     Start.
                  3. Unplug the Neon® Pipette and transfer your transfected cells into a tissue
                     culture vessel containing the appropriate medium.



Features           Important features of the Neon® Transfection System are listed below:
                   •   User-friendly Neon® device benchtop design that easily fits in your tissue
                       culture hood for easy, efficient transfection of a wide variety of
                       mammalian cells including primary and stem cells
                   •   Ability to transfect 1 × 104–5 × 106 cells per reaction in a sample volume of
                       10 µL or 100 µL in a variety of cell culture formats (60 mm, 6-well, 48-well,
                       and 24-well)
                   •   Utilizes a single buffer system for all cell types except primary suspension
                       blood cells
                   •   Simple touch screen interface for easy programming of electroporation
                       parameters
                   •   Available with one pre-programmed 24-well optimization protocol and
                       the option to customize up to 50 cell specific protocols
                   •   Built-in safety features in the device to enhance user safety
2 Neon® Transfection System
Description of parts
Neon® Device The Neon® device is a simple, user friendly benchtop electroporation device. When used with a Neon® Pipette Station and Neon® Kits, the Neon® device efficiently transfects mammalian cells including primary and stem cells. The device is preprogrammed with a 24-well optimization protocol and supports a database to store up to 50 user-specified protocols. See page vii for a front and rear view of the device.
Neon® Pipette The Neon® Pipette utilizes a positive displacement pipette mechanism for pipetting mixtures containing cells and nucleic acid or siRNA. The Neon® Pipette is a fixed volume pipette and permanently calibrated at the manufacturing stage and does not require any further calibration. The Neon® Pipette is designed for use with Neon® Tips only. Do not use any other tips with the Neon® Pipette.
Neon® Transfection System 3
Neon® Pipette The Neon® Pipette Station is a unique component of the Neon® Transfection Station system. It holds a Neon® Pipette during electroporation procedures. The Neon® Pipette Station is equipped with many safety sensors and protection mechanisms that protect the user from any exposures to an electrical shock. The Neon® Pipette Station is connected to the Neon® device using the high voltage and sensor connector (see page 6 for details). The Neon® Pipette Station also holds the Neon® Tube which has an electrode near the bottom that transfers the electric field from the electrode inside the Neon® Tip.

General guidelines
Recommended kits To use the Neon® device for electroporation of mammalian cells, you need to purchase the Neon® Kits. Ordering information is on page 40. Do not use any other kits with the unit.
               To obtain the best results, follow these recommendations:
               •   Based on your initial results, you may need to optimize the electroporation
                   parameters for your cell type and DNA/siRNA. A preprogrammed 24-
                   well optimization protocol is included in the device for your convenience.
               •   Before using the device with your samples, ensure that you are able to
                   insert and use the Neon® Pipette and Tip correctly into the Neon® Pipette
                   Station (see page 14 for details).
               •   Wear gloves, laboratory coat, and safety glasses during electroporation.
               •   Always use the Neon® device with Neon® Kits for electroporation of
                   mammalian cells.
               •   The Neon® Transfection System is compatible for use with most
                   mammalian cells including primary and stem cells.
               •   Use high quality DNA and siRNA to obtain good transfection efficiency.
               •   Follow the guidelines on pages 16–17 for cell preparation.
               •   Use an appropriate GFP (green fluorescent protein) construct or siRNA
                   control (see next page for details) to determine transfection efficiency.
               •   Discard the Neon® Tips after 2 usages and Neon® Tubes after 10 usages as
                   a biological hazard. We strongly recommend changing tube and buffer
                   when switching to a different plasmid DNA/siRNA or cell type.
               •   Visit www.lifetechnologies.com/neon for a library of electroporation
                   protocols for commonly used cell types.
Recommended The Neon® Kits contain two Resuspension Buffers. Use the appropriate buffers Resuspension Buffer based on the cell type as below. The cell-specific Neon® transfection protocols available on www.lifetechnologies.com/neon indicate the type of Resuspension buffer for use with each cell type. Resuspension Buffer R: Use Resuspension Buffer R with established adherent and suspension cell lines such as 3T3-L1, HEK293, Cos7, C2C12, HeLa, HCT-15, PC-12, MDCK, Raw264.7, U-2OS, CEM, HL-60, K-562, Jurkat, LCL, Ramos, U-937, as well as primary adherent cells such as neuronal cells, stem cells, hepatocytes, HUVEC, macrophage cells, dendritic cells. Resuspension Buffer T: Use Resuspension Buffer T with primary blood-derived suspension cells such as T-cells, B-cells, NK cells, PBMC, monocytes.
12 Neon® Transfection System
DNA quality and The quality and concentration of DNA used for electroporation plays an amount important role for the transfection efficiency. We strongly recommend using high quality plasmid purification kits such as PureLink™ HiPure Plasmid DNA Purification Kits (page 40) to prepare DNA. • Resuspend the purified DNA in deionized water or TE buffer (10 mM Tris- HCl, 1 mM EDTA, pH 8.0) at a concentration between 1–5 µg/µL. Concentrations may vary depending on cell type. • The DNA amount should not exceed 10% of total volume used. • Check the purity of the purified DNA preparation by measurement of the A260/280 ratio. The ratio should be at least 1.8 for electroporation. • The device has been routinely tested with 4–7 kb plasmids and plasmids up to approximately 20 kb should not be a problem. Using plasmids larger than 20 kb will most likely lower transfection efficiency. IMPORTANT! Do not precipitate DNA with ethanol to concentrate DNA. Concentrated DNA by ethanol precipitation shows poor transfection efficiency and cell viability due to salt contamination.
siRNA quality and The quality and concentration of siRNA used for electroporation plays an amount important role for the transfection efficiency. We strongly recommend using high quality siRNA such as Stealth™, Silencer® Select, or Silencer® siRNA. • The recommended starting siRNA concentration is 100–250 µM in nuclease- free water. • The siRNA amount should not exceed 10% of total volume used.
Controls GFP control To initially assess transfection efficiency for your cell type using fluorescent microscopy, we recommend using a plasmid encoding GFP (green fluorescent protein) or any colored variant of GFP (Clontech or equivalent). For best results, the vector encoding the GFP should have the following features: • Strong promoter active in a variety of mammalian cells such as the immediate early CMV (cytomegalovirus) promoter • SV40 polyadenylation signals downstream of the GFP gene for proper processing of the 3’ end of the GFP mRNA. • Antibiotic selection marker • pUC origin of replication for propagation in E. coli siRNA control For siRNA experiments, use BLOCK-iT™ Fluorescent Oligo for electroporation or Silencer® Select GAPDH Positive Control siRNA (page 40) to assess transfection efficiency.
Neon® Transfection System 13
Using the Neon® Transfection System
Introduction Instructions are provided in this section to use the Neon® device with the Neon® Pipette Station and Neon® Kits for electroporation of mammalian cells. General instructions to prepare cells for use with the Neon® Transfection System are described below. For primary and stem cell types, use the established methods developed in the laboratory. See page 22 if you wish to use the preprogrammed optimization protocol.
Materials needed Ordering information is on page 40. • Cells • Neon® Kits • High quality DNA at a concentration of 1–5 µg/µL in deionized water or TE buffer, or high quality RNAi duplex at a concentration of 100–250 µM in nuclease-free water (page 13) • Cell culture plates containing the appropriate medium • D-PBS or Phosphate buffered saline (PBS) without Ca2+ and Mg2+ (page 40) • Trypsin/EDTA or TrypLE™ Express (Cat. no. 12563) for adherent cells • Countess® Automated Cell Counter (page 40) or equivalent
               If you are a first time user of the Neon® Transfection System, we recommend
               that you review the protocol below and ensure that you are able to insert and

Optimization protocol for DNA and siRNA
Introduction Electroporation is mainly dependent on the combination of three electric parameters such as the electric field, pulse width, and pulse number. Based on your initial results, you may need to optimize the electroporation parameters for your cell type especially the hard-to-transfect cells. The Neon® device is preprogrammed with a 24-well optimization protocol using the 10 µL or 100 µL Neon® Tip that allows you to quickly optimize electric parameters for many adherent and suspension cell lines within days. For primary blood suspension cells, use the 18-well optimization protocol with Resuspension Buffer T as described on page 26.
Materials needed Ordering information is on page 40. • Neon® 10 µL or 100 µL Kit • Cells in Resuspension Buffer (prepared as described in pages 16–17) • High quality DNA at a concentration of 1–5 µg/µL in deionized water or TE buffer or high quality RNAi duplex at a concentration of 100–250 µM in nuclease-free water (page 13) • Cell culture plates containing the appropriate medium
Workflow General workflow for optimization is described below. For detailed protocols, see the next page. Optimization for plasmid 1. Perform 24-well optimization using the preprogrammed parameters. 2. Based on results from Step 1, perform optimization using narrower (bracket) parameters. 3. Based on results from Step 2, further refine the parameters to obtain optimal conditions (this is optional step). Optimization for siRNA 1. Perform 24-well optimization using the preprogrammed parameters. 2. Based on results from Step 1, perform optimization using narrower (bracket) parameters. 3. Based on results from Step 2, perform optimization by varying siRNA final concentrations to 10 nM, 30 nM, 100 nM, and 200 nM.

Tumor_Interstitial_Fluid
A New Method for Isolation of Interstitial Fluid from Human Solid Tumors Applied to Proteomic Analysis of Ovarian Carcinoma Tissue Hanne Haslene-Hox1, Eystein Oveland1, Kaja C. Berg1, Odd Kolmannskog1, Kathrine Woie2, Helga B. Salvesen2,3, Olav Tenstad1., Helge Wiig1.* 1 Department of Biomedicine, University of Bergen, Bergen, Norway, 2 Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, Haukeland University Hospital, Bergen, Norway, 3 Department of Clinical Medicine, University of Bergen, Bergen, Norway
Abstract
Major efforts have been invested in the identification of cancer biomarkers in plasma, but the extraordinary dynamic range
in protein composition, and the dilution of disease specific proteins make discovery in plasma challenging. Focus is shifting
towards using proximal fluids for biomarker discovery, but methods to verify the isolated sample’s origin are missing. We
therefore aimed to develop a technique to search for potential candidate proteins in the proximal proteome, i.e. in the
tumor interstitial fluid, since the biomarkers are likely to be excreted or derive from the tumor microenvironment. Since
tumor interstitial fluid is not readily accessible, we applied a centrifugation method developed in experimental animals and
asked whether interstitial fluid from human tissue could be isolated, using ovarian carcinoma as a model. Exposure of
extirpated tissue to 106 g enabled tumor fluid isolation. The fluid was verified as interstitial by an isolated fluid:plasma ratio
not significantly different from 1.0 for both creatinine and Na+, two substances predominantly present in interstitial fluid.
The isolated fluid had a colloid osmotic pressure 79% of that in plasma, suggesting that there was some sieving of proteins
at the capillary wall. Using a proteomic approach we detected 769 proteins in the isolated interstitial fluid, sixfold higher
than in patient plasma. We conclude that the isolated fluid represents undiluted interstitial fluid and thus a subproteome
with high concentration of locally secreted proteins that may be detected in plasma for diagnostic, therapeutic and
prognostic monitoring by targeted methods.

In the present study we asked whether a method developed for isolation of TIF in experimental animals [13] could be translated for use in human solid tumors. As an example we used ovarian carcinoma, representing the most lethal gynecological malignancy, with the majority of cases diagnosed with metastatic disease [4]. In order to verify the origin of the isolated fluid we quantified the admixture of intracellular fluid by relating the concentration of endogenous substances present predominantly in the extracellular fluid phase in isolated fluid to that of plasma, and were able to demonstrate that such admixture was negligible. We utilized the isolated fluid to determine for the first time interstitial fluid colloid osmotic pressure in a human solid malignant tumor, and could furthermore show that such fluid is a relevant substrate in a subproteome analysis when searching for tumor specific proteins. The presented new technique may serve as a useful tool in studies of the tumor cell microenvironment.

title: Protocol_Caecum_Orthotopic_MRC
text:
PROCEDURE: Orthotopic implantation into the Caecum wall
We will use an orthotopic implantation model for colon that requires implantation of colon cancer cells into the cecum of mice, as described by Céspedes MV et al., 2007. (See Orthotopic microinjection of human colon cancer cells in nude mice induces tumor foci in all clinically relevant metastatic sites, Am J Pathol. 2007 Mar;170(3):1077-85.). We would like to evaluate how direct orthotopic cell microinjection, between the mucosa and the muscularis layers of the cecal wall of mice, drives tumor foci to the most relevant metastatic sites and impacts the immune response.
Summary: Mouse colon cancer cells (e.g., MC-38 cells) will be grown to confluence using standard aseptic cell culture technique, harvested for injection, and resuspended in serum-free DMEM at a concentration of 4 x 10^7 cells/mL. Mice will be anesthetized with ketamine/xylazine, prepared in a sterile fashion, and the cecum will be exteriorized through a middle abdominal incision. 2 x 10^6 cells in 50μl will be slowly injected into the cecum wall between the mucosa and the muscularis layers through a 250-um diameter micropippette. Animals will be euthanized after 90 days, or when they appear lethargic, whichever occurs first.
Cecum injection:

Ketamine (100 mg/kg) / Xylazine (10 mg/kg) combination will be administered via intraperitoneal injection. Depth of anesthesia will be confirmed by verifying an absence of response to ear, toe, and/or tail pinch.
After induction of anesthesia, under sterile conditions (sterile instruments, surgical PPE per policy), the middle abdomen will be shaved with an electric razor, and scrubbed with Betadine, after which the surgical site is wiped with 70% ethanol, and re-painted with Betadine.
The animal is then draped appropriately, and using sterile gloves and instruments, a middle abdominal incision will be made and a a 250-um diameter micropippette will be used to inject 50μl of cell suspension (up to 2x10^6 cells resuspended in serum-free DMEM) into the cecum wall between the mucosa and the muscularis layers under a binocular lens (23 magnification), with an approximate 30° angle and its tip introduced 5 mm into the cecal wall. The delivery of tumor cells will occur within the subserosa. Alternatively, 2-10 mm3 tumor pieces derived from subcutanous tumors will be sutured to the caecum wall using 3-0 Vicryl.
Slight pressure with a cotton stick will be done at 32 mm from the injection point in the direction of the pipette axis. The pipette is pulled out and clean the area around the injection with 3% iodine to avoid seeding of unlikely refluxed tumor cells into the abdominal cavity. Any potential bleeding will be controlled by using a cotton swab.
The wound will be closed in two layers, with running 4-0 Vicryl, and nylon or polypropylene sutures for the skin. Mice will be monitored for anesthesia withdrawal as well as an increase or change in respiratory rate and/or pattern. The length of anesthesia will be approximately 20 minutes so the variance from normothermic conditions should be minimal. A heat lamp will be used if the mice do not begin to recover and move after 20 minutes of anesthesia. Care will be taken to ensure the mice do not overheat by keeping the lamp far enough away that it is comfortable for surgeon’s hands to rest there.
Respiratory rate and depth will be monitored until mouse is able to right itself after mouse is subject to surgery. The animal is then placed back into its cage, observed until fully recovered from anesthesia, and returned to its rack.
Mice will be weighed at the time of surgery and once a week following orthotopic implantation. If an animal appears to be losing weight, then the frequency of weighing will increase to every other day. Pain will be assessed as described in IACUC guidebook, 2002ed, (http://grants.nih.gov/grants/olaw/GuideBook.pdf) and treated by analgesia Buprenorphine (0.05-0.1mg/kg) administered initially at time of surgery and then SC or IP twice daily or more frequently if pain is indicated, but no more than every 6 hours as needed for at least 48 hours. We give this with ketoprofen SC 1-2 mg/kg given before surgery and again 24 hours later. If an animal loses greater than 20% of their body weight, or if it appears that the animal is in distress as outlined by the criteria above in “monitoring of clinical signs”, it will be euthanized prior to the planned time point.

Significant differences between groups will be determined using a Student’sttest (two-tailed unpaired) when the data met the normal distribution tested by the D’Agostino test. If the data does not meet this test, a Mann-Whitney test will be used.

title: LLB_GutPrep2017
text:
Lara Labarta-Bajo (Zuniga Lab) - Protocol is a combination of the Surh lab and Goldrath lab protocols
Materials:
- Hot-plate stirrer (Scilogex)
- Tissue chopper - McIlwain tissue chopper
- 50ml pyrex conicals
- Stirring magnets
- Stripping buffer:
PBS1x + 3% FBS + 10mM EDTA + 20mM HEPES + Pen/Strep (100u/ml pen, 100ug/ml strep), 1mM Na-pyruvate
- Enzyme media:
RPMI + 3% FBS, 20mM HEPES, Pen/Strep (100u/ml pen, 100ug/ml strep), 1mM Na-pyruvate +*on day of harvest add
0.4mg/ml Collagenase D (Roche) and DNAse I 10ug/ml (Roche)
- Percoll 100% (9 parts of Percoll from commercial bottle + 1 part of PBS 10x)
d-1 Prepare:
- Rinse 50ml conicals with ddw
- Prepare stripping buffer (30ml/sample per IEL).
- Prepare RPMI 5% FBS (as re-suspension media)
- Prepare PBS 5% FBS (to wash)
- Prepare enzyme media w/o enzymes (20ml per sample)
d0 Harvest
- Turn on stirrer and set at 37ºC
- Put stripping buffer at 37ºC
- Enzyme media at 37ºC
- Set centrifuge at RT. Pull out Percoll and keep at RT
- Set up big collection container (waste)
- Thaw collagenase and DNase at RT
- Collect SI and colon, remove fat (cotton swabs are useful), remove PP’s, empty fecal contents by gently pressing it down with your scissors. Cut it longitudinally, fold and cut in 1cm pieces. 
*Keep tissues in PBS- they should never be dry
- Wash x3 with PBS5% directly into 50ml Pyrex conical
- Add 30ml Stripping buffer and stir for 20min at 37ºC
- Shake a bit and collect soup (these are your IEL!) into 50ml falcon. Add RPMBI5% to Pyrex conical and collect some more. Add RPMI5% up to 50ml in conical and keep on ice until Percoll.
- Wash remaining tissue in PBS5% once and strain through tea strainer
- Pick gut pieces and Chop 2x with tissue chopper and add to 30ml enzyme media (in pyrex conical)
- Stir for 45min at 37ºC
- Pipette up and down 3 times with automatic pipette (10ml glass pipette) and
- Filter through cell strainer & spin down
- Re-suspend in 5ml 44% Percoll then add up to 2ml of 67% Percoll below
- Spin 20min 2,000 rpm (NO brake) and collect interphase with Pasteur pipette
- Collect interphase in 15ml falcon tubes, fill up with 5%RPMI and spin down at 2,000rpm for 8min.
- Re-suspend pellet in desired counting volume and continue with your staining.

Number of assays: Each kit provides sufficient reagents for approximately 500 assays using a fluorescence microplate reader and reaction volumes of 100 μL per assay, based on the protocol below.
Approximate fluorescence excitation/emission maxima: Amplex® Red reagent: ~571/585 in nm. * 1 unit = the amount of enzyme that will form 1.0 mg purpurogallin from pyrogallol in 20 seconds at pH 6.0 at 20°C. † 1 unit = the amount of enzyme that will oxidize 1.0 μmole of cholesterol to 4-cholesten-3-one per minute at pH 7.5 at 25°C. ‡ 1 unit = the amount of enzyme that will will hydrolyze 1.0 μmole of cholesteryl oleate to cholesterol and oleic acid per minute at pH 7.0 in the presence of taurocholate.
MAN0002087 Revised: 05–May–2010 | MP 12216
Introduction
           The Amplex® Red Cholesterol Assay Kit provides a simple fluorometric method for the
           sensitive quantitation of cholesterol using a fluorescence microplate reader or fluorometer.
           Because a large portion of cholesterol in blood is in the form of cholesteryl esters, the assay
           is based on an enzyme-coupled reaction that detects both free cholesterol and cholesteryl
           esters. Cholesteryl esters are hydrolyzed by cholesterol esterase into cholesterol, which is
           then oxidized by cholesterol oxidase to yield H2O2 and the corresponding ketone product.
           The H2O2 is then detected using 10-acetyl-3,7-dihydroxyphenoxazine (Amplex® Red reagent),
           a highly sensitive and stable probe for H2O2.1 In the presence of horseradish peroxidase
           (HRP), Amplex® Red reagent reacts with H2O2 with a 1:1 stoichiometry to produce highly
           fluorescent resorufin.1,2 Because resorufin has absorption and fluorescence emission maxima
           of approximately 571 nm and 585 nm, respectively (Figure 1), there is little interference from
           autofluorescence in most biological samples.

           The Amplex® Red cholesterol assay can detect cholesterol at a concentration of 200 nM
           (80 ng/mL) or lower (Figure 2) and can accurately measure the cholesterol content in the
           equivalent of 0.01 μL of human serum.3 Because the assay is continuous and requires no
           separation steps, the procedure is particularly well suited to the rapid and direct analysis of
           cholesterol in blood and food samples using automated instruments. By performing reactions
           in the presence and absence of cholesterol esterase, the assay is also potentially useful for
           determining the fraction of cholesterol that is in the form of cholesteryl esters within a
           sample. In addition, the assay can be adapted to detect the activity of cholesterol oxidase by
           providing an excess of cholesterol in the reaction.3

                                            reaction contained 150 μM Amplex® Red reagent, 1 U/mL HRP, 1 U/mL cholesterol
                                            oxidase, 0.1 μM cholesterol esterase and the indicated amount of the cholesterol in 1X
                                            Reaction Buffer. Reactions were incubated at 37°C for 30 minutes. Fluorescence was
                                            measured with a fluorescence microplate reader using excitation at 560 ± 10 nm and

Before Starting
Materials Required But Not Provided • Deionized water (dH2O)
   Storage and Handling         • Upon receipt, the kit should be stored frozen at ≤–20°C, protected from light. Stored
                                  properly, the kit components should remain stable for at least six months.
                                • Allow reagents to warm to room temperature before opening vials.
                                • The Amplex® Red reagent is somewhat air sensitive. Once a vial of Amplex® Red reagent is
                                  opened, the reagent should be used promptly.
                                • Protect the Amplex® Red reagent from light.


                 Caution        DMSO is known to facilitate the entry of organic molecules into tissues. Handle reagents
                                containing DMSO (e.g., Amplex® UltraRed reagent stock solution in DMSO) using equipment
                                and practices appropriate for the hazards posed by such materials. Dispose off the reagents in
                                compliance with all pertaining local regulations.



     Preparing Solutions
                                20 mM Amplex® Red reagent stock solution

                            1.1 To prepare a 20 mM stock solution of Amplex® Red reagent, allow one vial of Amplex® Red
                                reagent (Component A) and the DMSO (Component B) to warm to room temperature.
                                Immediately prior to use, dissolve the contents of the vial of Amplex® Red reagent (1 mg) in
                                200 μL DMSO. Each vial of Amplex® Red reagent is sufficient for approximately 250 assays,
                                with a final reaction volume of 100 μL per assay. Store the stock solution frozen at ≤–20°C,
                                protected from light.




                                                                                                    Amplex® Red Cholesterol Assay Kit | 3

                              1X Reaction Buffer working solution
                          1.2 To prepare a 1X working solution of Reaction Buffer, add 2.5 mL of 5X Reaction Buffer
                              stock solution (Component E) to 10 mL of deionized water (dH2O). This 12.5 mL volume of
                              1X Reaction Buffer is sufficient This 12.5 mL volume of 1X Reaction Buffer is sufficient for
                              approximately 100 assays of 100 μL each, with a 2.5 mL excess for making stock solutions and
                              dilutions.

                              200 U/mL horseradish peroxidase (HRP) stock solution
                          1.3 To prepare a 200 U/mL stock solution of horseradish peroxidase (HRP), dissolve the contents
                              of the vial of HRP (Component C) in 1 mL of 1X Reaction Buffer. After use, divide the
                              remaining solution into small aliquots and store frozen at ≤–20°C.

                              20 mM H2O2 working solution
                          1.4 To prepare a 20 mM H2O2 working solution, dilute the ~3% H2O2 stock solution
                              (Component D) into the appropriate volume of dH2O. The actual H2O2 concentration is
                              indicated on the component label. For instance, a 20 mM H2O2 working solution can be
                              prepared from a 3.0% H2O2 stock solution by diluting 23 μL of 3.0% H2O2 into 977 μL of
                              dH2O.

                              Note: Although the ~3% H2O2 stock solution has been stabilized to slow its degradation, the
                              20 mM H2O2 working solution is less stable and should be used promptly.

                              200 U/mL cholesterol oxidase stock solution
                          1.5 To prepare a 200 U/mL solution of cholesterol oxidase, dissolve the entire vial of cholesterol
                              oxidase (Component F) in 250 μL of 1X Reaction Buffer. After use, divide the remaining
                              solution into small aliquots and store frozen at ≤–20°C.

                              Note: The cholesterol oxidase solution may appear cloudy. This does not interfere with the
                              assay.

                              200 U/mL cholesterol esterase stock solution
                          1.6 To prepare a 200 U/mL stock solution of cholesterol esterase, dissolve tthe entire vial of
                              cholesterol esterase (Component G) in 250 μL of 1X Reaction Buffer. Cholesterol esterase is
                              added to the reaction to allow detection of cholesterol in the form of cholesteryl esters. After
                              use, divide the remaining solution into small aliquots and store frozen at ≤–20°C.

                              2 mM resorufin stock solution
                          1.7 To prepare a 2 mM stock solution of resorufin, add 1 mL dH2O directly to the vial of
                              resorufin solid (Component I). This solution can be used to prepare a standard curve to
                              determine the moles of product produced in the Amplex® Red reaction. Store the resorufin
                              stock solution frozen at ≤–20°C, protected from light.
Experimental Protocols
 General Considerations       • The following procedure is designed for use with a fluorescence multiwell plate reader. For
                                use with a standard fluorometer, volumes must be increased accordingly.
                              • The product of the Amplex® Red reaction is unstable in the presence of thiols such
                                as dithiothreitol (DTT) or 2-mercaptoethanol. For this reason, the final DTT or
                                2-mercaptoethanol concentration in the reaction should be no higher than 10 μM.




                                                                                      Amplex® Red Cholesterol Assay Kit | 4

                    • The absorption and fluorescence of resorufin are pH-dependent. Below the pKa (~6.0), the
                      absorption maximum shifts to ~480 nm and the fluorescence quantum yield is markedly
                      lower. In addition, the Amplex® Red reagent is unstable at high pH (>8.5). For these
                      reasons, the reaction should be performed at pH 7–8.
                    • We recommend using the included Reaction Buffer (pH 7.4) for optimal performance of
                      the Amplex® Red reagent.
Cholesterol Assay The following protocol describes the cholesterol assay in a total volume of 100 μL per microplate well. The volumes recommended here are sufficient for ~100 assays.
                2.1 Prepare a cholesterol standard curve: Dilute the appropriate amount of 2 mg/mL (5.17 mM)
                    cholesterol reference standard (Component H) into 1X Reaction Buffer to produce
                    cholesterol concentrations of 0 to 8 μg/mL (0 to ~20 μM). Use 1X Reaction Buffer without
                    cholesterol as a negative control. A volume of 50 μL will be used for each reaction.

                    Note: The cholesterol concentrations will be two-fold lower in the final reaction volume.
                    The cholesteryl esters are digested by cholesterol esterase to free cholesterol, which is then
                    detected in the enzyme-coupled reaction with Amplex® Red reagent. The solution has been
                    calibrated to yield the equivalent of 2 mg/mL cholesterol.

                2.2 Dilute the cholesterol-containing samples in 1X Reaction Buffer. A volume of 50 μL will be
                    used for each reaction.

                2.3 Prepare a positive control by diluting the 20 mM H2O2 working solution to 10 μM in 1X
                    Reaction Buffer.

                2.4 Pipet 50 μL of the diluted samples and controls into separate wells of a microplate.

                2.5 Prepare a working solution of 300 μM Amplex® Red reagent containing 2 U/mL HRP,
                    2 U/mL cholesterol oxidase, and 0.2 U/mL cholesterol esterase by adding 75 μL of Amplex®
                    Red reagent stock solution (prepared in step 1.1), 50 μL of the HRP stock solution (prepared
                    in step 1.3), 50 μL of the cholesterol oxidase stock solution (prepared in step 1.5), and 5 μL
                    of the cholesterol esterase stock solution (prepared in step 1.6) to 4.82 mL of 1X Reaction
                    Buffer. This 5 mL volume is sufficient for ~100 assays.

                    Note: Final concentrations of each component will be two-fold lower in the final reaction
                    volume.

                2.6 Begin the reactions by adding 50 μL of the Amplex® Red reagent/HRP/cholesterol oxidase/
                    cholesterol esterase working solution to each microplate well containing the samples and
                    controls.

                2.7 Incubate the reactions for 30 minutes or longer at 37°C, protected from light. Because the
                    assay is continuous (not terminated), you may measure fluorescence at multiple time points
                    to follow the kinetics of the reactions.

                2.8 If desired, prepare a resorufin standard curve: Dilute the appropriate amount of 2 mM
                    resorufin stock solution in 1X Reaction Buffer to yield resorufin solution ranging from 0 to
                    20 μM resorufin. Pipet 100 μL of each resorufin standard into individual (empty) wells of a
                    microplate at any time prior to measuring fluorescence.

                2.9 Measure the fluorescence in a fluorescence microplate reader using excitation in the range of
                    530–560 nm and emission detection at ~590 nm (see Figure 1).

            2.10 For each point, correct for background fluorescence by subtracting the values derived from
                 the no-cholesterol control.




                                                                            Amplex® Red Cholesterol Assay Kit | 5

text:
Retroviral transduction of CD8+ T cells

Have virus ready or start making virus following our protocol at day -1.
Day 1 (4-5pm). Anti-CD3/anti-CD28 stimulation
Purify CD8s by negative selection – Follow our protocol
Day 2 (3-4pm). Retroviral Transduction (24hours post stimulation; mitotic phase is 22-26 hrs post stim, which is the optimal time for transduction)

*Pre spin centrifuge at 4000rpm, 40C– to get it up to 37C or as close to it as possible


*If making virus: Collect viral media and filter with a 0.45 um syringe filter to remove cell debris (alternatively centrifuge at 3000 rpm 10 min). Store it at -80 C.

*If virus was stored at -80, pre-warm at 37C.

Remove ~1.8 ml of media (from the 2ml on the 6well plate). And set it aside for after spin infection.
Add 1 mL viral media (filtered) supplemented with 8ug/ml polybrene (1/1000) and BME 50 mM (1/1000) to each well. Double polybrene if double transduction (1/500).
Spin at 2000 rpm for 60 min at 37° (or as close as practical) to infect cells (120 min for double transduction).
Place them in the incubator for 2h.
Remove ~900 uL of viral media or aspirate, and replace with 2 mL old CD3/CD28 activation media + 2ml of fresh TCM media. Put in incubator.

Day 3 (8-9am) - Add IL-2 (10 ng/mL r-human IL-2),

Pool CD8 T cells from the 6 well plates into a 50 ml conical and centrifuge 1600 rpm 5 min.
Resuspend in 20 ml of TCM media containing 10 ng/ml r-human IL-2 and transfer to T75 flask
Day 4 (5-6pm). Transfer activated T cells




Wash CD8 T cells from the flask in cold PBS 2x




Resuspend in 1ml an count them in the hemocytometer

(D10): DMEM, 10%v/v FBS, 1% v/v L-glut or “Glutamax”, 1% v/vPen/Strep

5 ml 1% v/v Glutamax,
5 ml 1% v/v P/S,
5ml 1% v/v NEAA,
5 ml 1% v/v NaPy,
500 ul BME 50uM ( stock 50 mM)

title: STAINING PROTOCOL FOR FLOW
text:
STAINING PROTOCOL FOR FLOW
- Obtain your cells after TIL isolation
- Count them
- Pellet cells you want to stain onto a 96-well plate. For staining it is always best to use a U-bottom or a V-bottom plate, rather than flat-bottom plates.
1) L/D staining: re-suspend cells at 100 million cells/ml* (it will be around 25-50ul per sample) in 1xPBS + 1/1000 Live/Dead dye. 
Note: if you are staining a spleen or an organ with lots of cells, stain 5 million cells. If you were looking at rare, non-abundant populations you would have to stain 10 million or more. 
Note*: staining concentrations of up to 200milion cells/ml will work just fine.
2) Incubate for 10min on ice (or at 4C) (in the dark)
3) After the 10 min, add 200ul of PBS1x+3%FBS (no need to re-suspend), and spin down 1,500rpm 5min. Flick plate to remove SNT (this is just a washing step)
4) Add surface antibody mix**, re-suspend pellets and incubate for 20min on ice (or at 4C) and in the dark. After that, add 200ul of PBS1x+3%FBS (no need to re-suspend), and spin down 1,500rpm 5min. Flick plate.
   - **Surface antibody mix consists of surface antibodies diluted in Facs buffer.
5) Re-suspend pellet in 25-50ul of Foxp3 fix solution (contains 1 part of fixation/permeabilization concentrate + 3 parts of fixation/permeabilization diluent - make it fresh every time you need it). Incubate for at least 30min (and up to overnight). 
6) Add 200ul of PBS1x+3%FBS (no need to re-suspend), and spin down at 2,000 rpm for 5min (you can spin down faster now because your cells are dead). Flick plate. 
   - Add 250ul PBS1x and leave cells like that if you want to leave them overnight.
7) On the next day (or same day after fixation), spin down at 2,000rpm 3-5min, flick to remove SNT.
8) Re-suspend cells in antibody mix containing intracellular and intranuclear antibodies. IMPORTANT: this antibody mix has to be made in 1X Permeabilization buffer (it is made of the detergent saponin, that will reversibly permeabilize the membrane to allow antibodies to go in). To make 1X permeabilization buffer, dilute 10XPermeabilization buffer (brown color) in ddw. 
9) Incubate cells with intracellular/intranuclear antibodies in 1XPerm buffer for 30min-1h at room temp. Note: standard staining time for intracellular antibodies (such as cytokines, granzymes) is typically 30min and for transcription factors is 1h. I personally tend to mix all of them in my stainings, so I end up staining everything for 1h at RT (and it looks great).
**Some tips for this protocol:
- To ensure intracel/intranuclear antibodies give me the brightest signal, I always stain for them the day I will run FACS. 
- If you are only doing intracellular staining for proteins that are in the cytoplasm, the Foxp3 ebio kit is not required. It would be enough to, after L/D and surface stain, to fix your cells for 10min in 1% PFA (in PBS1x), wash it off, then leave in PBS1x overnight until you are ready to stain intracellularly. Then, stain intracellularly in saponin solution (1XPerm buffer) for 30min-1h at RT (I prefer 1h)
- If you follow the vendor’s protocol for intracellular/intranuclear staining kits, they typically add washing steps with the saponin. I personally never do them because 1) you lose cells the more you wash/flick, 2) vendors try to make you use more reagent so that you have to re-stock faster.

title: MYCO_PCR

MYCO-PCR
MRC 10/2019
Order Primers
You will need to order multiple forward and reverse primers to detect multiple species of mycoplasma.
Forward primers

   Myco-5-1   CGCCTGAGTAGTACGTTCGC
   Myco-5-2  CGCCTGAGTAGTACGTACGC
   Myco-5-3  TGCCTGAGTAGTACATTCGC
   Myco-5-4  TGCCTGGGTAGTACATTCGC
   Myco-5-5  CGCCTGGGTAGTACATTCGC
   Myco-5-6  CGCCTGAGTAGTATGCTCGC

 Reverse primers

   Myco-3-1  GCGGTGTGTACAAGACCCGA
   Myco-3-2  GCGGTGTGTACAAAACCCGA
   Myco-3-3  GCGGTGTGTACAAACCCCGA

Prepare Primer Mix
Dissolve each primer to a final concentration of 100 µM. Mix all forward primers together to reach a final concentration of 10 µM each. For example, if you want to prepare 100 µl primer mix, take 10 µl of each forward primer and add 40 µl of water. Mix all reverse primers in a similar fashion.
Prepare Sample
Take 100 µl of cell culture supernatant from a dense culture (80-100% confluent) into a 1.5ml tube (or media, sera, whatever you want to test). Heat the sample for 5 min at 95°C (to denaturate it) and spin it for 2min in a bench centrifuge at maximum speed.
Set up PCR
Prepare the PCR reaction mix using the following table (may need some adjustment depending on the manufacturer). Remember to include a negative control sample with water to exclude false positives and a positive control if you have one (If you identify an infected culture you can also use this supernatant as a positive control.)

title: Cell Trace Violet labeling
text:
Cell Trace Violet labeling

Prepare CTV stock by adding 20ul DMSO to one vial of reagent.
Warm cells in PBS (w/o Ca++ and Mg++) for 10min at 37’C
Dilute cells to 10x10^6cells/ml
Add 1ul of CTV in DMSO to each ml of cell suspension in PBS.
Vortex gently to ensure equal exposure to dye
Incubate cells for 20min at 37’C in the dark
Add 5X of staining volume of culture medium containing at least 1% protein to cells. Incubate for 5 min.
Pellet cells by centrifugation and wash 2X
Resuspend and plate out.

title: Genotyping PCR info
text:
Genotyping PCR info
Vhl flox
The following primers were used to detect 1-lox and 2-lox alleles of Vhlh: FwdI (5′-CTGGTACCCACGAAACTGTC-3′), FwdII (5′-CTAGGCACCGAGCTTAGAGGTTTGCG-3′), and Rev primer (5′-CTGACTTCCACTGATGCTTGT CACAG-3′). The Vhlh 2-lox allele was identified as a ∼460-bp band, the 1-lox allele was detected as a ∼260-bp band, and the wild-type allele was detected as a ∼290-bp band.
For some reason we only use the two highlighted primers. I assume because we’re not attempting to detect the ~260 bp band of the 1-lox allele.
These are also different from the JAX PCR primers will generate similar product sizes though. Although JAX PCR protocol does not utilize 3 primers.
hif1a flox
Hif-1α 1-lox and 2-loxalleles were detected with following primers: Fwd1 (5′-TTGGGGATGAAAACATCTGC-3′), Fwd2 (5′-GCAGTTAAGAGCACTAGTTG-3′), and Rev (5′-GGAGCTATCTCTCTAGACC-3′). The wild-type allele was identified as a ∼240-bp band, the 2-lox allele was detected as a ∼260-bp band, and 1-loxallele was detected as a ∼270-bp band.
Same for the HIF1a PCR, we for some reason do not check for the 1-lox allele which is approximately 270 bp
hif2a flox
The WT, 2-loxP, and 1-loxP allele can be distinguished by a multiplex PCR [primer (P) 1: 5′-CAGGCAGTATGCCTGGCTAATTCCAGTT-3′; P2: 5′-CTTCTTCCATCATCTGGGATCTGGGACT-3′; P3: 5′-GCTAACACTGTACTGTCTGAAAGAGTAGC-3′]. The WT allele produces a 410-bp fragment (P1 and P2), the 2-loxP allele produces a 444-bp fragment (P1 and P2), and the 1-loxP allele produces a 340-bp fragment (P1 and P3)
Andrew ordered truncated versions of these primers, which are different than the genotyping primers suggested on the jax website. These are labeled as hif2380, hif2 381, and hif2430.
Have had issues with these primers so will order the Jax pair of primers as well, will label these HIF2FJax and HIF2RJax.
HIF2FJax: 5’ GAG AGC AGC TTC TCC TGG AA 3’
HIF2RJax: 5’ TGT AGG CAA GGA AAC CAA GG 3’
Yields different band sizes as follows:
Mutant = ~220 bp
Heterozygote = 182 bp and ~220 bp
Wild type = 182 bp

title: RNA extraction using Trizol
text:
RNA extraction with Trizol (adapted from Kyla Omilusik)


Thaw Trizol sample at RT.


Add 2ul glycoblue


Add chloroform


For 500ul Trizol, use 100ul chloroform
For 1000ul Trizol, use 200ul chloroform


Shake vigorously for approx 15s


Incubate 2-3 min at RT


Centrifuge 15 min at 12000g, 4C


Carefully transfer aqueous phase to a fresh tube (work on ice from this point)


Pipet in circular motion, avoid interphase by leaving generous amount of aqueous phase
For 500ul Trizol, transfer ~250ul
For 1ml Trizol, transfer ~500ul


Add isopropanol (flick, do not pipette)


For 500ul Trizol, add 250ul isopropanol
For 1ml Trizol, add 500ul isopropanol


Centrifuge 20 min at 12,000g, 4C


Then remove supernatant with pipette tip


Wash with 1ml cold 75% EtOH (make fresh using DNAse/RNAse-free water)


Flick to loose pellet


Centrifuge 15 min at 7,400g, 4C


Pipette of as much EtOH as possible. Use 10ul micropipettor for small volume
Dry 10-15 min


Resuspend RNA pellet in 10ul nuclease-free water


Incubate 10-15 min at 55-60C.


Optional: DNAse I digestion (from Turbo DNA-free procedure)


Add 1ul 10X Turbo Dnase buffer and 1ul Turbo Dnase to sample. Mix gently.


Incubate 20-30 min at 37C


Add 2ul of resuspended DNA Inactivation Reagent and mix well.


Incubate 5 min, RT. Mix occasionally.


Centrifuge 1.5 min at 10,000g


Transfer the supernatant to a fresh tube. Avoid pellet.

title: Th differentiation in vitro
text:
Th cell differentiation in vitro protocol
Antibodies and reagents
Media is RPMI 1640 (for Th1 and Th2) or IMDM (for Th17) supplemented with 10% FBS, 0.5% penicillin/streptomycin, 2 mM L-glutamine, 1 mM sodium pyruvate, 10 mM Hepes, non-essential amino acids and 50 μM β-Mercaptoethanol.
Mouse specific anti-CD3 (2C11), anti-CD28 (PV1) and anti-IFNγ (R4/GA2) antibodies were from Bio Express (West Lebanon, NH, USA). Human IL-2 was from NCI Biological Resources Branch (Frederick, MD, USA). Mouse IL-4, IL-12 and IL23 and mouse-specific anti-IL-4 (11B11) antibody were from eBioscience. Mouse IL-6 and human TGF-β1 were from R&D Systems.
Helper T cell (Th) differentiation
Coat a 24-well plate O/N @ 4 °C with 1 μg/ml anti-CD3 and 2 μg/ml anti-CD28 antibodies. This is Day -1!
Prior to use wash once with sterile PBS.
Naïve T cells were isolated from mouse spleens and lymph nodes using the CD4+CD62L+ MACS kit from Myltenyi Biotec (Bergisch Gladbach, Germany) and seeded into plates anti-CD3/anti-CD28 coated plates @ 106/ml in 2ml/well. This is Day 0!
Helper T cell differentiation was induced by the following reagents:
- for Th1 in complete RPMI:
IL-2 (100 u/ml),
IL-12 (10 ng/ml) and
anti-IL-4 antibody (10 μg/ml);
- for Th2 in complete RPMI:
IL-2 (100 u/ml),
IL-4 (10 ng/ml) and
anti-IFNγ antibody (10 μg/ml).
On Day 3, expand each well of Th2 into a well of a 6-well plate containing 2 more ml of fresh media with IL-2 (same as above). Pool 2 wells of Th1 into a well of a 6-well plate containing 2 more ml of fresh media with IL-2 (same as above).
Th1 and Th2 cells were analyzed on Day 5 or Day 7.
Th17 were grown in complete IMDM with IL-6 (20 ng/ml), IL-23 (10 ng/ml), TGF-β1 (0.3 ng/ml), anti-IL-4 antibody (10 μg/ml) and anti-IFNγ antibody (10 μg/ml).
Th17 cells were analyzed on Day 4 (no pooling or change of media necessary!).
Th cell analysis
Cells can be analyzed before re-stimulation (“naïve” Th1, 2 or 17 cells) or after re-stim – the re-stim can be done with either anti-CD3 (can be coated on a plate (preffered) or added in solution; no anti-CD28 is necessary at this step!) or with PMA (50 ng/ml) plus Ionomycin (1 μM), depending on which function is analyzed!
Typically, PMA/I stim is used if cells are analyzed for intracellular cytokines for FACS (5h @ 37 °C stim – add Brefeldin A for entire duration of stim! Follow intracellular cytokine FACS protocol afterwards!), and anti-CD3 stim is used for cytokine analysis by ELISA (24 h @ °C stim).

title: Fetal Liver Chimeras
text:
Fetal Liver Chimeras
Day 1:

Any timed mating females pregnant on day E14-14.5 can be used.
Sac pregnant female and remove both horns of the uterus from the abdominal cavity.
Cut along the bottom of the horns, avoiding blood from the surrounding vessels (this is maternal blood and can contaminate the fetal samples). Place uterus in a petri dish with RP5 media to rinse.
Remove the embryos from the uterus and amniotic sac. This is most easily done with forceps. Be careful to keep the embryo intact and to avoid contamination with maternal blood.
Place separated embryos in another petri dish with media to rinse.
Store each embryo in a 12 or 24 well plate in a couple of mLs of RP5. Wrap the edges of the plate in parafilm and store at 4C. Be careful to avoid knocking the plate over.
For genotyping take a hand or foot from each embryo. PCRs must be completed as soon as possible.

Day 2:

Remove the fetal liver (using forceps) and place in 500ul of RP5. Be more concerned with getting all of the liver cells, extra tissue taken during this step will be filtered out later.
Pipet up and down vigorously to resuspend the liver cells. Filter sample into a new tube.
Use 5ul to count cells and 5ul to stain for congenic markers (CD45.1 and CD45.2).
When staining fetal liver ALWAYS Fc block for five minutes and stain the cells for a full 15. It’s usually hard to see 45.1 and 45.2 positive cells at this stage.
Select recipient mice based on congenic markers. Mice should be no younger than four weeks, six is better. Males preferable
Irradiate recipient mice with 1000 rad (900 if they are really small).
Process RAGko bone marrow in media (Id2ko mice have a defect in APCs so we use RAGko cells to solve this problem).
Each mouse should receive an absolute minimum of 3x10^6 fetal liver cells. 5x10^6 is optimal. Even up to 10x10^6 is fine. However, normalize the number of fetal liver cells per mouse for each group (EG: make sure recipients getting KO cells get the same number of cells as recipients getting WT cells). Add 1/10th the number of RAGko bone marrow cells (EG: if you’re injecting 5x10^6 fetal liver cells add 5x10^5 RAGko bone marrow cells).
Wash the cells with sterile PBS (media can cause rejection. However, since the mice have been irradiated if you have very few cells you can skip this step). Resuspend in correct amount of PBS (each mouse should receive it’s cells in 200ul).
Inject cells ASAP into the tail veins of recipient mice (cells don’t do too well in PBS for long periods of time).
Recipient mice should receive antibiotics in their drinking water for 2 weeks (changed weekly).

title: LP Isolation (updated April 2012)
Liver Preparation Protocol
text:
Liver Preparation Protocol
1. Chop livers into small pieces with a razor blade. Push liver pieces through a 70um filter into a 50ml conical tube using plenty of 5% BGS + PBS to wash through. Push through using the bottom of a syringe.
2. Wash all liver cells twice in 40 mL PBS+5% BGS. Spin at 1600rpm for 8 minutes each time (centrifuge should be at room temp). The second washing step is actually worthwhile as it leads to better separation.
3. Spin cells in 25 mL 37% Percoll at 1750rpm for 25 minutes. To make a Percoll working solution, add 8.5ml Percoll to 16.5ml PBS (25ml total).
4. At this point the lymphocytes will be at the bottom of the conical with a layer of hepatocytes near the top of the gradient. You can aspirate off the hepatocytes at this point and proceed with the lymphocytes as normal.
5. Ack the lymphocytes. I normally do this for 2-3 minutes, as the erythrocytes are hard to get rid of in the liver. I resuspend in 250ul 5% BGS in order to count the cells.
6. Stain as normal.

title: Listeria production-KPC
text:
Listeria production for Infection
Do everything in a BSL2 TC hood.

Thaw a frozen stock from -80oC- 2nd shelf, 1st rack. (I usually stick in a 37 degree H20 bath).
Dilute 1:50 in tryptic soy broth (no more than 1 month old). For 5 ml broth, use 100ul listeria stock.
Grow in 50ml conical. Do not cap conical tightly as air needs to circulate. Secure loose cap with tape. Put biohazard sticker on tube, and put a sign on the shaker as well, warning about biohazard.
Grow in bacterial shaker at 37 oC until you reach OD600 of approx. 0.1 (this is mid log phase) then stick culture on ice to stop growth. Anything between .09-.11 is OK.

At a 1:50 dilution of the frozen stock this usually takes between 1.5 and 2.5 hours.
Use disposable plastic 1 ml cuvettes to OD bugs. Parafilm around the top of them before carrying out of the hood.
Take an aliquot of tryptic broth alone for control.

Calculate concentration of listeria. An OD600 of 0.1=2x10e8 cfu/ml. Calculate appropriate ratio. Final concentration should be 5000 cfu/mouse in 200ul. That is 2.5 x 10^4 pfu/ml.


0.1 / 2x10e8 cfe = your O.D / cfe
Usually should have to perform a dilution in the range of about 1:7000. Anything a lot lower or higher is probably incorrect. Since the dilution ratio is so high, perform serial dilution. Do not attempt to dilute entire 5ml of listeria.


Perform serial dilutions in sterile PBS to inject.

If OD yields concentration of 2.52 x 10^8 cfu/ml, do a 1:100 dilution.

Take 10ul in 990ul RPMI- concentration now is 2.52 x 10^6 cfu/ml

Then from diluted stock, do 1:100 dilution again.

Take the total dilution you have to do and divide by the dilution you already did. That is the rest of the dilution you have to do. Take 80ul of diluted stock and add to 7920ul RPMI. This is the 2nd 1:100 dilution, which should result in 2.52 x 10^4 cfu/ml. Now you can use this to infect.


5000 cfu iv for B6 mice (for balbs the typical dose is 2000). Peak CD8 response for primary is day 7. I often got about 8-13% of CD8s in the spleen responding by tetramer or IFNg.
Bleach all tips and pipets, etc in 10% bleach before disposing as biohazard. When I do FACS staining of cells from infected mice, I flick plates into a 2 L beaker with bleach in the bottom and always use a plate with a lid (until fixed of course). I know this is overkill compared to Bevan Lab procedures, but there’s always someone pregnant around here!

title: Guava Instructions

Guava User Instructions
Hello Guava users, if you use the Guava for any amount of samples (even ONE), you must clean the machine afterwards.
For a few samples (5 or less):

For 5 or more samples:
-A long clean must be done after counting

title: RNP_Electroporation_Protocol_GoldrathLab
text:
Cas9 RNP Electroporation Protocol (Seki and Rutt, JEM, 2018)_v2.4
Generated by Katia Faliti
Modified by Jinyong Choi
Re-Modified by Tianda Deng*
*Note: I chose to leave in some components (colored gray) that aren’t necessarily relevant to us now, but could potentially be utilized in the future. So if you’re confused by things that don’t really pertain to you, don’t worry.
Materials

Spleen + I.Ns C57BL/6 mouse.
For activated CD4 T cells:
0.5 x 106 cells/ml
8 ug/ml anti-CD3 (clone l45-2c11, BD)
8 ug/ml anti-CD28 (clone 37.51)
Pre-activation for 2 days before transfection.
For resting CD4 T cells:
Preincubated with 2 ng/ ml rhlL-7 for 24h before transfection.
crRNA and tracrRNA from IDT:
Alt-R CRISPR-Cas9 TracrRNA
Alt-R CRISPR-Cas9 TracrRNA-ATTO 550
(ATTO 550: a fluorochrome excited by yellow laser, PE channel)
Alt-R CRISPR-Cas9 crRNA NTC negative control
Cas9 Protein
IDT Cas9 v3 (10 mg/ml) or
TrueCut Cas9 Protein v2 (5 mg/ml; Invitrogen) or
Cas9 (6.4 mg/ml; QB3 Berkley Lab) *We use this one, it is greatly discounted for UCs.
Neon Transfection System
Neon Transfection System 100uL Kit

Catalog #: MPK10096
*Crispr Guide Design

I use CHOPCHOP for guide design: https://chopchop.cbu.uib.no/ because I think it’s simple to use, there are many alternatives (just google “crispr guide generator”)
When ordering crRNA from IDT, you can check your guides again on their website
Make sure to order crRNA and NOT sgRNA. To learn the difference on more on RNPs, this is a great resource: https://www.idtdna.com/pages/education/decoded/article/crispr-guide-rna-format-affects-genome-editing-outcomes

(Optional if you start from IVT) Preparation of In Vitro Transcription
A 0.3 uM target oligonucleotide mix working solution was prepared by diluting l uL of each target oligonucleotide stock solution (10 uM) in 32 uL nuclease free water.
Use GeneArt Precision gRNA Synthesis kit:
PCR reaction in 25 uL in the following order:

12.5 uL Phusion HF PCR Master Mix 2X
1 uL Tracr Fragment + T7 Primer Mix
1 uL 0.3 uM Target F1/R1 oligonucleotide mix
10.5 uL nuclease-free water

PCR cycles:

Denaturation 98 °C, 10 sec
Denaturation 32 cycles at 98 °C, 5 sec
Annealing at 55 °C, 15 sec
Extension at 72 °C, I min

Purify the PCR products from agarose gel.
16-24 ng for PCR product was used in the IVT reaction (MegaShortScripts T7 Kit), following the instruction.
Incubation at 37 °C for 4 h.
Add 1 uL of Turbo DNAse to the reaction to remove DNA template. Incubate 37 °C for 15 min.
sgRNA was purified using the GeneArt precision kit and eluted in 40 uL RNAse-free water.
(D0)
Isolation SM CD4 T cells and stimulation
Activate with anti-CD3 and anti-CD28 (We have an activation protocol on the server)
*I personally like using 6 well plates for activation and seed between 1-2x106 cells/well.
(D2)
Preparation of crRNA-tracrRNA duplex
To prepare the duplex, each Alt-R crRNA and Alt-R tracrRNA or Alt-tracrRNA-ATTO550 were reconstituted to 100 uM with Nuclease Free Duplex buffer (IDT).
100 μM = 100 pmol/uL = 10 nmol/100 uL = 2 nmol/20 uL
*If you order 10 nmols from IDT, this means resuspend with 100 uL of NF Duplex Buffer (IDT)
Mix oligos at equimolar concentrations in a sterile PCR tube (e.g. 3 uL Alt-R crRNA + 3 uL Alt-R-tracrRNA).
Annealing oligos by heating at 95C for 5 min in a PCR machine, then cool down at RT at least 1 h.
After duplexing, the concentration of crRNA-tracrRNA duplex in solution is now 50 uM (50 pmol/uL).
Precomplexing of Cas9 / RNP
TrueCut Cas9 Protein v2 concentration: 5 mg/mL (1 ug = 6.1 pmol; 30.5 pmol / uL)
IDT Cas9 Protein v2 concentration: 10 mg/mL (1 ug = 6.1 pmol; 61 pmol / uL)
QB3 Berkley Lab Cas9 Protein: 6.4 mg/mL (1 ug = 6.1 pmol; 39 pmol / uL)
Mix gRNA and Cas9 at ~3:1 molar ratio
In a PCR strip, mix 4.8 uL crRNA-tracrRNA duplexes (240 pmol) and 2.0 uL QB3 Cas9 (80 pmol) by gentle pipetting up and down and incubated RT for at least 20 min. Now total 6.8 uL mixture generated per reaction.
*During this 20 minute incubation is typical when I start prepping the activated cells for Electroporation
or
In a PCR strip, mix 4.8 uL crRNA-tracrRNA duplexes (240 pmol) and 1.3 uL IDT Cas9 v3 (80 pmol) by gentle pipetting up and down and incubated RT for at least 10 min. Now total 6.1 uL mixture generated per reaction.
Note: Check the amount of crRNA, tracrRNA and Cas9 protein mixture before the reaction *(meaning make sure you have enough volume).
~2.4 uL crRNA, ~2.4 uL tracrRNA, and ~2.0 uL Cas9 protein are needed per reaction.
For Electroporation with Neon Transfection System

Harvest activated cells and count cell number
Wash with sterile PBS twice: it’s important to remove as much serum as possible since it could interfere with the electroporation
Resuspend cells @ 2x106 cells / 110 uL “R Buffer” (from Neon Kit)


*I have also resuspended at 1.5x106 cells and it worked as well


Aliquot 6.8 uL of RNP mixture into sterile Eppendorf tubes
Carefully add 110 uL of cells (now in R buffer) into each Eppendorf: do not introduce bubbles or you will regret it
Mix carefully with pipette (NO BUBBLES) then incubate the cells and RNP mixture for 3-5 mins
Very carefully fill the Neon Pipette with the cell/RNP mixture without introducing any bubbles!
Electroporate with following settings:

Voltage: 1600
Width: 10 ms
Pulses: 3
*If there are bubbles in the pipette tip during the electroporation, the bubbles will spark and kill off A LOT of cells. Observe the tip as you start the electroporation and if you see a spark, expect dead cells.

After electroporation, transfer the cells into 2mL of TCM + hIL2 in a 6 well plate and move to 37C incubator.

For Electroporation with MaxCyte ATX

Aliquot 57 uL of complete media/well in 24 well plate.
Wash cells with electroporation buffer (Hyclone) once and resuspend the cells at 4 x 107 cells / mL in electroporation buffer.
Aliquot 50 uL of cells into Eppendorf tubes (2 x 106 cells / rxn)
Add 6.8 uL RNP into the cells and mix well. Now total approx. 57 uL.
Transfer the cells/RNP mixture to cuvette (OC-100).
Electroporation with Expended-5 protocol

title: Generation of V… CV-1 Cells
text:
Generation of Vaccinia Recombinants in CV-1 Cells

Start with a confluent T-25 flask of CV-1 cells. Figure about 5 x 106. These cells are grown in DMEM with FCS, Splitting requires trypsin (1X concentration) with no special considerations. The cells grow somewhat slowly, so during heavy usage, 1:5 splits are appropriate. However, the cells can be reseeded quite sparsely for maintenance.
Wash the cells 1X with DPBS. Infect the cells with normal WR vaccinia virus (CR19) at 0.05 pfu/cell or 2.5x105 pfu total in BSS/BSA. Incubate at 37C/9% CO2 for 2 hours rocking every 15-20 min. Note: I use 1ul of CR19, with titer ~1x108pfu/ml.
30 min. before the end of infection, start transfection of DNA. We used to use Cellphect kit by Pharmacia, but I find that Lipofectamine 2000 or Fugene works about 5-10 X better. For LF2000, we use about 5ul miniprep DNA, 6ul LF2000. Note: Centrifuge the (nonsterile) DNA minipreps at high speed for 1 min. to pellet any infectious contaminants prior to pipetting.
Aspirate off virus and add 3.5ml DMEM +7.5% FCS plus 3.5ul gentamycin (1:1000) (optional)
Add the DNA/lipofectamine and incubate for 48 hours.
Harvest the cells by trypsinization with versene. Pellet cells by centrifugation. Resusp. in 0.5 ml BSS/BSA and freeze thaw (dry ice/37C water bath) three times. Sonicate for 2 min. in a cup horn sonicator at maximal intensity. Store at –80C. Follow with three plaque purifications.

title: Extraction of D…cinia V[1]
text:
Extraction of DNA from Purified Vaccinia Virus
1. Measure OD260 of purified virus. (Separate protocol) 1 OD260=64ug/ml virus. DNA is equivalent to 4% of the virus mass. Therefore, 1 OD260 equals about 2.5ug DNA.
2. Suspend virus at 50-200ug DNA/ml in 50mM Tris pH 7.8 in a volume of 1.2ml.
3. Add to virus suspension:
0.1ml 1M Tris pH 7.8
0.1ml 10% SDS
0.2ml 60% sucrose (wt/vol)
0.4ml proteinase K (10mg/ml)
Incubate for 4 hours at 37C
4. Carefully extract the DNA. The DNA is very sensitive to shearing.

2X phenol (equilibrated in 50mM Tris pH 7.8)
1x phenol:chloroform (1:1)
1x chloroform

Mix gently by rolling or rocking tube. DO NOT SHAKE. Spin 10 min. at 3000 rpm between extractions. Remove aqueous phase by sucking up gently using pipet tip that has its end cut off.
5. Add Sodium Acetate (pH 7.0 to 0.1M and then 2.5 volumes of ethanol. Mix gently and leave for several hours at -20C.
6. Recover DNA by centrifugation. Wash twice in 95% ethanol and dry. Then dissolve in sterile double distilled water. Measure OD at 260 and 280.
Note: from crude stock use Rnase.
-——
The above is from our lab protocol notebook. My own changes are as follows:
Don’t bother measuring Ods. Do step 2 at 1/10 scale, for 200ul final volume (do duplicates if you’re worried this won’t give you enough DNA). Use sucrose and proteinase K powder, so that you can substitute virus stock for the volume of water they would otherwise take up. Protease K treatment is better at 50C. Extract once with 200ul phenol, once with 500ul chloroform is plenty. I add 16.5ul 3.5M NaAcetate pH 5.2. After thoroughly mixing ethanol, spin at room temperature, freezing is unnecessary. Washing once with 100% ethanol is plenty. Resuspend final DNA in 50ul TE (10mM tris, 1mM EDTA, pH 7). RNAse is not necessary. PCR with 5ul DNA in 50ul reaction volume.
The oligo sequences we use for amplification of any pSC11 insert are:
pSC11-6369 CCACCCGCTTTTTATAGTAAG
pSC11-6610-minus ACGTTGAAATGTCCCATCGAG

title: Vaccinia Titration Plaq[1]
text:
Vaccinia Titration Plaques


Start with confluent 6-well plates of TK- cells. (Generally two 175 cm2 flasks can be plated out in eight 6 well plates for use 24 hours later)


Aspirate the media from TK- cells.


Place 250 ul of each virus dilution per well, with duplicate wells of each dilution, to ensure good counts. 10 fold dilutions are performed in 24 well plates using 1 ml total volumes. 100 ul transfer volume and then mix with a 200-1000 ul pipettor, changing tips with each dilution. Normally, 105, 106, 107 dilutions are plated. Occasionally 108 is needed.


Incubate for 2 hours, rocking every 15 min.


Overlay well with 3.0 ml of 1:1 mixture of 2X EMEM and 1.8% agar.

2X EMEM (500 ml) with
25 ml fetal calf serum
10 ml 100X glutamine
1 ml gentamycin

After 3 days, stain with 2 ml/well of 1.5% neutral red in 1:1 mixture of 2X EMEM and 1.8% agar.


Stain for 6 hours or overnight and count plaques. Remember to include a multiplication factor of 4 because you initially infected with 250 ul of virus.

title: Isolate splenocytes
text:
Isolate spleenocytes

Harvest mouse spleen in eppie tube containing cell media.
Fill petri dish with 5 ml T cell media (TCM).
Transfer spleen into petri dish.
Use rough sides of 2 microscope slides to grind the spleen.

*tips: keep the 2 slides at 90 angle to avoid too much capillary action

Rinse slides with 1 ml TCM before discarding.
Pipet up and down to dissociate cells
Transfer to 15 ml conical tube.
Rinse petri dish with 1 ml TCM and transfer to conical. Discard dish.
After a few seconds, debris will settle.
Transfer sup to a new conical.
Filter through nitrex (70 um)
Spin down at 1600 rpm, 4 min. Discard sup.
Ack pellet using 2 ml Ack for 7 mins.
Fill up the tube with TCM and spin down (same settings). White pellet should be visible.
Resuspend in 1 ml TCM.
Mix 10 ul of cells in 10 ml sheath for counting.

title: Cell Trace Violet
text:
This composite protocol combines:

CellTrace Violet protocol (protocols/t_cells/ctv.md)
Cell Trace Violet labeling protocol (protocols/Goldrath Protocols/The Master Folder/Anthony/Cell Trace Violet labeling.md)




Prepare the dye stock. Immediately before use, add the appropriate volume of DMSO to one vial of CellTrace reagent and mix well; frozen stock may also be used. The Goldrath protocol specifies adding 20 µL DMSO to one vial. [Source: protocols/Goldrath Protocols/The Master Folder/Anthony/Cell Trace Violet labeling.md]
Prepare the cells. Pellet cells by centrifugation and remove the supernatant. The Goldrath protocol additionally warms cells in calcium- and magnesium-free PBS for 10 minutes at 37°C, then dilutes them to 10 × 10^6 cells/mL. [Source: protocols/Goldrath Protocols/The Master Folder/Anthony/Cell Trace Violet labeling.md]
Prepare the staining solution. Dilute the CellTrace DMSO stock in pre-warmed (37°C) PBS or another protein-free buffer to a working concentration of 1–10 µM. The t_cells protocol notes that 5 µM is used as a 1:1,000 dilution of stock; the Goldrath protocol specifies 1 µL CTV stock per mL of cell suspension. [Source: concentration guidance from protocols/t_cells/ctv.md; volume guidance from protocols/Goldrath Protocols/The Master Folder/Anthony/Cell Trace Violet labeling.md]
Label the cells. Gently resuspend cells in the dye solution. Vortex gently to ensure equal dye exposure, as specified in the Goldrath protocol. [Source: protocols/Goldrath Protocols/The Master Folder/Anthony/Cell Trace Violet labeling.md]
Incubate. Incubate for 20 minutes at 37°C, protected from light. The t_cells protocol also permits room-temperature incubation. Gentle agitation during staining can improve uniform labeling. [Source: room-temperature option and agitation note from protocols/t_cells/ctv.md]
Quench free dye. Add at least 5× the original staining volume of culture medium containing at least 1% protein and incubate for 5 minutes.
Wash and resuspend. Pellet cells by centrifugation, then resuspend in fresh, pre-warmed complete culture medium. The Goldrath protocol specifies washing cells twice. [Source: twice-wash instruction from protocols/Goldrath Protocols/The Master Folder/Anthony/Cell Trace Violet labeling.md]
Recover and use. Incubate for at least 10 minutes before analysis to allow acetate hydrolysis, then proceed with stimulation, incubation, or analysis. The Goldrath protocol instead concludes by resuspending and plating the cells. [Source: recovery/analysis instruction from protocols/t_cells/ctv.md; plating instruction from protocols/Goldrath Protocols/The Master Folder/Anthony/Cell Trace Violet labeling.md]












Topic
protocols/t_cells/ctv.md
protocols/Goldrath Protocols/The Master Folder/Anthony/Cell Trace Violet labeling.md




Dye stock preparation
Appropriate DMSO volume; frozen stock is acceptable.
Specifies 20 µL DMSO per vial.


Cell preparation
Pellet and remove supernatant.
Warm cells in Ca/Mg-free PBS for 10 minutes at 37°C and use 10 × 10^6 cells/mL.


Dye concentration
Recommends 1–10 µM; notes 5 µM as a 1:1,000 stock dilution.
Uses 1 µL CTV stock per mL of cell suspension; does not state final µM.


Mixing
Gentle resuspension; gentle agitation is suggested.
Specifies gentle vortexing.


Staining temperature
Room temperature or 37°C.
37°C only.


Post-stain handling
Quench, pellet, resuspend in fresh medium, and allow at least 10 minutes for hydrolysis before analysis.
Quench, pellet, wash twice, resuspend, and plate.


Guidance for tracking generations
5–10 µM for five or more generations; 1–2 µM for fewer than five.
No generation-based concentration guidance.
