text:
Maximilian Heeg — Retroviral transduction
This page is a focused composite of the Polybrene-related steps from Maximilian Heeg’s source protocol. Among the four supplied source files, it is the only file containing a Polybrene workflow.

title: Transduction Polybrene
text:
Maximilian Heeg — Retroviral transduction
This page is a focused composite of the Polybrene-related steps from Maximilian Heeg’s source protocol. Among the four supplied source files, it is the only file containing a Polybrene workflow.

title: Transduction Polybrene
text:
1. Activate T cells
Derived from: Maximilian Heeg.
Activate T cells using CD8 Selection and Activation before transduction.

title: Transduction Polybrene
text:
2. Prepare virus and Polybrene mixture
Derived from: Maximilian Heeg.

Prewarm the centrifuge to 37°C.
Thaw 2 mL retrovirus in a water bath. See Make Retrovirus for virus production.
Make a 70× Polybrene mixture for each 100 µL needed:

8 µL Polybrene
10 µL BME (mercaptoethanol)
82 µL Optimem

Combine virus and Polybrene mixture at 2 µL mixture per 140 µL virus; for example, 2 mL virus requires 28.5 µL mixture.

title: Transduction Polybrene
text:
3. Transduce cells
Derived from: Maximilian Heeg.

Transfer medium from the 6-well plate into a 15 mL Falcon tube and keep it warm. Keep media for different congenic groups separate.
Add virus/Polybrene mixture to activated T cells.
Spin at 37°C for 1 hour at 2000 RPM.
Incubate cells at 37°C for an additional 1–4 hours.
Carefully remove the virus mixture. Pellet the retained original medium, return it to the cells, and add an equal volume of fresh TCM to reach 4 mL per well.

title: Transduction Polybrene
text:
4. Use or culture cells
Derived from: Maximilian Heeg.

For mixed transfer on Day 3, transfer 500,000 total P14 cells and target a 1:1 congenic ratio among Ametrine-positive T cells.
For culture, transfer cells to a T75 flask on Day 3, wash wells with 2 mL TCM into the flask, then add 6 mL TCM plus IL-2 at a final 1:2000 concentration. Add 12 mL more TCM plus IL-2 on Day 4. Day 5 can be used for downstream work such as FACS sorting for RNA isolation.

title: Transduction Polybrene
text:
Source differences
Among the four specified input files, only Maximilian Heeg’s source provides a Polybrene-containing workflow; therefore there are no conflicting Polybrene parameters to compare within this source set. Source: Maximilian Heeg

title: Growing a Listeria stock
text:
Note



This is a protocol that I got from Maurice, Nicholas J (nmaurice@fredhutch.org) for the Lm-OVA variants (N4, Q4, T4)

title: Growing a Listeria stock
text:
Procedure

Inject 3000-4000 CFU into hosts (I just start with the vial in ~3-4mL Brain-heart infusion (BHI) media, with no antibiotic and move to step 9)
Sacrifice mice between 48 and 60 hrs post-infection
Harvest and tease apart spleen in 5ml PBS+0.1% NP40
Plate 200ml of spleen solution onto BHI+erythromycin plate [spread out sequentially to get single colonies]
Incubate for 48 hours
There should be little to no growth after 24 hours – the presence of large colonies at this time point suggests contamination.
Do not grow past 48 hours – overgrowth may occur
Harvest a single colony into 200ml of BHI+ erythromycin (in mc tube)
Take several medium-sized colonies (growth will be heterogeneous)
Grow for 4 hr with shaking 37°C (set speed higher to ensure agitation in mc tubes)
Inoculate 4ml of BHI (no antibiotic at this step) with LM-OVA from previous step
Expand with shaking until broth is mildly cloudy

Add 4ml of bacteria to 26ml of BHI broth in a 50ml Falcon tube (or 200ml flask) (depending on growth kinetics, you could set this up as an overnight)
Expand with shaking for several hours until broth is cloudy, add erythromycin for the last 45-60min of culturing (once the OD is at about 0.6) (I don’t bother with erythromycin since these are stable/do everything sterile)
Read OD: should be at 0.6 – 0.8 before moving on to step 13 (OD can be pushed a little higher; if overgrowth occurs, just add BHI and allow to re-enter log-phase of growth)
Add 15ml of the 40% glycerol stock (40% glycerol stock is 20mL glycerol in 30mL BHI; I sterile filter mine and use fresh) to the 30ml of cloudy bacteria culture
mix gently on ice and aliquot 1ml in screw top cryotubes (keep on wet ice while aliquoting) (I like my LM to be on wet ice to facilitate glycerol uptake for a bit before moving them into the -80°C freezer).
Freeze -80°C

title: Infection with Listeria
text:
Listeria production for Infection






Important



Do everything in a BSL2 TC hood.



Thaw a frozen stock from -80°C (I usually stick in a 37°C H20 bath).
Dilute 1:50 in tryptic soy broth or BHI (no more than 1 month old). For 5 ml broth, use 100μl listeria stock. Grow in 50ml conical. Do not cap conical tightly as air needs to circulate. Secure loose cap with tape. Put biohazard sticker on tube, and put a sign on the shaker as well, warning about biohazard.

Grow in bacterial shaker at 37°C until you reach OD600 of approx. 0.1 (this is mid log phase) then stick culture on ice to stop growth. Anything between .09-11 is OK.

Depending on the dilution of the frozen stock this usually takes between 1.5 and 2 hours


Use disposable plastic 1 ml cuvettes to OD bugs. Parafilm around the top of them before carrying out of the hood.
Take an aliquot of tryptic broth alone for control.


Calculate concentration of listeria. An OD600 of 0.1=2x10e8 cfu/ml. Calculate appropriate ratio. Final concentration should be 5000 cfu/mouse in 200μl. That is 2.5 x 104 pfu/ml.

\(\frac{0.1}{2*10^8} = \frac{[your OD]}{cfu}\) –> \(cfu = [your OD]*2*10^9\)
Usually should have to perform a dilution in the range of about 1:7000. Anything a lot lower or higher is probably incorrect. Since the dilution ratio is so high, perform serial dilution. Do not attempt to dilute entire 5ml of listeria.

Perform serial dilutions in sterile PBS to inject.

Example:

If OD yields concentration of 2.52 x 108 cfu/ml, do a 1:100 dilution
Take 10μl in 990μl PBS concentration now is 2.52 x 106 cfu/ml.
Take the total dilution you have to do and divide by the dilution you already did. That is the rest of the dilution you have to do.

Take 80μl of diluted stock and add to 7920μl PBS. This is the 2nd 1:100 dilution. which should result in 2.52 x 104 cfu/ml. Now you can use this to infect.







Note



Use the interactive calculator at lab.beetletun.de










Important



Bleach all tips and pipets, etc in 10% bleach before disposing as biohazard. When I do FACS staining of cells from infected mice, I flick plates into a 2 L beaker with bleach in the bottom and always use a plate with a lid (until fixed of course).

title: Tail prep
text:
Tail prep

Cut ~1 cm mouse tail.
Thaw tail juice at 37C and turn on shaker calibrated at 55C.
Add 400 ul tail juice into tail sample.
Shake at 55C for at least 1 hour.
Add 150 ul of 5M NaCl. Spin max speed, 5 min.
Transfer sup to new tube.
Add 250 ul isopropanol. Invert.
Pellet: max speed, 5 mins. Discard sup.
Wash pellet with 500 ul 70% EtOH.
Spin max speed, 5 mins.
Discard sup and air dry pellet.
Resuspend in 200 ul water.

title: Western2
text:
Thaw cell pellets on ice
Prepare RIPA buffer


Add 1:100 phosphatase inhibitor set I
1:100 phosphatase inhibitor set II
1:500 protease inhibitor set III
(I usually take 500 µl RIPA and add 5 µl phos inhib I, 5 µl phos inhib II, and 1 µl prot inhib III)


Add 20-30 μl RIPA buffer + inhibitors to each pellet (typically, for 5x106 cells, I add 25 μl)
Incubate on ice 10-30 minutes
Freeze/Thaw (optional step)


MeOH/dry ice 3 min
37°C water bath 3 min
Repeat 3 times

title: Extraction of D…cinia Virus
text:
Extraction of DNA from Purified Vaccinia Virus
1. Measure OD260 of purified virus. (Separate protocol) 1 OD260=64ug/ml virus. DNA is equivalent to 4% of the virus mass. Therefore, 1 OD260 equals about 2.5ug DNA.
2. Suspend virus at 50-200ug DNA/ml in 50mM Tris pH 7.8 in a volume of 1.2ml.
3. Add to virus suspension:
0.1ml 1M Tris pH 7.8
0.1ml 10% SDS
0.2ml 60% sucrose (wt/vol)
0.4ml proteinase K (10mg/ml)
Incubate for 4 hours at 37C
4. Carefully extract the DNA. The DNA is very sensitive to shearing.

2X phenol (equilibrated in 50mM Tris pH 7.8)
1x phenol:chloroform (1:1)
1x chloroform

Mix gently by rolling or rocking tube. DO NOT SHAKE. Spin 10 min. at 3000 rpm between extractions. Remove aqueous phase by sucking up gently using pipet tip that has its end cut off.
5. Add Sodium Acetate (pH 7.0 to 0.1M and then 2.5 volumes of ethanol. Mix gently and leave for several hours at -20C.
6. Recover DNA by centrifugation. Wash twice in 95% ethanol and dry. Then dissolve in sterile double distilled water. Measure OD at 260 and 280.
Note: from crude stock use Rnase.
-——
The above is from our lab protocol notebook. My own changes are as follows:
Don’t bother measuring Ods. Do step 2 at 1/10 scale, for 200ul final volume (do duplicates if you’re worried this won’t give you enough DNA). Use sucrose and proteinase K powder, so that you can substitute virus stock for the volume of water they would otherwise take up. Protease K treatment is better at 50C. Extract once with 200ul phenol, once with 500ul chloroform is plenty. I add 16.5ul 3.5M NaAcetate pH 5.2. After thoroughly mixing ethanol, spin at room temperature, freezing is unnecessary. Washing once with 100% ethanol is plenty. Resuspend final DNA in 50ul TE (10mM tris, 1mM EDTA, pH 7). RNAse is not necessary. PCR with 5ul DNA in 50ul reaction volume.
The oligo sequences we use for amplification of any pSC11 insert are:
pSC11-6369 CCACCCGCTTTTTATAGTAAG
pSC11-6610-minus ACGTTGAAATGTCCCATCGAG

title: Vaccinia Stock Production
text:
Vaccinia Stock Production


Begin with 10 – 175 cm2 flasks of confluent TK- cells. (They must be totally confluent)


Aspirate the media (DMEM) and infect each flask with 10 ml of balanced salt solution (BSS) with 0.1% BSA and 0.5-1.0x107 PFU of vaccinia virus. (Stock for the 10 ml is generally made by adding 0.5-1.0x108 PFU to 100 ml of BSS + 0.1% BSA.


Incubate for 2 hours at 37C. Rock flasks every 20 minutes.


Aspirate off BSS/0.1% BSA and virus.


Add 25-30 ml of DMEM with 7.5% fetal bovine serum.


Incubate for 48 hours. All cells should demonstrate marked CPE. If not, incubate until they do.


Collect supernatants from flasks and trypsinize (trypsin versene) any cells that still adhere. Pool cells and supernatants in two 250 ml centrifuge tubes. One wash of flasks with BSS/BSA may be needed. Pellet cells and discard the supernatant. Resuspend in 10mls of BSS/0.1% BSA.


Freeze thaw three times. Sonicate in cup horn sonicator at a setting of 5 for 2 minutes. Vortex well. Total virus yield will usually be about 1-5X1010 pfu.


Dilute in BSS/0.1% BSA to 130 ml, aliquot in 1 ml samples and freeze at –85C.


Note: When making new recombinants, take 0.5 ml of final plaque purification and add 1-1.5 ml BSS/BSA. Infect a confluent 50 cm2 flask of TK- cells for 2 hours. Incubate for 48 hours until CPE is demonstrated. Harvest and pellet virus. Resuspend in 5-6 ml of BSS/BSA. Infect one 175 cm2 flask of TK- with 5 ml of above. From the virus collected from one 175 cm2 flask you can continue with stock production (10 flasks).

title: Generation of V… CV-1 C[1]
text:
Generation of Vaccinia Recombinants in CV-1 Cells

Start with a confluent T-25 flask of CV-1 cells. Figure about 5 x 106. These cells are grown in DMEM with FCS, Splitting requires trypsin (1X concentration) with no special considerations. The cells grow somewhat slowly, so during heavy usage, 1:5 splits are appropriate. However, the cells can be reseeded quite sparsely for maintenance.
Wash the cells 1X with DPBS. Infect the cells with normal WR vaccinia virus (CR19) at 0.05 pfu/cell or 2.5x105 pfu total in BSS/BSA. Incubate at 37C/9% CO2 for 2 hours rocking every 15-20 min. Note: I use 1ul of CR19, with titer ~1x108pfu/ml.
30 min. before the end of infection, start transfection of DNA. We used to use Cellphect kit by Pharmacia, but I find that Lipofectamine 2000 or Fugene works about 5-10 X better. For LF2000, we use about 5ul miniprep DNA, 6ul LF2000. Note: Centrifuge the (nonsterile) DNA minipreps at high speed for 1 min. to pellet any infectious contaminants prior to pipetting.
Aspirate off virus and add 3.5ml DMEM +7.5% FCS plus 3.5ul gentamycin (1:1000) (optional)
Add the DNA/lipofectamine and incubate for 48 hours.
Harvest the cells by trypsinization with versene. Pellet cells by centrifugation. Resusp. in 0.5 ml BSS/BSA and freeze thaw (dry ice/37C water bath) three times. Sonicate for 2 min. in a cup horn sonicator at maximal intensity. Store at –80C. Follow with three plaque purifications.

title: growing sphingomonas and pneumococcus
text: S. pneumoniae URF918 cultured in Todd-Hewitt broth (BD) at 37 °C in an incubator at 5% CO2 were collected at a mid-log phase and then washed twice in PBS. For induction of pulmonary infection, mice were anesthetized with isoflurane and restrained on a small board. Mice were inoculated with S. pneumoniae (1 × 106 to 1 × 107 colony-forming units in a volume of 50 μl per mouse) by insertion of a 24-gauge catheter into the trachea. For induction of systemic infection, S. pneumoniae (1 × 107 colony-forming units) were injected intravenously into mice. At 6 h (spleen) spleen cells were collected and CD19− cells positive for the α-GalCer-loaded CD1d tetramer were analyzed immediately after isolation for intracellular cytokines without restimulation or pretreatment with brefeldin. Bacteria is plated at 100 μl on 5% (vol/vol) sheep blood Mueller-Hinton agar plates and cultured for 18 h, followed by colony counting.

title: CD8 activation protocol
text:
CD8+ T Cell Enrichment from Spleen + Lymph Nodes
Prepared by Hannah Tsunemoto
Updated February 15, 2016
Background:
This protocol is for the enrichment of CD8+ T cells collected from mouse spleen and lymph node tissues for cell cultures in 96-well plates.
Caution:

CAUTION: Comply with all biological and chemical safety guidelines, including disinfection of all materials contacting cultures by autoclaving or by contact (15 minutes) with 70% ethanol or 10% household bleach.
All steps should be performed to preserve sterility in the Tissue Culture (TC) room in the biological safety cabinet using aseptic techniques
CD3 and CD28 Antibodies are kept in 4oC box in 4oC fridge in TC room
Biotin-Abs are kept in 4oC fridge in main lab area

What you need:

Biotin-Abs (see Table 1)
Goat Anti-Hamster IgG Abs (GAH-IgG)
CD3 Abs
CD28 Abs
Phosphate buffered saline (PBS)
MACS buffer
T-Cell Media (TCM)
Ammonium-Chloride-Potassium Lysing Buffer (ACK)
Streptavidin beads
MACS column
Magnet (located in Hedrick Lab)
Round-bottom 96-well plate
15 mL Falcon tubes

Procedure:

2Hrs before plating: prepare 96-well plate with GAH-IgG

Dilute GAH-IgG Ab 1:30 in sterile PBS
Aliquot 50 uL/well into a round-bottom 96-well plate; tap plate to distribute liquid equally across bottom of wells
Incubate at 37oC for 2 hrs

Process spleen and/or lymph node tissues collected from mouse

Homogenize tissue(s) in PBS with frosted glass slides and place solution in 15 mL tube
Centrifuge at 1600 rpm for 4 min and discard supernatant
Resuspend pellet in 1-2 mL ACK and incubate at room temperature for 5-6 min
Neutralize with 3-4 mL MACS
Centrifuge at 1600 rpm for 4 min and discard supernatant

Treatment of cells with Biotin-Ab stain (see Table 1)

Resuspend pellet in 500 uL Biotin-Ab stain
Incubate at 4oC (fridge) for 15 min protected from light
Fill tube with MACS buffer
Centrifuge at 1600 rpm for 4 min and discard supernatant
Resuspend pellet with 50 uL streptavidin-beads and 500 uL MACS Buffer
Incubate at 4oC for 15 min protected from light
Fill tube with MACS buffer
Centrifuge at 1600 rpm for 4 min and discard supernatant
Resuspend pellet in 500 uL MACS buffer

Column purification of streptavidin-bound cells

Attach MACS column to magnet
Pre-treat MACS column with 3 mL MACS buffer and discard flow-through
Run cell solution through column, collecting flow-through
Wash column three times (3X) with 3 mL MACS buffer
Centrifuge at 1600 rpm for 4 min and discard supernatant
Resuspend pellet in 500 uL TCM
Count cells (1:1000 dilution) using Beckman Coulter Cell Counter
Dilute cells to wanted concentration of 2x106 cells/mL

Plating cells in pre-treated 96-well plate (see step 1)

Wash GAH-Ab with 100-200 uL TCM twice (discard supernatant into cell bucket)
Plate 100 uL of 2x106 cell/mL solution [final conc. 2x105 cells/well]
Dilute CD3 and CD28 Abs 1:500 in TCM
Add 100 uL CD3/CD28 Ab mixture to each well, pipette to mix
Incubate at 37oC until further processing

title: Labeling T cells with CFSE
text:
Labeling T cells with CFSE…Beautiful Peaks Guaranteed

Wash lymphocytes in PBS 0.1%BSA twice to remove FCS.
Resuspend at 2x 107 cells/mL in PBS 0.1%PBS which has been prewarmed to 37C. Add 2μL of 5mM CFSE stock (in DMSO) per mL of cells while vortexing for 10μM final. This step is very important for getting good, tight peaks: you want all of the cells to get exposed to the same concentration of CFSE at the same time (use a 50 mL tube if labeling more than 5 mLs of cells, also I would not suggest labeling more than 10 mLs at a time if possible).
Incubate t 37C in dark for 10 minutes.
Top off tube with cold RP20% FCS spin down and wash twice more.
For last wash, put cells through nytex and wash in RPMI no FCS, count before spinning down and resuspend in RPMI (no FCS) at appropriate concentration (don’t do this last wash until you are headed to the mousehouse).

text:
Stimulation of Peripheral T cells with anti-CD3 and CD28
COAT THE PLATE

Coat 24 well plate with goat anti-hamster Ig (IgG H+L Cat#6061-01 Southern Biotech goat anti hamster))

Dilute 1:100 in carbonate buffer
Add 250ul/well (6 well plate use 1 ml)
Incubate at 37’ for 1 hour

Add anti-CD3 (Clone#145.2C11)

For maximal stimulation use 200ng/250ul
Incubate 1 hour at 37’C

Harvest cells from lymph node and spleen in HBSS
Lyse red blood cells with 5 ml ACK ~2 min RT
Add 5 ml PBS
Spin
Wash with 5 ml PBS
Purify if necessary, otherwise resuspend in RP10 and count

ADD CELLS TO PLATE

Plate cells in wells 0.5-5 x 106
Add 0.5 ml soluable anti-CD28 (Clone#37.51) diluted in RP10 at 1:1000 final concentration
Incubate plate at 37’ C for desired amount of time

to 1.0 L; pH to 9.5. Freshly prepare or use within 7 d of preparation, stored at

title: Goldrath IEL and LPL Isolation
text:
IEL Isolation:
1. Turn on hot plate and add DTE to DTE solution
2. Bring reagents to appropriate temperature
-CMF on ice (ice bucket)
-DTE solution and collagenase solution (if isolating LP)to 37oC (water bath)
-Percolls to RT (bench)
3. Resect small intestine from mouse (we put it in RPMI+5% serum on ice until ready to isolate cells)
4. Cut out peyers patches; Push out fecal content; Cut longitudinally to flatten intestine and then cut intestine into ~ 1cm pieces (laterally)
5. Place pieces into 125ml Erlenmeyer flask w/30ml CMF. Let pieces settle; pour off supernatant. (discard). Repeat wash with another 30ml CMF; pour off supernatant. (discard)
6. Add 35ml DTE solution and a stir bar; spin on hot plate for 30 min@37oC
7. Pour off supernatant through a cell strainer into clean 50ml conical. Wash flask/intestine pieces with additional DTE solution and top up the 50ml conical. Put on ice. (These are your IEL’s)

*if you are isolating cells from LP start this prep now by returning all intestine pieces to the flask and adding 30ml collagenase Type I solution (see LP protocol).

8. Spin down IEL and discard supernatant. Resuspend pellet in 5ml 44% Percoll + transfer to 15 ml round bottom tube. Underlay 2ml of 67% Percoll (we do this with Pasteur pipettes).
9. Centrifuge @RT for 20 min @2000rpm (4 Acceleration and 0 BRAKE!)
10. Remove lymphocyte interface into 15ml conical and top off tube with RPMI+5% serum.
11. Centrifuge @4 oC for 10min @2000rpm (with brake). The resultant pellet are your purified IELs.
LPL Isolation
1. Add Collagenase to solution
2. Bring reagent to appropriate temperature
-Collagenase to 37oC (water bath)
-Percolls to RT (bench)
3. Add 30ml Collagenase solution to intestine pieces (post-IEL prep); spin on hot plate for 45min @37<sup>oC
4. Pour off supernatant through cell strainer into new 50ml conical (These are your LP cells)
5. Centrifuge @4 oC for 5 min @1600rpm; Resuspend pellet in 5 ml 44% Percoll; transfer to 15 ml
round-bottom tube; Underlay with 2ml of 67% Percoll (with Pasteur pipette)
6. Centrifuge @RT for 20 min @2000rpm (4 Acceleration and 0 BRAKE!)
7. Remove lymphocyte interface into 15ml conical and top off tube with RPMI+5% serum.
8. Centrifuge @4 oC for 10min @2000rpm (with brake). The resultant pellet are your purified LPLs.

title: Western Blot Protocol
text:
Western Blot Protocol
Quantify Protein (BCA Protein Assay)

Dilute Standard in 96 well flat bottom plate

Add 184 ul of H2O to the first well of the column then 100ul to the rest of the wells in the column. Add nothing to the last well
Add 16ul of BSA (2mg/ml) to the first well and then do 1:2 dilutions down the column (transfer 100ul).
Standard curve 16ug, 8ug, 2ug, 1ug, 0.5ug

Dilute samples in 96 well flat bottom plate

Add 2ul of sample to 98ul of H2O

Mix reagent A to B in a 50:1 mixture (5mL A to 100mL B) and add 100ul to samples. Add to lowest [BSA] up to highest [BSA] then add to samples.
Incubate at 37°C for 15min (or until samples turn purple)
Read in plate reader @ 560nm
Determine protein concentration using standard curve. Calculate volume of sample needed for 15ug.

Sample Preparation:










Sample Volume
Sample Buffer (4x 1x)
Reducing Agent (10x1x)
H2O
Total Volume




Volume determined above
5ul
2ul
Make up volume
20ul




Heat @ 70°C for 10mins
Spin down for about 1 min@ max speed
Store at -20°C

If stored at -20°C, thaw samples then heat for a few minutes @ 70°C and spin down @ max speed


Electrophoresis

Make 1L of running buffer (20X1X)

50mL running buffer, fill to 1L in graduated cylinder with water
Take 200mL and place in a second graduated. Add 500ul of antioxidant (do this immediately before you are going to run you gel).

Set up gel apparatus

Wash gel wells with running buffer and take the tape off
Place 200ml of running buffer with antioxidant solution from 1b. in the middle part of the gel box and check for leaks
Pour running buffer from 1a. on the outside

Load 7ul of ladder and 20ul of sample (all of sample that you prepared above)
Run @ 100V for 5 minutes, check, then turn up

Transfer

Set up transfer apparatus
Make up transfer buffer

Add 100mL 10X transfer buffer into a graduated cylinder. Fill to 500mL with H2O then add 200mL methanol. Fill to 1L with H2O (if you add methanol directly to undiluted 10X transfer buffer, you will cause precipitation)

Cut membrane to size slightly smaller than filter paper. Do not touch the membrane (the membrane will get dirty from protein from your hands).
Set up 3 small plastic containers and fill with methanol, dH2O, or transfer buffer respectively

Place membrane in methanol for 30sec to 1 min, then rinse in dH2O, then transfer buffer, allowing it to sit transfer buffer while you proceed

Fill large glass dish with transfer buffer and put in transfer holder black side down

Crack open gel and cut off wells at the bottom
In holder place foam, 2 filter papers, gel, membrane, 2 filter papers, and then foam. Roll out the bubbles and close holder under transfer buffer

Place holder in apparatus (black to black), then place in cold room on stir plate. Pour transfer buffer from bowl into the apparatus
Run at 70V (around 200mA) for 80min.

Check after 5min that the timer is working
May check periodically to make sure that the transfer is running and no errors have occurred.


Blocking

Make up blocking buffer in 50mL conical

BSA (5%) or milk in TBS-0.1% tween-20 (ex. 2.5g BSA per 50ml)

Take blot out and place in container. Pour blocking buffer (10-20mL) to cover blot. Do not pour directly on the blot.
Place on shaker 1-2 hrs @ RT or @4°C overnight

Primary

Dilute primary Ab in blocking buffer from above.
If you need to work with a small volume of Ab, Place blot in a bag that is sealed on 3 sides, then add ~ 2ml of diluted Ab and seal the top. Label the blot then place face down on the shaker. Shake 1-2hr @ RT or @4°C overnight (this will depend on the primary antibody you are using).
If you can work in a larger volume of Ab. Add 10ml of diluted Ab to container that you blocked in. Shake 1-2hr @ RT or @4°C overnight (this will depend on the primary antibody you are using).
Cut open bag and place blot in container (or pour of primary Ab from container) and rinse the blot 3x quickly with TBS-0.1% Tween-20. Depending on your primary Ab, you may be able to reuse it several times so you can store it at 4°C until next use otherwise discard down sink).
Wash 3x in TBS-0.1% Tween-20 for at 15-20 mins each time

Secondary

Dilute secondary Ab (1:10,000) in blocking buffer from above. Add secondary Ab for 45mins shaking @RT.
Rinse blot in TBS-0.1% Tween-20 3x for 15- 20mins each time

Developing

Remove all liquid from container that blot was washing in.
More sensitive ECL kit

Make 4mL of a 1:1 mixture of the reagents and add to the blot
Leave on for 5 mins then aspirate off

Less sensitive ECL kit

Make 4mL of a 1:1 mixture of reagents and add to the blot
Leave on for 1 min then aspirate off

Pick up blot with forceps (make sure you pick up by edge of blot) and let drip onto a kimwipe to remove last bits of developing reagent. Place blot into a plastic divider inside cassette and gently remove bubbles with fingers.
Develop in dark room as soon as possible

Draw ladder before removing membrane from cassette


Stripping

Add 174ul β-Mercaptoethanol to 25ml of stripping buffer – work in fumehood as this will stink.
Place blot in hybridization tube and add stripping buffer (in hood). Place in heated spinner @ 70°C for 30 min with counter balance tube.
Discard buffer in fume hood with water running.
Rinse tube with dH2O water until there are no bubbles and you can’t smell the stripping buffer anymore.
Place blot in container with TBS-0.1% Tween-20 and shake for 2-3x 15-20mins @ RT.
Start at blocking step

30.3g Tris
144.1g glycine
up to 1L dH20
10X TBS
24g Tris
88g NaCl
up to 1L of dH20
pH 7.6
1X TBS-0.1% Tween-20
100ml 10x TBS
900ml dH20
1ml Tween-20
Stripping Buffer
62.5mM Tris-HCl pH6.8
2% SDS
100mM mercaptoethaol (stock at 14N – add before each use)

title: Diallo et al vsv propagation
text:
Download the original PDF

Diallo et al vsv propagation
                                                                                           Chapter 10
Propagation, Puriﬁcation, and In Vivo Testing of Oncolytic Vesicular Stomatitis Virus Strains Jean-Simon Diallo, Markus Vähä-Koskela, Fabrice Le Boeuf, and John Bell
Abstract Oncolytic viruses are self-amplifying therapeutics that speciﬁcally replicate in and kill cancer cells. We have previously shown that vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) can be used as an oncolytic virus. A strain of VSV harboring a mutation in the M protein (VSV$51) was found to exhibit enhanced tumor selectivity over its wild-type counterpart due to its inability to overcome antiviral programs in normal cells and due to the frequent defects in antiviral signaling pathways observed in the majority of tumors. VSV$51 can harbor transgenes, is easily propagated and puriﬁed to high titers, and shows potent oncolytic activity in several mouse models, including syngeneic CT26-lacZ subcutaneous colon carcinoma models. However, VSV- neutralizing antibodies targeting mainly the VSV-G surface glycoprotein arise within 3–5 days following the initial dose. This should be considered for strategies aiming at increasing the effectiveness of VSV through delivery of additional doses of virus or aiming to prolong VSV replication in vivo.
 Key words: Vesicular stomatits virus, Oncolytic, Puriﬁcation, Syngeneic mouse model, Neutralizing
 antibodies

Introduction
                           Vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) is a small negative-strand RNA
                           virus belonging to the Rhabdovirus family. The VSV genome
                           (approximately 11 kbp) encodes ﬁve distinct genes referred to as
                           the nucleocapsid (N), polymerase proteins (P and L), the matrix
                           protein (M), and the surface glycoprotein (G). The VSV virion is
                           bullet-shaped and consists of viral RNA wrapped tightly within the
                           ribonucleocapsid (an array of N, P, L proteins) to which binds M
                           protein. The virion becomes enveloped with G protein trimers

David H. Kirn et al. (eds.), Oncolytic Viruses: Methods and Protocols, Methods in Molecular Biology, vol. 797, DOI 10.1007/978-1-61779-340-0_10, © Springer Science+Business Media, LLC 2012
                                                          127
128 J.-S. Diallo et al.
                            upon budding from the host cell, which is the main target of
                            neutralizing antibodies generated against the virus (1).
                                 VSV has been explored as an oncolytic virus due in part to its
                            rapid life cycle and its potent cytolytic activity. Being an RNA virus
                            that replicates in the cytoplasm, VSV is unlikely to recombine with
                            cellular DNA and cannot integrate the genome. Combined with
                            low human exposure to the virus and the absence of preexisting
                            immunity in the population, this makes VSV an attractive candi-
                            date for human cancer therapy (2).
                                 Interferon (IFN) signaling is thought to be defective in approx-
                            imately 70–75% of all tumors (3). In light of this, we and others
                            have explored VSV strains that exploit this tumor-speciﬁc defect to
                            enhance tumor targeting (4, 5). One of these mutant strains is
                            VSV$51 which harbors a mutation in the M protein at methionine
                            51. Whereas wild-type M protein can block the nuclear export of
                            cellular antiviral genes and their subsequent expression, the M$51
                            protein cannot and so VSV$51 replication is quickly subdued in
                            normal cells that have intact antiviral signaling pathways (4).

Materials

2.1. Cell Culture and 1. HyQ High glucose Dulbecco’s modiﬁed Eagle medium Virus Propagation (DMEM) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) (HyClone, Waltham, MA). 2. Solution of trypsin (0.25%) and ethylenediamine tetraacetic acid (EDTA) (1 mM) from Gibco/BRL. 3. ViCell (Beckman/Coulter) automated cell counter (alternately any standard hemocytometer can be used). 4. Phosphate buffer saline (PBS, HyClone). 5. 0.20 Mm Bottle top ﬁltration unit (Millipore).
2.2. Virus Puriﬁcation 1. OptiPrep 60% (w/v) (Sigma). 2. Tris stock solution (100 ml): Dissolve 12.1 g Tris base into 100 ml ddH2O. Filter and store at 4°C. 3. EDTA stock solution (100 ml): Dissolve 3.72 g EDTA Na2·2H2O into 100 ml ddH2O. Filter and store at 4°C. 4. NaCl stock solution (100 ml): Dissolve 5.84 g NaCl into 100 ml ddH2O. Filter and store at 4°C. 5. Solution B (100 ml): To 50 ml water, add 30 ml Tris stock solution and 3.0 ml EDTA stock solution. Adjust pH to 7.4 with 5 M HCl, and adjust volume to 100 ml with ddH2O. Filter and store at 4°C.
               10   Propagation, Puriﬁcation, and In Vivo Testing of Oncolytic Vesicular…       129

                          6. Solution C (100 ml): To 50 ml water, add 10 ml NaCl stock
                             solution, 5.0 ml Tris stock solution, and 0.5 ml EDTA
                             stock solution. Adjust pH to 7.4 with 1 M HCl, and adjust
                             volume to 100 ml with ddH2O. Filter and store at 4°C.
                          7. Solution D: Add 5 volumes of OptiPrep (Sigma) to 1 volume
                             solution B.
                          8. Gradient maker (e.g., Auto Densi-Flow, LabConco).
                          9. Ultra-clear thinwall Beckman ultra-centrifuge tubes (11-ml
                             maximum volume) for use with Beckman SW41Ti rotor.
2.3. Virus Titering 1. 2× concentrated DMEM prepared from powder (Gibco/BRL) supplemented with 20% FBS. 2. 1% agarose dissolved in deionized water. 3. 3:1 methanol: Glacial acetic acid ﬁxative solution. 4. Coomassie brilliant blue solution: 0.5 g Coomassie Brillant Blue R (Sigma) is dissolved in 250 ml 40% methanol and sub- sequently ﬁltered on Whatman paper. 250 ml 20% acetic acid is then added to the ﬁltered solution.
2.4. Mouse Tumor 1. Syringes. Implantation, 2. IVIS200 Series Imaging System (Xenogen). Treatment with 3. 3% Isoﬂurane (Baxter). Virus, and Imaging 4. D-Luciferin, 10 mg/ml in PBS (Molecular Imaging Products). 5. Electronic caliper.
2.5. Collection 1. Restraint tube (perforate 50-ml Falcon tube). of Mouse Serum 2. Vaseline. and Neutralizing 3. Beveled syringe needle. Antibody Assay 4. Heparinized collection tubes.

Methods
                      A key consideration in using VSV or VSV$51 for both in vitro and
                      in vivo experimentation is starting from a pure high-titer stock of
                      virus containing as little defective uninfectious particles as possible.
                      To this end, virus is propagated by infecting sensitive cells (e.g.,
                      Vero cells) at a low multiplicity of infection and then collected
                      from supernatants prior to extensive cell lysis. The virus is subse-
                      quently puriﬁed on gradient to eliminate cellular contaminants,
                      such as DNA, protein, and cellular exosomes (6, 7), which can
                      induce antiviral programs and impact the permissiveness of cells

130 J.-S. Diallo et al.
                           in vitro or induce immune responses in vivo. It is possible to
                           quantify how many infectious VSV particles have been obtained
                           using viral plaque assays. Once viral titers have been assessed, virus
                           can then be used for in vitro or in vivo testing alone or in combina-
                           tion with other agents (8, 9). In vitro, virus spread can be followed
                           easily when VSV is engineered to express ﬂuorescent proteins using
                           ﬂuorescence microscopy. For example, we use VSV variants in
                           which have been inserted green ﬂuorescent protein (GFP) or ﬁreﬂy
                           luciferase (FLuc) between the G and L genes driven by an inter-
                           genic VSV promoter. FLuc-expressing variants are useful as they
                           can be imaged in vivo in real time using injectable luciferin and
                           in vivo imaging systems (IVISs).
                                The oncolytic properties of VSV can be observed in xenografts
                           implanted in immunocompromised animals or in immunocompe-
                           tent mice harboring syngeneic tumors. The latter is preferred since
                           immune responses can both positively and negatively impact onco-
                           lytic virus efﬁcacy (10, 11). Subcutaneous models are convenient
                           since tumors can be injected directly and volumes post infection
                           can be followed using a caliper (Fig. 3). Viral replication can be
                           followed by IVIS as well. Infection of mice with VSV leads to pro-
                           duction of neutralizing antibodies from B cells that typically recog-
                           nize the G-protein. These antibodies effectively inactivate the virus
                           and generally arise 4–5 days post infection when virus is given
                           intravenously (Fig. 4). VSV-neutralizing antibody titers can be eas-
                           ily measured from sera extracted from mouse blood obtained by
                           saphenous vein bleeds at various times post infection.
3.1. Propagation of 1. Prior to infection with VSV, Vero African green monkey kid- VSV in Cell Culture ney cells are seeded at 1 × 104 cells per cm2 in FBS supple- mented with DMEM in 150-mm cell culture petri dishes (25 ml per plate). 2. When cultures have reached roughly 95% conﬂuency (~3–4 days), they can be infected with a preexisting virus stock at 2 × 105 plaque forming units (PFUs) per 150-mm petri (an MOI of ~0.01, see Note 1). 3. For infection of ten plates (see Note 2), 2 × 106 PFUs of stock is diluted in 50 ml of serum-free DMEM and vortexed thor- oughly (see Note 3). 4. Supernatant is removed from each petri dish and 5 ml of virus mixed in serum-free DMEM is added to each plate. Petris are then placed in a 37°C 5% CO2 humidiﬁed incubator for 45 min (see Note 4). 5. After incubation, the serum-free media is removed and 25 ml of DMEM containing 10% FBS is added to each petri. Infected cultures are then placed in a 37°C 5% CO2 humidiﬁed incubator.
            10   Propagation, Puriﬁcation, and In Vivo Testing of Oncolytic Vesicular…   131

                       6. When approximately 50% cytopathic effect (CPE) (cell
                          rounding) is observed (usually, after approximately 24 h), the
                          supernatants are collected in 50-ml Falcon tubes (see Note 5).
                       7. The supernatants are centrifuged at 780 × g for 5 min to pellet
                          heavy cellular debris.
                       8. Cleared supernatants are ﬁltered through 0.2 Mm membranes
                          (Millipore) and then either used directly or puriﬁed further
                          (see Note 6).
3.2. Puriﬁcation of VSV Puriﬁed VSV crude obtained in Subheading 3.1 should be further concentrated by ultracentrifugation prior to gradient puriﬁcation. 1. Virus can be pelleted using a Beckman Coulter Avanti J25I Ultracentrifuge at 14,000 rpm (28,000 × g) for 1 h 30 min at 4°C in polypropylene centrifuge bottles (JA-14 rotor). The virus pellet should be visible at this stage and supernatant should be carefully discarded, removing as much media as pos- sible without disturbing the pellet (see Note 7). 2. To purify the virus using OptiPrep® (see Note 8), the virus pel- let isolated following ultracentrifugation is resuspended in maximum 2 ml of solution C (see Note 9). 3. For a single 12-ml gradient (accommodating up to 2 ml of resuspended virus), prepare 5 ml of 15% OptiPrep® solution by diluting 1.5 ml of solution D (which is 50% OptiPrep®) with 3.5 ml of solution C. Also prepare 5 ml of 35% OptiPrep® solu- tion by diluting 3.5 ml of solution D with 1.5 ml of solution C. 4. Transfer 5 ml of the 35% OptiPrep® solution into the ﬁrst chamber of a gradient maker (the chamber closest to the exit valve on a LabConco Auto Densi-Flow model gradient maker) and 4.5 ml of the 15% OptiPrep® solution into the second chamber (furthest away from the exit valve). 5. Let ~0.5 ml of the 35% solution leave the exit valve before opening the valve connecting the two gradient chambers. This generates 9.5 ml 15–35% continuous OptiPrep® gradient which can be collected in clear SW-41 Ti thin-walled ultracen- trifuge tubes (Beckman # 344059). 6. When the gradient has been obtained, carefully layer up to 2 ml of virus suspension onto the gradient. 7. Ultracentrifuge virus and gradient at 36,000 rpm (160,000 × g) for 1.5 h at 4°C. 8. If the pellet has been properly dispersed, a single band should be visible roughly mid-gradient (see Fig. 1). Collect this band by ﬁrst removing the OptiPrep® above it and then aspirating the band carefully using a P 1000 pipet (should take at least 600 Ml).
132 J.-S. Diallo et al.
                           Fig. 1. VSV puriﬁcation on OptiPrep® Gradient. VSV band in a 5–50% OptiPrep Gradient
                           obtained starting from 10 × 150-mm petris of Vero cells following a 24-h incubation. Note
                           that a single band is obtained approximately mid-gradient. Multiple bands, some with
                           macroscopic ﬂakes, may be observed if pellet is insufﬁciently dispersed in solution C prior
                           to gradient puriﬁcation.




                            9. To avoid repeated freeze-thawing, make many small-volume
                               aliquots (e.g., 10 Ml) and store at least at −80°C. This virus
                               should remain stable for several months.
3.3. Quantiﬁcation VSV obtained from various sources, including infected cell cul- of Infectious VSV tures, tissues, and puriﬁed virus stocks, can be quantiﬁed by viral Particles by Viral plaque assays. Plaque Assay 1. Vero cells are plated in six-well plates at densities such that they have reached approximately 95% conﬂuence the following day. In six-well plates, this equates to approximately 1 × 106 cells per well (see Note 10). 2. Serum-free media is then used to do serial dilutions of virus (see Note 11).
                10    Propagation, Puriﬁcation, and In Vivo Testing of Oncolytic Vesicular…                          133
Fig. 2. Viral plaque assay for quantifying VSV titers. Vero cells were plated and inoculated with serial dilutions of a super- natant obtained from VSV$51-infected cells then coated with an agarose/DMEM overlay. Twenty-four hours later, wells were ﬁxed with methanol–acetic acid ﬁxative, agarose overlay was removed, and ﬁxed cells were stained with Coomassie brilliant blue. The arrow points to a typical plaque. The middle well contains 25 plaques, an appropriate number to calculate viral titers which in this case comes to (25/10−5) × 2 = 5 × 106.
                               3. The media covering the plated Vero cells is then removed and
                                  500 Ml of diluted virus stock (for each dilution) is used to infect
                                  Vero cells which are then incubated for 45 min at 37°C in a 5%
                                  CO2 humidiﬁed incubator.
                               4. During this time, a 1% agarose solution prepared in sterile-
                                  deionized H2O should be brought to a boil and put in a 42°C
                                  water bath. 2× concentrated DMEM containing 20% FBS
                                  should be warmed in a 37°C water bath as well.
                               5. After the 45-min incubation, the media covering infected Vero
                                  cells should be removed. 1:1 volumes of 1% agarose: 2×
                                  DMEM, 20% FBS at 42°C should then be mixed together and
                                  1–2 ml of this mixture should be used to cover each well of
                                  Vero cells infected with virus dilutions (see Note 12).
                               6. Cells should then be put back in a 37°C 5% CO2 humidiﬁed
                                  incubator for another 24 h (see Note 13).
                               7. After incubation, 1 ml methanol–acetic acid ﬁxative (3:1 ratio)
                                  is added on top of the agarose layer in each well and allowed to
                                  incubate at room temperature for 1 h.
                               8. Subsequently, the agarose can be washed or lifted off the wells
                                  using a strong water current (e.g., under a tap).
                               9. Fixed Vero cells are stained using 1 ml of a Coomassie blue
                                  solution and incubated for 30 min at room temperature on a
                                  plate shaker (at low speed).
                             10. Resulting viral plaques can be easily visualized (see Fig. 2) and
                                 plates can be stored indeﬁnitely.
                             11. To calculate viral titers, plaques are counted ideally at a dilu-
                                 tion step, where between 10 and 100 plaques are visible.
134 J.-S. Diallo et al.
                            12. The number of plaques is then divided by the appropriate
                                dilution and the resulting number is multiplied by 2 to give a
                                titer in PFU/ml (since 500 Ml were used to infect cells). For
                                example, if 25 plaques were counted in the well where a 1/106
                                dilution was used, the titer of the initial undiluted sample is
                                (25/(10−6)) × 2 = 5 × 107 PFU/ml.
3.4. In Vivo Testing of VSV$51 has been shown to be an effective oncolytic in several Oncolytic VSVD51 tumor models. Because it is well-recognized that immune responses play a major role in oncolytic virus efﬁcacy, it is best to study this oncolytic strain in immunocompetent models. One model we fre- quently use is the CT26 colon carcinoma model, which is synge- neic in Balb/C mice (see Note 14). This model is convenient because tumors grow homogenously with relatively good repro- ducibility without ulcerating or metastasizing too quickly. As such, they are particularly suitable for measuring tumor volumes. 1. Balb/C mice can be injected subcutaneously in the ﬂanks with 3 × 105 cells (>95% viable) resuspended in 100 Ml serum-free media or PBS. 2. Ten days later, tumors reach approximately 200 mm3 as measured using a caliper and the formula Volume = (Length × (Width)2)/2. 3. VSV$51 can be injected either intratumorally or intravenously at doses of up to 1 × 109 PFU (see Note 15). 4. Tumor volumes may be measured at regular intervals. Delayed tumor progression can be observed even after a single injection of VSV$51 delivered intratumorally (Fig. 3). 5. Virus replication can be followed in vivo using IVIS if VSV$51- expressing Fluc is used. To do this, mice are injected with 200 Ml of luciferin substrate (10 mg/ml) intraperitoneally. Five minutes later, mice are anesthetized using isoﬂurane and then put in the IVIS for photon measurement (see Note 16). Exposure times vary generally between 30 s and 3 min. 6. If so desired, tumors or other organs (for toxicity studies, for example) can be collected by dissection and used as a starting material for viral plaque assays to conﬁrm the presence (or absence) of virus. 7. To do this, tissues (whole or partial) are dissected, weighed, and homogenized in 500 Ml PBS. It is important to drench mice in ethanol 70% prior to dissection to minimize the risk of contamination (see Note 17). 8. A fraction of this homogenate can be used for viral plaque assays (Subheading 3.3, see Note 18).
           10    Propagation, Puriﬁcation, and In Vivo Testing of Oncolytic Vesicular…                  135




                      Fig. 3. Injection of VSV$51 intratumorally delays progression of syngeneic CT26 tumors.
                      Mice were implanted with 3 × 105 VSV$51-sensitive CT26-lacZ cells (see Note 14). Tumors
                      were injected with 5 × 107 PFU of VSV$51 (in 50 Ml PBS) 11 days following tumor implan-
                      tation. Tumor volumes were measured every 2–3 days using an electronic caliper. Volumes
                      are expressed in mm3 and were calculated according to the formula in Subheading 3.4,
                      step 2. Five and six mice were included in PBS (full lines) and VSV$51 (dashed lines)
                      groups, respectively.
3.5. Following the VSV is quite sensitive to neutralizing antibodies present in the serum Production of VSV- of immunized individuals; as such, additional doses of VSV may not Neutralizing reach tumors following the rise of neutralizing antibody titers. It Antibodies In Vivo may be useful for investigators to monitor neutralizing antibody titers, for example in response to cotreatment with drugs that can impact innate and elicited immune responses, such as cyclophosph- amide (12). To measure VSV-neutralizing antibodies, fresh whole blood from infected animals or individuals is required. In mice, whole blood can be collected repeatedly by saphenous bleed. 1. Mice are put facing downward in a restraint tube (e.g., perfo- rated 50-ml Falcon tube). 2. The mouse tail is wrapped around the index ﬁnger and held by the middle ﬁnger. 3. Light pressure is applied by the index ﬁnger and the middle ﬁnger on the lower abdomen and legs toward the wall of the restraint tube, securing the mouse in place. At this stage, the mouse should have its head in the restraint tube and its hind legs sticking out of the tube. 4. Using the thumb, light pressure is applied just above the hip, extending the leg. 5. Vaseline is then applied to the extended leg so that the saphen- ous vein can be easily visualized.
136 J.-S. Diallo et al.
                         6. A small puncture at a 45° angle is done directly on the saphenous
                            vein and blood is drawn using heparinized collection tubes (see
                            Note 19).
                         7. Blood contained within the capped heparinized collection
                            tubes is spun down at 3,400 × g in an Eppendorf minifuge for
                            5 min to separate serum from blood cells.
                         8. Serum (fraction on top) should be transferred gently to a fresh
                            tube using a micropipet (see Note 20).
                         9. Collected serum can be tested for its ability to neutralize VSV
                            infection (see Note 21).
                        10. For the neutralizing antibody assay, Vero cells are plated in
                            96-well plates at a density of 12,500 cells per well in 100 Ml of
                            FBS supplemented with DMEM and incubated overnight at
                            37°C in a 5% CO2 humidiﬁed incubator.
                        11. The following day, each serum sample is diluted 1/50 in
                            serum-free medium (see Note 22).
                        12. 100 Ml of the diluted serum preparation is plated into an empty
                            96-well microtiter plate.
                        13. In each subsequent row, 50 Ml of serum-free DMEM is plated.
                        14. 50 Ml from the 1/50 dilution is transferred and serially diluted
                            (1:2) across the plate. 50 Ml is discarded from the last row.
                        15. Subsequently, 2 × 105 PFU VSV per 50 Ml serum-free DMEM is
                            added to each well (see Note 23). A negative control, where virus-
                            free DMEM is used, and a positive control, where no serum is put
                            in the initial 1/50 dilution, should also be included. A schematic
                            representation of a typical dilution setup is shown in Fig. 4a.
                        16. The mixtures of serum dilutions and virus are incubated for
                            1 h at 37°C.
                        17. Media is removed from 96-well plates containing Vero cells,
                            and the contents of the 96-well plate containing virus:serum
                            mixtures are immediately transferred.
                        18. Cells and virus:serum mixtures are incubated at 37°C in a 5%
                            CO2 humidiﬁed incubator for 1 h.
                        19. 100 Ml of DMEM containing FBS is then added to all of the
                            wells, and the plates are further incubated for 48 h.
                        20. After this time, CPEs can be visualized or quantiﬁed by a vari-
                            ety of methods, including visual inspection (cell rounding),
                            Coomassie blue stain, or using metabolic dyes, such as MTT or
                            Alamar Blue®.
                        21. Antibody titers in a given serum sample can be determined by
                            assessing the dilution at which 50% CPE is observed. Figure 4b
                            shows the progression of neutralizing antibody titers collected
                            form Balb/C mice injected intravenously with 1 × 107 PFU of
                            VSV$51. In this case, the same virus was used for the neutral-
                            ization antibody assay.

Fig. 4. VSV-neutralizing antibody titers following intravenous administration of VSV$51 in mice. (a) Typical experimental setup for determining neutralizing antibody titers. (b) Balb/C mice were injected with 1 × 107 PFU of VSV$51 (in 100 Ml PBS). Serum was collected over time by saphenous vein bleed, and VSV-neutralizing antibody titers were determined using the method described in Subheading 3.5. In this case, Alamar Blue® metabolic dye was used to assess Vero cell viability. Five mice were included in each group and error bars represent standard error. Note that in this experiment, neutralizing antibody titers remained at their high plateau for at least 56 days post infection.
138 J.-S. Diallo et al.

Notes
                          1. In general, high-titer seed stocks tend to yield more viral
                             progeny.
                          2. Typically, we use 10 × 150-mm petris which are sufﬁcient for
                             routine use, although more stock may be necessary for in vivo
                             experiments.
                          3. Brief vortexing of stocks prior to dilution is always recom-
                             mended as concentrated viruses may deposit or clump.
                             Vortexing after each dilution is also recommended.
                          4. Low-volume infection is necessary in order to optimize virus
                             adsorption. During this step, it is important that cells do not
                             dry and so the best results are obtained when plates are shaken
                             lightly every 5 min.
                          5. Longer incubation times give higher yields, but also increase
                             the number of defective particles and potential cellular
                             contaminants.
                          6. The ﬁltrate contains VSV crude that can be titered (see
                             Subheading 3.3) and used in in vitro experiments if so desired.
                             It is nonetheless recommended to further purify and concen-
                             trate the virus by ultracentrifugation and better yet to purify
                             the virus on gradient.
                          7. At this stage, if so desired, the virus pellet can be resuspended
                             in 1 ml PBS solution and frozen at −80°C for use at a later
                             time. This puriﬁed crude can be titered and used directly
                             in vitro or in vivo. Because some contaminants can remain in
                             puriﬁed crude, best results are obtained following puriﬁcation
                             on either sucrose or optiprep gradient.
                          8. Because sucrose can be toxic when injected in mice, we use
                             OptiPrep® (Iodixinol) in order to be able to use the same virus
                             stock for in vitro and in vivo experiments. Puriﬁcation on
                             optiprep gradient yields the highest titers when initiated from
                             fresh puriﬁed crude (as opposed to frozen) since each freeze–
                             thaw cycle of virus stocks leads to approximately two- to ﬁve-
                             fold decreases in titers.
                          9. Obtaining a homogenous virus preparation without clumps is
                             critical at this stage since clumps may lead to multiple bands to
                             extract in the gradient. To this end, it is recommended to allow
                             the resuspended pellet to disperse overnight at 4°C. Also, rig-
                             orous aspiration and vortexing may help. Ultimately, virus and
                             protein aggregates may not be dispersed completely, and thus
                             it is more important to collect the homogenous band from the
                             gradient.

      10. Alternately, 12-well plates can be used in which case
          ~2.5 × 105 Vero cells in 1 ml can be used. To keep consistent
          titers between formats, infection volumes should be adjusted
          accordingly and considered in the calculation of titers.
      11. Usually, one in ten dilutions are used, although this can be
          further reﬁned if more precision is required. Importantly, best
          results are obtained when tips are changed after each dilution
          step as the virus can stick to the tips and carry over to more
          diluted samples, leading to overestimations in titers.
      12. This must be done fairly quickly since the agarose/DMEM
          mixture congeals rapidly as it cools. If several six-well plates
          need to be done simultaneously, it is best to do several small
          batches and make small quantities of agarose/DMEM mix-
          tures each time.
      13. After 24 h, viral plaques should be clearly visible by eye and can
          be counted directly. To facilitate the counting of plaques, we
          recommend ﬁxing and staining Vero monolayers.
      14. There exist several variants of the CT26 cell line. The CT26
          cell line that can be obtained directly from ATCC is very resis-
          tant to VSV$51 infection. Some CT26 strains that have been
          subcloned, for example the CT26 clone 25 and CT26-lacZ
          strains, can be more sensitive to VSV$51.
      15. Doses above 1 × 109 can lead to hind limb paralysis if the mice
          have not been previously immunized with the virus.
      16. Typically, VSV replication can be observed at early time points
          (as early as 8–10 h) in the liver and spleen of mice, but this
          signal is transient. In contrast, replication in subcutaneous
          tumors increases over 24–72 h.
      17. Do not drench tissues directly in ethanol as this may inactivate
          virus present at the surface.
      18. For viral plaque assays starting from tissue homogenates, 2×
          DMEM media should be supplemented with penicillin–
          streptomycin in order to minimize the potential for
          contamination.
      19. Up to 150 Ml of sample can be collected at once using this
          method; however, serum can be easily obtained from as little as
          20 Ml.
      20. Care should be taken not to collect any blood cells at this step.
      21. Serum can be kept at 4°C for extended periods of time (easily
          up to a year).
      22. It is important that the serum does not contain red blood cells
          as this leads to abnormally high viability values if a metabolic
          assay is used (e.g., spin down tubes ﬁrst and take serum from
          the top).

                                between samples is expected, more VSV is better as long as the

title: Mouse Saliva Test Protocol (Sjogren’s Syndrome Project)
text:
Mouse Saliva Test Protocol
Using Schirmer’s test and Saliva Weight test

Preparing Pilocarpine solution:


*Note: Powdered Pilocarpine found in chemical stock
*Note: Can prepare/store at 4°C stock solution at 5 mg Pilocarpine/mL PBS.


For injections, dilute the 4°C stock solution 1:100 in ddH20 or PBS.
For a 5 mL solution, do the following:

Add 4950 ul ddH20
Add 50 ul Pilocarpine (of 5 mg/mL PBS solution)

Injections:

Use 10 ul/g body weight of mouse.




Inject Pilocarpine solution s.c. under sterile conditions.

Wait at least 5 minutes after pilocarpine injection before tests.

Schirmer’s test (zone quick test)

Wipe excess saliva from mouth of mouse prior to test.
Using forceps, place hook of phenol thread behind the teeth and on the tongue.
Place mice on its side on dry surface. Time for 2 minutes duration.
Measure thread (in mm) according to complete red color change.

Saliva Weight test (epi-kimwipe)

Have pre-weighed 1.5 mL eppendorf tubes filled with rolled up quarter sized kimwipes (roughly 2’’ x 2’’) ready.
Wipe excess saliva from mouth of mouse prior to test.
Using forceps, place kimwipe roll behind teeth. Place mice facedown onto dry surface. Time for 5 minutes duration.
Post-weigh eppendorf-kimwipe tubes to calculate saliva (in mg).

title: Transfection Protocol
text:
Transfection-96 well plate format
Day 1

Plate 2-4x104 Plat E cells/well in 96-well flat bottom plate (total volume 200uL/well)

Only use middle 60 wells, fill outer 36 wells with 100uL media
For six well plates- we typically use ~0.8-1.2x106 cell per well in 2mL and typically scale everything up by 10

Plate cells in Plat E media without Pen/Strep

Plat E media = DMEM + L-glut, 10% FBS, 50uM BME, 10mM HEPES


Day 2

Remove 150uL of media from Plat E cells and add back 50uL of fresh, warm Plate E media without Pen/Strep

At least 1 hr prior to transfection

Prep for transfection

Warm mirus transfection agent and opti-mem to room temperature
Tube 1

Add 1uL of 100ng/uL of Pcl-Eco (helper plasmid) + 9uL of Opti-mem media per transfection well

i.e. if you are transfecting 10 wells, add 90uL of Opti + 10uL of Pcl-Eco to Tube 1

Add 200ng of shRNA plasmid per well (2uL of 100ng/uL) to Tube 1

i.e. for 10 transfection wells add 20uL


Tube 2: mirus/Opti Mix

Add 0.6 uL of mirus transfection reagent +9.4 uL of Opti-mem per transfection well

i.e. for 10 wells add 6uL mirus + 94uL of Opti-mem to Tube 2


Add Tube 2 to Tube 1 and mix well

Always add mirus/opti mix (Tube 2) last and mix well

Incubate for 20min rm temp

After 20min incubation add shRNA mixture to Plat E cells dropwise

Day 3

Replace 70uL of Plat E media with 70uL of warm T cell media

Day 4

Harvest 70uL of RV supernatant and replace with 70uL of fresh T cell media
We typically activate CD8 T cells here for transducing the following day

Typically getting 40-80% transduction with this protocol


Day 5

Harvest all of RV supernatant and pool for transduction (final 170uL/well)

in vitro stim of T cells by plate bound anti­CD3 and soluble anti­CD28 antibodies Goldrath Laboratory Andrew Doedens
Materials: (all located in TC 4 degree…Ab in box, binding buffer is in a filter flask) ­Bicarbonate Binding buffer, pH9.6 ­Goat anti hamster antibody, Vector Laboratories, Cat# AI‐9100 Follow instructions for resuspension (add 500ul H20, NOT PBS) This makes a 3mg/ml solution. It contains azide. Comes in a small brown bottle with a grey rubber lid. ­anti­CD3 (clone 2C11) we have a large amount from UCSF Ab core @ 1.8mg/ml (CONTAINS NO AZIDE…KEEP STERILE!) ­anti­CD28 (clone 37.51) we have a large amount from UCSF Ab core @ 1.0mg/ml (CONTAINS NO AZIDE…KEEP STERILE!)
Procedure: Coat wells with 1/100 goat anti hamster antibody in binding buffer. Place in the 37 degree TC incubator for 1 hour. Suggested volumes sufficient to cover the bottom of the well yet not waste antibody are listed in the table below. Coating Volumes After the 1 hour at 37 degrees, aspirate and rinse in PBS (use about ~2X the volume you used to coat…the bicarbonate buffer 96well 50ul contains sodium azide, which you want to wash out) 48well 100ul Aspirate PBS (be careful not to let plate dry after aspiration) 24well 250ul Add anti‐CD3 (2C11) diluted in PBS and incubate 1 hour at 37 12well 500ul degrees
6well 1ml Aspirate and rinse in PBS (with ~2X the volume you used to coat)
Dilute cells in media (1 million per ml is a good density) and add 1ug/ml soluble CD28 Ab if costimulation is desired. Add cells+media to coated wells. Of course have an uncoated well for a negative control. T cell density in your culture will affect proliferation. So unpurified splenocytes plated at 1 million per ml will proliferate less than purified T cells at the same density. title: DNA Prep for Genotyping
text:
DNA Prep for Genotyping


Cut a small piece of mouse tail (0.5-1 mm)


Add 400ul tail juice. Shake at 55C for a minimum of 45 min or until tail dissolved.


Add 150ul 5M NaCl to each tube.


Vortex and spin at max speed for 5 min


Take off ~400ul supernatant and place in a clean new epp. Discard pellet.


Add 250ul isopropanol to each tube of supernatant. Vortex and spin max speed for 5 min. DNA pellet should be visible (maybe small).


Remove supernatant from pellets and discard.


Add 500ul 70% EtOH to each pellet. Spin 5 min max speed.


Remove 70% EtOH and allow pellets to dry for 30 min to overnight.


Resuspend in 250ul water.

title: Goldrath_ChIP protocol with dynabeads
text:
Goldrath Lab ChIP Protocol
Fixation:
-Harvest cells (between 5-10 million the more the better) and place them in 10mL media or PBS
-Add 270ul 37% formaldehyde (to make 1% formaldehyde) and incubate (better rotate) for 10 minutes at RT
-Stop the reaction with 500ul 2.5M glycine (to make .125M glycine) and incubate (better rotate) for 5 minutes at RT
-Spin the cells down and wash once with ice cold 10 mL PBS. You can flash freeze the cells at this point if you wish to sonicate at a later time.
-Spin again and resuspend in 300ul Lysis Buffer. Add 3ul each of fresh protease inhibitors (PIC cocktail [100x] and benzamidine[0.1M]) to the solution. Incubate on ice for 5 minutes.
Sonication:
-Sonicate 20 cycles 30s on/off by Bioruptor-plus [10 cycles 2x with a brief jostle in between]
-Spin down sonicated lysate (5min at 13K rpm 4°C) to get rid of debris. Put the supernatant (the lysate) in a new eppendorf tube. The lysate can be stored at -80°C or used immediately.
-To test the sonication efficiency take 30ul of lysate. Add 100ul of NFW and incubate overnight at 65°C to reverse the crosslinks (shake for the first hour).
-Add 1 ul RNase A (stock at 100mg/ml) and incubate at 37C for 30 minutes. Add 2ul proteinase K (stock at 20mg/ml) and incubate at 55C for 1 hour.
-Extract DNA using Zymo DNA Clean & Concentrate kit. (DNA fragment)
-Measure DNA with nanodrop
-run 10ul of DNA on a 1% agarose gel to test sonication (should see a smear around 300-500 bp).
-Can use the remaining DNA as input
Binding Ab to dynabeads for CHIP (4 hours or overnight)
-Make Blocking solution: 0.5%w/v BSA in PBS
-Suspend the dynabeads well
-Transfer 30uL of suspension (per ChIP) into a 1.5mL EP tube containing 1mL blocking solution
-Rotate to wash the beads with the blocking soluton for 5 minutes
-Place the tube on the magnet then remove the supernatant by pipette
-Repeat wash
-suspend the beads with 200uL Blocking solution
-Add Ab and rotate at 4 degree for more than 4 hours or O/N
-Wash the beads twice with blocking buffer and then WBI buffer
Immunoprecipitation:
-use 5-10ug of DNA/Immunoprecipitation (using more can decrease the efficiency of the pulldown). (Around 2-2.5x106 cells)
-Dilute with 9 volumes of Dilution Buffer. Add protease inhibitors (PIC cocktail and benzamidine) to the solution.
-Add it to washed dynabeads and rotate overnight at 4°C. Remember to save an input sample (leave at 4C until elution step).
-Spin down complexes for 30 seconds at 8000rpm and put on magnet and discard the supernatant. Resuspend the beads in 1mL WBI, rotate at 4C for 5minutes and spin as before.
-Repeat wash with WBII, WBIII and two times with 1X TE buffer.
-Elute with 200ul Elution Buffer and shake for 30 minutes at 65C then reverse the crosslinks overnight at 65C. Remember to reverse crosslink your input sample as well (add 30ul of input to 200ul of Elution Buffer).
DNA extraction:
-Add 1ul of RNase A (stock at 100mg/ml) and incubate at 37C for 30minutes. Add 2ul of proteinase K (stock at 20mg/ml) and incubate at 55C for 1 hour.
-Spin down sample as before and transfer the supernatant to a new tube (this is the eluted DNA/protein complexes. Discard the beads).
-Extract DNA with Zymo DNA Clean & Concentrate kit. Follow the instruction of the kit and Elute in 55ul elution buffer.
Reagents:

title: Infection with LMGP33
text:
Infection with LM-gp33

Swipe glycerol stock with sterile pipette tip. Grow overnight in 5ml BHI (brain heart infusion) media in shaker at 37’C.
In the morning, add 50ul of overnight stock to 5ml BHI media. Take 1ml and measure the OD. Should be pretty low ~.02-.03 OD600.
Place new mixture in shaker. It should reach around 0.1 OD in 2.5-3 hours.
Make calculations based on OD600 of 0.1=2x10^8 cfu/ml.
Infect i.v at 3x10^4 pfu/mouse.

Note:
LM-gp33 is much less virulent than LM-OVA. It needs to be grown overnight for it to reach optimal growth point.
Adjust infection concentration up for rechallenge.
Rechallenge? 5x10^5 pfu/mouse i.v

title: General Seahorse Protocol
text:
Goldrath Lab – XF96 – Seahorse protocol
Materials needed:
XF Calibrant (catalog #100840-000 individually or in pack with sensor cartridge)
XF Cell Plate (catalog #101085-004 individually or in pack with sensor cartridge)
XF Sensor Cartridge (FluxPak catalog #102310-001 [18 sensor plates])
Buffer and glucose free media of Choice pH = 7.4 (we have Seahorse XF Assay Media catalog #102352-000)
Glucose – Final Concentration 2g/L
L-glutamine – Final concentration 2mM
Optional materials (depending on tests needed to be run on cells):
XF Cell Mito Stress Test Kit (catalog #101706-100)
Purpose is to evaluate mitochondrial function of cells (all these chemicals could be ordered separately from Sigma)

Components:


Oligomycin – PORT A (10 uM in port)



FCCP – PORT B (10 uM in port)
Antimycin A – PORT C (10 uM in port)
Rotenone – PORT C (10 uM in port)

XF Glycolysis Stress Test Kit (catalog #102194-100)
Purpose is to evaluate glycolytic function of cells
Components:

Glucose – PORT A (10 mM in port)
Oligomycin - PORT B (10 uM in port)
2-Deoxy-D-glucose PORT C (1 M in port)

Procedure:

Turn on instrument and start the Seahorse software (at least 4 hours ahead of time) to allow it to prewarm to 37°C.
XF Sensor Cartridge must be hydrated from 4-72 hrs prior to running the assay on the XF96 instrument. Cartridges cannot be hydrated for longer than 72 hours as this results in breakdown of the materials in the cartridge itself.


Equilibrate the sensor cartridge by adding 200 μl of XF Calibrant pH 7.4 to each well of the utility plate that comes with the sensor cartridge.


Incubate up to 72 hours at 37°C without CO2 (if incubating for longer than 24 hours they recommend parafilming the plate to avoid evaporation)


Prepare and add compounds to XF Sensor Cartridge injection ports (optional)





Prepare all solutions as recommended by assay kit protocols and add to injection ports as needed.


Allow compounds to incubate in a non-CO2 37°C incubator as well once added to the Sensor Cartridge.


Prepare Cell Plate to be read

Prewarm your assay media (add glucose if necessary for assay DO NOT ADD if running Mitochondrial Stress Test) to 37°C.
Coat cell plate with BD Cell-Tak prior to plating of T cells

20 μl of Cell-Tak solution is necessary to coat the XF 96 well cell plates.
To coat a whole plate, make the Cell-Tak solution by combining:

2000 μl 0.1M pH 8.0 bicarbonate buffer (filter-sterilized if growing cells in plate)
12.58 μl 1N NaOH
25.15 μl Cell-Tak




Mix solution well and coat all wells within 10 minutes
Incubate for a minimum of 20 minutes at 37°C (longer is not a problem, even if everything evaporates)
Pour off/aspirate Cell-Tak solution and wash with 200 μl sterile water 2x to remove all bicarbonate (very important step may affect readings on Seahorse if residual bicarbonate is present)
Plates can be air dried and stored at 2-8°C for up to two weeks for later use.




Count T cells and prepare single cell suspension for even seeding. For the XF96 we have yet to test in vivo activated cells, but for in vitro activated T cells a density of 2x10^5 - 2.5x10^5 has been optimal for achieving good ECAR and OCR readings.
Add cells to wells of cell plate as needed in a volume of 50 μl and spin plate down at 200 RCF for 5 minutes to gently plate them into the Cell-Tak.
Bring volume of each well carefully up to necessary volume for measurements to be done.

225 μl if not adding compounds or performing stress tests.
150 μl if performing mitochondrial or glycolytic stress tests.

Place cell plate in 37°C non CO2 incubator for at least 30 minutes to warm up and equlibrate (if plate has not been in a CO2 incubator up to this point, it can be immediately read if it is warm).




Begin protocol on XF96 Instrument and begin calibration of the sensor plate.



After ~25 minutes calibration will be complete and cell plate can be added for measurement of cells.



Depending on assay, measurements will take possibly ~2 hrs then software will produce a message asking you if the assay is complete and whether you’d like to eject the sensor and cell plate. Click yes and logout and exit the software. If no one else is using the Seahorse please turn off the heater within the instrument (Software will ask if you’d like to leave it on).

title: Determining Bacterial Burden
text:
Asymmetric T Lymphocyte Division in the Initiation of Adaptive Immune Responses
Four days after infection, quantitative bacterial burdens in spleens were determined. Mean bacterial burden of recipient mice (left to right, n = 3, 4, 4, 4) is expressed as a percentage relative to the burden of untransferred control mice. All groups were significantly protected relative to untransferred controls (P ≤ 0.006). After delayed challenge, distal daughters afforded significantly better protection than proximal daughters (*P = 0.03).
4d after challenge, recipient mice were sacrificed and quantitative bacterial burdens in the spleens were determined. Briefly, spleens were homogenized in 1% Triton X (Roche), and serial dilutions plated on brain-heart infusion (Sigma) agar plates
incubated overnight at 37C. P
The generation of protective memory-like CD8+ T cells during homeostatic proliferation requires CD4+ T cells
Bacterial infections.
Recombinant L. monocytogenes strains LM-OVA (expressing secreted ovalbumin protein) and wild-type strain 10403s were provided by H. Shen (University of Pennsylvania School of Medicine, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania) and J.T. Harty (University of Iowa, Iowa City, Iowa)34, 43. Bacteria were grown in tryptic soy broth (TSB) with 50 mug/ml of streptomycin to an absorbance at 600 nm of about 0.1. For challenge experiments about 0.61 times 105 to 1.0 times 105 CFU were injected intravenously. The actual number of bacteria injected was confirmed by dilution and growth on tryptic soy agar plates containing streptomycin.
Determination of CFU.
On various days after infection, spleens and livers were removed and placed in a 0.2% IGEPAL (Sigma) solution. Organs were homogenized and serial dilutions were plated onto TSB plates containing 50 mug/ml of streptomycin. Bacterial colonies were counted after plate incubation for about 24 h at 37 °C. Dashed lines on graphs (Figs. 1, 5 and 6) indicate the limit of detection (approximately 100 organisms).
